question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS (United States, current rule)

Answers
1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 pounds (the aircraft's maximum takeoff weight must be not more than 12,500 lb).
2. Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7 (not more than 7 occupants, including any required flightcrew members).
3. Passengers on board: 6 (no more than 6 passengers on board).

Controlling authority
14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), current text:
'(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter; and'

Source chain:
- eCFR, 14 CFR 61.113 (current as of the fetched text, 2026-11-16), including the amendment history line: '... Docket FAA-2024-2580; Amdt. 61-158, 89 FR 90577, Nov. 18, 2024; Docket FAA-2023-1377, Amdt. 61-159, 90 FR 35218, July 24, 2025'.
- FAA BasicMed page: 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants'; 'Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds'; 'Carries not more than six passengers'.
- Final rule, 89 FR 90577 (Nov. 18, 2024), implementing FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 sec. 828: raised occupants from 6 to 7, maximum certificated takeoff weight from 6,000 lb to 12,500 lb, passengers from 5 to 6, and added the part 29 transport-category rotorcraft exclusion.

How the three numbers fit together
- 'Occupants' is the aircraft-level authorization: the number of persons the aircraft is authorized under Federal law to carry, counting required flightcrew. 7 is the airframe limit.
- 'Passengers' is the operation-level limit on the flight: 6. With one pilot, 1 pilot + 6 passengers = 7 occupants, so the two limits are mutually consistent and neither is violated by the other.
- If the aircraft is type certificated for two required pilots, the practical passenger count drops (2 required crew + up to 5 passengers = 7 occupants). The binding constraint in that case is the 7-occupant authorization, not the 6-passenger number.
- 12,500 lb is a ceiling: the aircraft's maximum takeoff weight must be at or below 12,500 lb. The rule text in the current regulation uses 'maximum takeoff weight' (the word 'certificated' was deliberately omitted so that experimental aircraft, which are not type certificated, can qualify); the FAA's web page and the 2024 preamble phrase it as 'maximum certificated takeoff weight.' For type-certificated aircraft, the design approval (TC, STC, or amended TC) establishes both the authorized occupant count and the maximum certificated takeoff weight.

Additional conditions in the same paragraph (context, not part of the three asks)
- Not a transport category rotorcraft certificated to part 29 airworthiness standards.
- Flight, including each portion, not above 18,000 ft MSL; not outside the United States unless authorized by the country where the flight is conducted; not above 250 knots indicated airspeed.
- No operation for compensation or hire; the pilot must hold a valid U.S. driver's license, meet 61.23(c)(3), and carry the CMEC and course-completion certificate in the logbook.
- The aircraft's own operating limitations still apply; where they conflict with 61.113(i)(1), the aircraft must comply with its operating limitations.

Superseded figures — do not use
- 6 occupants / 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight / 5 passengers. This was the pre-2024 BasicMed standard (FESSA sec. 2307 as originally enacted, implemented 2017). It appears in FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1 (1/9/17), the 'BasicMed One Departure' chart (1 MAY 17), and the July/August 2017 FAA Safety Briefing. Those documents predate the 2024 amendments and are outdated on all three numbers. Anyone quoting 6,000 lb, 6 occupants, or 5 passengers is quoting the pre-November-2024 rule.

Verification note
All three values were read from the current regulatory text and cross-checked against the FAA's own BasicMed page and the 2024 final rule preamble; the numbers are internally consistent (7 occupants = 1 pilot + 6 passengers) and no stated value breaches a limit stated elsewhere in this answer.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 7 on faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med and 6 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/fr-2024-11-18/html/2024-26935.htm. The first reads: "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 12500 on faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med and 6000 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/fr-2024-11-18/html/2024-26935.htm. The first reads: "Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds"

question: M3
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — HOURS OF SERVICE, PASSENGER-CARRYING CMV (US, INTERSTATE)

SCOPE AND BASIS
The controlling rule is 49 CFR 395.5 ('Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles'), made subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 49 CFR 395.1. This is the passenger-carrier rule set; it is materially different from the property-carrying rule set in 49 CFR 395.3, and the property figures (11-hour driving, 14-hour window) must not be substituted. The determination below reflects the current text of § 395.5 as published in the eCFR (last amended at 70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005) and FMCSA's own passenger-carrier guidance (FMCSA-E-06-006, July 2022; 'Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service').

Assumed (state it to the driver/carrier so the answer is not misapplied): the driver operates a passenger-carrying CMV in interstate commerce in the 50 states and is therefore subject to federal FMCSA jurisdiction; no exception in § 395.1 applies (no adverse driving conditions, no Alaska operation, no sleeper-berth split). Intrastate-only passenger operations are governed by the state's adopted version of Part 395 and may differ; non-US regimes differ and are outside this answer.

THE THREE LIMITS (ANSWERS)

1) Maximum driving: 10 hours. Citation: § 395.5(a)(1) — no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV 'more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.' The 10 hours is cumulative driving time within the duty period; it may be taken in one block or split into shorter segments, but the total may not exceed 10.

2) Minimum consecutive off-duty time before driving: 8 hours. Citation: § 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2), both of which condition the 10-hour and 15-hour limits on '8 consecutive hours off duty.' The 8 hours may consist of off-duty time, sleeper-berth time, or any combination of the two, but must contain no on-duty or driving time. Note the figure is 8, not the 10 required of property-carrying drivers.

3) On-duty point after which driving is prohibited: 15 hours. Citation: § 395.5(a)(2) — no driving 'for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.' At the 15-hour mark the driver must stop driving; the driver may continue non-driving work, but may not drive again until another 8 consecutive hours off duty have been taken.

Important measurement point specific to passenger carriers: the 15-hour limit is counted in on-duty hours, not elapsed clock time. FMCSA guidance states that off-duty time taken during the day (a lunch break, a nap) does not count toward the 15-hour limit, and the FMCSA summary table states 'Off-duty time is not included in the 15-hour period.' This is the opposite of the property-carrying 14-hour window, where off-duty time does not extend the window. Do not convert the passenger 15-hour rule into an elapsed-time window.

WORKED EXAMPLE (from FMCSA's passenger guide)
Driver has 8 consecutive hours off, comes on duty at 06:00. Driver may drive up to a cumulative 10 hours. Driver may not drive after accumulating 15 on-duty hours (i.e., 21:00 in this example). The driver may perform non-driving work after 21:00 but may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty have been taken.

RELATED LIMITS THE DRIVER WILL ALSO BE CHECKED AGAINST (context, not part of the three answers)
- 60/70-hour limit, § 395.5(b): no driving after 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days (carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week), or after 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days (carrier operates every day of the week). This applies regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, and all compensated work for any employer counts as on-duty time.
- No 34-hour restart for passenger carriers. The restart in § 395.3(c) is a property-carrying provision. A passenger driver who reaches 60/70 hours must drop below the limit over the rolling 7/8-day period before driving again; FMCSA's comparison table lists the restart only in the property-carrying column.
- No 30-minute driving break requirement for passenger carriers. The break requirement in § 395.3(a)(3)(ii) is a property-carrying provision and is likewise listed only in the property-carrying column of FMCSA's table. Passenger drivers should not be cited for failing to take a 30-minute break, and should not be told a break resets or extends anything other than as described above.

EXCEPTIONS IN § 395.1 THAT CHANGE THE NUMBERS (apply only when their conditions are met; otherwise the 10/8/15 figures stand)
- Adverse driving conditions, § 395.1(b)(1): the 10-hour maximum driving time and the 15-hour on-duty limit may each be extended by up to 2 hours — i.e., a maximum of 12 hours driving and 17 hours on duty — where the driver encounters adverse driving conditions as defined in § 395.2. The 8-hour off-duty requirement is not reduced.
- Alaska, § 395.1(b)(2): a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV driving in Alaska is not subject to § 395.5(a) and instead may not drive more than 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, nor after being on duty 20 hours or more following 8 consecutive hours off duty, with 70-hour/7-day and 80-hour/8-day outer limits; after an adverse-conditions run in Alaska the passenger driver must be off duty at least 8 consecutive hours before driving again. These figures apply only to operation in Alaska.
- Sleeper berth, § 395.1(g)(3): a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth as defined in § 393.76 may be used to accumulate the equivalent of the 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the four conditions of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met; per FMCSA's passenger guidance, neither period may be less than 2 hours and the periods must total at least 8 hours.
- Short-haul / 150 air-mile exception, § 395.1(e): relieves qualifying drivers of the record-of-duty-status (and ELD) requirement when operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released from duty within 14 consecutive hours. This is a records exception only; it does not enlarge the 10-hour driving limit, the 8-hour off-duty requirement, or the 15-hour on-duty limit.
- Travel/'cushioning' time, § 395.1(j): travel at the carrier's direction but not driving is on-duty time unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival at destination, in which case the entire travel period is treated as off duty. This affects how the 15-hour on-duty total is computed, not the limits themselves.

COMMON MISAPPLICATIONS TO AVOID
- Using the property-carrying 11-hour driving limit or 14-hour window for a motorcoach driver (wrong rule set).
- Treating the 15-hour passenger limit as an elapsed-time window that off-duty breaks do not extend (wrong; it is an on-duty accumulation).
- Applying the 34-hour restart or the 30-minute break to passenger drivers (neither applies).
- Reading '8 consecutive hours off duty' as 8 hours of any non-driving time; it must be off-duty and/or sleeper-berth time with no on-duty or driving time in the period.
- Applying the Alaska or adverse-conditions figures as the default rather than as conditional exceptions.

RECORDKEEPING NOTE
Drivers subject to Part 395 must record duty status (§ 395.8) and generally use an ELD; non-business private motor carriers of passengers are not subject to the records requirements. Multiple-employer/intermittent drivers require a signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty (§ 395.8(j)).

PRIMARY SOURCES
- 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1), (a)(2), (b) — https://ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.5
- 49 CFR 395.1(b), (e), (g)(3), (j) — https://ecfr.gov/current/title-49/part-395
- FMCSA, 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' (FMCSA-E-06-006, July 2022)
- FMCSA, 'Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service'
- FMCSA, 'Summary of Hours of Service Regulations' (passenger-carrying column)
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.5 and 15 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/part-395. The first reads: "(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty;"

question: M5
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — FLIGHT ATTENDANT REST AFTER A DUTY PERIOD OF 14 HOURS OR LESS (14 CFR PART 135 ON-DEMAND CHARTER)

BOTTOM LINE

| Ask | Determination | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Rest owed after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | At least 12 consecutive hours of rest (measured from release from the duty period to the next report for duty) | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(7) |
| 2. Permitted reduction | To not less than 10 consecutive hours, and only if a subsequent rest period of at least 14 consecutive hours is provided; that subsequent rest must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. When the reduction is used, the certificate holder may not schedule the flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest period. | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(8), (b)(9) |

No provision of § 135.273 authorizes fewer than 10 consecutive hours of rest in any circumstance. Ten hours is a hard floor, not a target.

1. WHY § 135.273 GOVERNS THIS OPERATOR

1.1 Coverage. Section 135.261(e) states: "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part." The elections in § 135.261(b)–(c) (scheduled passenger-carrying operations under § 135.265; unscheduled/on-demand and Alaska-only operations under §§ 135.267 and 135.269) allocate the flight-crewmember rules only. They do not remove flight attendants from § 135.273, and an on-demand charter operator cannot argue that because it is not a "scheduled passenger-carrying operation" no flight-attendant rest rule applies.

1.2 Who is a flight attendant. Section 135.273(a) defines "flight attendant" as an individual, other than a flight crewmember, who is assigned by the certificate holder — either in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications or in addition to that minimum complement — to duty in an aircraft during flight time, and whose duties include but are not necessarily limited to cabin-safety-related responsibilities. FAA AGC-220 (memorandum dated June 10, 2014, "Applicability of part 135 flight, duty, and rest rules to flight attendants assigned in addition to the minimally-required crew complement") confirms that individuals voluntarily added to a Part 135 flight and given cabin-safety duties during flight time are flight attendants for § 135.273 purposes even though § 135.107 does not require flight attendants on aircraft with 19 or fewer passenger seats. Practical consequence: a cabin crewmember carried "voluntarily" on a large-cabin jet is fully covered by the 12/10 rest scheme.

1.3 Verification the operator must complete before adopting manual language. (a) Confirm from the operations specifications whether flight attendants are required for the aircraft (more than 19 passenger seats, § 135.107) or are assigned in addition to the minimum complement; (b) confirm no OpSpec, management specification, deviation, exemption, or approved procedure under § 135.273(c) modifies the § 135.273(b) scheme; (c) confirm whether any collective bargaining agreement or company policy is more restrictive (a contract minimum above 12 hours governs as a matter of contract compliance even though it is not the regulatory minimum).

2. THE OPERATIVE RULE

2.1 Baseline rest — § 135.273(b)(7). The certificate holder must provide the flight attendant a rest period of at least 12 consecutive hours following the duty period. "Rest period" is defined in § 135.273(a) as "the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise." "Duty period" is defined in § 135.273(a) as the elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder, computed in UTC or local time.

2.2 Reduced rest — § 135.273(b)(8). Verbatim: "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(7) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 10 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 14 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period." Four elements must all be satisfied: (i) the reduced rest is at least 10 consecutive hours; (ii) a subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours is in fact provided; (iii) that subsequent rest is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period; (iv) that subsequent rest falls between completion of the scheduled duty period and the start of the next duty period. Note the rule permits the reduction to be either "scheduled" (planned in advance in the pairing/roster) or "reduced" (effected operationally), but in both cases the 14-hour recovery rest is mandatory.

2.3 Duty cap that attaches to a reduced rest — § 135.273(b)(9). Verbatim: "Notwithstanding paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, if a certificate holder elects to reduce the rest period to 10 hours as authorized by paragraph (b)(8) of this section, the certificate holder may not schedule a flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest period." A reduced rest therefore buys 2 hours of schedule flexibility but forfeits any extended-duty authority for the following 24 hours.

2.4 Prohibitions — § 135.273(b)(10) and (b)(11). No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section, and no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during any required rest period. Assigning duty during required rest is itself the violation; it is not cured by later giving extra rest.

3. COMPUTATION EXAMPLES (used to test the scheduler logic)

3.1 No reduction. Report 06:00, release 20:00 (duty period 14.0 hours). Rest begins at release, 20:00. Earliest next report: 08:00 the following day (12 consecutive hours). Cycle length 26 hours.

3.2 Scheduled/reduced rest. Same duty period, release 20:00. Reduced rest 20:00 to 06:00 (10 consecutive hours). Consequences: (a) the subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours must be scheduled to begin no later than 20:00 the next day (24 hours after the 20:00 start of the reduced rest) and must fall between completion of the duty period (20:00 day 1) and the start of the next duty period; (b) during 20:00 day 1 to 20:00 day 2 the flight attendant may not be scheduled for a duty period longer than 14 hours, notwithstanding any other extended-duty authority the operator may otherwise hold. Arithmetic check: 10 hours reduced rest + a 14-hour duty brings the crewmember back to the original report time exactly 24 hours later, which is precisely the exposure § 135.273(b)(9) caps.

3.3 The § 135.273(c) election (alternative, only if approved). A certificate holder may instead apply the flight crewmember flight time, duty, and rest requirements of Part 135 to flight attendants for all operations, but only if it establishes written procedures that apply to all flight attendants used in its operation, incorporate the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (rest facilities on board not required), add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each flight crewmember above the aircraft type certificate data sheet minimum, and are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications. Absent that approval and OpSpec reference, the flight-crewmember figures (for example, the 9/10/11-hour scheduled-rest tiers of § 135.265(b), or the 10 consecutive hours immediately preceding and following a regularly assigned duty period of no more than 14 hours under § 135.267(c)(1)) do NOT apply to flight attendants. This election, if made, would change the answer from 12/10 to the flight crewmember figure — it is the single most important item to check in the OpSpecs.

4. WHAT THIS DETERMINATION IS NOT

4.1 It is not § 121.467. The 10-consecutive-hour flight attendant rest rule with reduction to 9 hours (and a 12-hour subsequent rest) is a Part 121 rule. It does not apply to a Part 135 certificate holder and must not be used as the planning minimum.

4.2 It is not the flight crew rest rule. Sections 135.263 through 135.271 govern flight crewmembers. They reach flight attendants only through the § 135.273(c) election described in 3.3.

4.3 It is not a substitute for OpSpecs or contract terms. Operations specifications, FAA-approved procedures, and collective bargaining agreements may impose more; where they do, the more restrictive term governs the operation.

5. IMPLEMENTATION CONTROLS (what the compliance file should contain)

5.1 Manual/GOM revision. Insert the 12-hour baseline, the 10-hour reduced-rest floor with all four (b)(8) conditions stated conjunctively, the (b)(9) 14-hour duty cap for the 24 hours following a reduced rest, and the (b)(10)/(b)(11) prohibitions. Cite § 135.273(b)(7)–(b)(11) verbatim in the revision so the requirement is auditable by paragraph number.

5.2 Scheduling-system rules. (i) Default hard stop of 12 consecutive hours from release to next report; (ii) a reduced-rest flag that cannot be set unless a linked recovery rest of at least 14 consecutive hours is also entered, with a begin time no later than 24 hours after the reduced rest begins and a begin time after completion of the scheduled duty period; (iii) a block on any duty period exceeding 14 hours that starts within the 24-hour window commencing at the beginning of a reduced rest period.

5.3 Timekeeping and records. Record report and release times (duty period per § 135.273(a)) and rest start/end times in a single time standard (UTC or local) consistently, per flight attendant per duty period; flag reduced-rest events and their paired recovery rest; retain per the certificate holder's approved record-retention program and make the records retrievable for FAA inspection.

5.4 Rest integrity. Because "rest period" means free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise, do not count as rest: standby/reserve availability, required phone or email responsiveness, company-directed travel, training, administrative duty, or any assignment the flight attendant is subject to during the period. A 12-hour block that contains a required check-in is not 12 hours of rest.

5.5 Training and audit. Brief flight attendants and schedulers on the difference between the 12-hour baseline and the 10-hour reduced rest, and audit a monthly sample of pairings that contain a reduced rest for compliance with (b)(8)(iii)–(iv) and (b)(9).

5.6 Source control. Cite § 135.273(b)(7) and (b)(8) by paragraph in the manual and re-verify the quoted text against the current eCFR at each manual revision cycle, together with the OpSpecs check in 1.3 and 3.3.
cautions: The answer gives 12 hours for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: M7
answer:
Current specification of HTTP/2: RFC 9113.

RFC 9113 ('HTTP/2', June 2022, Standards Track / Proposed Standard) is the current core HTTP/2 specification. Its header states:

  Obsoletes: 7540, 8740

Its abstract states:

  This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740.

Therefore, the RFCs obsoleted by the current HTTP/2 specification are:

  - RFC 7540 (HTTP/2, May 2015)
  - RFC 8740 (Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2)

Scope note: 'obsoletes' here means the direct obsoletes relationship declared in RFC 9113's header, not an 'Updates' relationship and not a transitive obsolescence chain. RFC 9113 does not obsolete RFC 7541 (HPACK), RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2), or RFC 8336 (The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame); those remain separate HTTP/2-related specifications.

Currency note: this reflects the RFC Editor and IETF datatracker records as fetched on 2026-11-16. If a later RFC supersedes RFC 9113, this answer would need to be updated.
cautions: The recompute vote disagrees with this answer on ask 2.

question: M9
answer:
UK statutory minimum wage rates effective 1 April 2026

HEADLINE ANSWERS

1. National Living Wage (NLW), workers aged 21 and over, from 1 April 2026: GBP 12.71 per hour (gross).
   Increase on the 2025-26 rate of GBP 12.21: +GBP 0.50, +4.1%.

2. National Minimum Wage (NMW), 18-20 Year Old Rate, from 1 April 2026: GBP 10.85 per hour (gross).
   Increase on the 2025-26 rate of GBP 10.00: +GBP 0.85, +8.5%.

Both are statutory gross hourly rates, before income tax and National Insurance, set by the UK Government on the recommendation of the Low Pay Commission (LPC) and applying across the UK (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland — NMW/NLW is a reserved matter). They are the Government's National Living Wage, not the Living Wage Foundation's independently calculated 'real Living Wage'.

FULL TABLE OF RATES FROM 1 APRIL 2026

| Band | Rate from 1 Apr 2026 | Change (GBP) | Change (%) | Rate 1 Apr 2025 - 31 Mar 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | GBP 12.71 | +0.50 | 4.1 | GBP 12.21 |
| 18-20 Year Old Rate | GBP 10.85 | +0.85 | 8.5 | GBP 10.00 |
| 16-17 Year Old Rate | GBP 8.00 | +0.45 | 6.0 | GBP 7.55 |
| Apprentice Rate | GBP 8.00 | +0.45 | 6.0 | GBP 7.55 |
| Accommodation Offset | GBP 11.10 (per hour equivalent; GBP 77.70 per week / GBP 11.10 per day) | +0.44 | 4.1 | GBP 10.66 (GBP 74.62/week) |

(The accommodation offset is expressed by the LPC as an hourly-equivalent figure; the daily figure equals that amount and the weekly figure is 7 x the daily figure: 11.10 x 7 = 77.70.)

EFFECTIVE DATE AND APPLICABILITY
- Rates change on 1 April each year; the 2026 rates came into force on 1 April 2026 and run to 31 March 2027.
- NLW applies to workers aged 21 and over. Workers aged 20 and under receive the NMW rate for their age band, not the NLW.
- The 18-20 Year Old Rate applies to workers who have reached school leaving age and are aged 18, 19 or 20, who are not apprentices entitled to the Apprentice Rate.
- Apprentice Rate applies to apprentices aged under 19, or aged 19+ in the first year of their apprenticeship. Apprentices aged 19+ who have completed the first year move to the rate for their age (e.g. an apprentice aged 21 who has completed year one is entitled to GBP 12.71).

ARITHMETIC VERIFICATION (internal consistency of the stated figures)
- NLW: 12.21 + 0.50 = 12.71; 0.50 / 12.21 = 4.095% -> 4.1% as published.
- 18-20: 10.00 + 0.85 = 10.85; 0.85 / 10.00 = 8.5% as published.
- 16-17 / Apprentice: 7.55 + 0.45 = 8.00; 0.45 / 7.55 = 5.96% -> 6.0% as published.
- Accommodation offset: 10.66 + 0.44 = 11.10; 0.44 / 10.66 = 4.13% -> 4.1% as published; 11.10 x 7 = 77.70.
- Band ordering holds: 12.71 > 10.85 > 8.00 = 8.00.
- Note the GOV.UK rates page also lists an April 2027 row (GBP 13.21 / GBP 11.27 / GBP 8.31 / GBP 8.31). Those are the following year's rates and are NOT the answer to this request; the April 2026 row is the applicable one.

SOURCES (all GOV.UK / Low Pay Commission, fetched 16 November 2026)
1. 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026', Low Pay Commission report, published 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026 — table 'National Minimum Wage rates to apply from 1 April 2026': NLW (21 and over) GBP 12.71 (+GBP 0.50, 4.1); 18-20 Year Old Rate GBP 10.85 (+GBP 0.85, 8.5); 16-17 GBP 8.00; Apprentice GBP 8.00; Accommodation Offset GBP 11.10.
2. Publication landing page, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026 — same table; confirms rates 'follow recommendations made by the Low Pay Commission in October 2025' and apply 'From 1 April 2026'.
3. 'Minimum wage rates for 2026', Low Pay Commission advice to Government, published 26 November 2025 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026 — same table; confirms the Government accepted the LPC recommendations in full.
4. Press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', published 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/news/national-living-wage-increases-to-1271-per-hour — same table; notes recommendations submitted 27 October 2025 and accepted at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025.
5. 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates' guidance — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates — 'The rates change on 1 April every year'; April 2026 row: 21 and over GBP 12.71, 18 to 20 GBP 10.85, under 18 GBP 8, apprentice GBP 8.
6. nidirect (Northern Ireland) 'The National Minimum Wage and Living Wage' — https://nidirect.gov.uk/articles/national-minimum-wage-and-living-wage — corroborates GBP 12.71 (21+) and GBP 10.85 (18-20) 'from April 2026'.

CAVEATS AND DISCREPANCIES NOTED
- The nidirect page's narrative sentence states that apprentices under 19 are entitled to GBP 7.55 per hour. That sentence is stale and contradicts both its own April 2026 table and GOV.UK; the correct 2026 Apprentice Rate is GBP 8.00. The headline answers above are unaffected.
- Northern Ireland agricultural workers are covered by separate Agricultural Minimum Wage rates, but no worker may be paid less than the NMW/NLW, so the GBP 12.71 / GBP 10.85 floors still apply.
- All figures are pence-precision gross hourly statutory minima; employers may pay more, and voluntary 'Living Wage Foundation' rates (a different, higher, independently calculated figure) are out of scope of this answer.
- No assumption table, falsifier list or kill trigger is included because the request does not ask for one.

question: M11
answer:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION — THE TWO THRESHOLDS

ANSWER
1. Radius: the driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. 150 air miles = 172.6 statute ("roadmap") miles.
2. Release from work: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

Controlling authority: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) — the "150 air-mile radius driver" exception, which exempts the driver from the records-of-duty-status requirement in 49 CFR 395.8 and the supporting-documents requirement in 49 CFR 395.11.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), as published on eCFR and govinfo)

"(e) Short-haul operations —
(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
  (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
  (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
  (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
       (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
  (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing:
       (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day;
       (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day;
       (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and
       (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

Both thresholds are therefore fixed numbers in the rule text, not interpretations: 150 air miles and 14 consecutive hours.

2. HOW THE RADIUS IS MEASURED
- "Air mile" is a straight-line (great-circle) measure, not road distance. Per FMCSA's driver guide: 1 air mile = 6,076 ft versus 1 statute mile = 5,280 ft; 100 air miles = 115.08 statute miles. The regulation prints the conversion for this exception: 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles.
- The radius is measured from the normal work reporting location — the location where the driver reports to and is released from work — not from the driver's residence, the terminal generally, or the first stop.
- The limit is a boundary, not a route length or a round-trip distance. A driver whose route length is 280 road miles but who never crosses the 150-air-mile boundary still satisfies (e)(1)(i); a driver with a short route who crosses the boundary does not.
- Any operation outside the radius on a given day defeats the exception for that day, regardless of total miles driven.

3. HOW THE 14 HOURS IS COUNTED
- The clock starts when the driver comes on duty. Within 14 consecutive hours thereafter the driver must both (a) physically return to the normal work reporting location and (b) be released from work.
- Both events must occur inside the window; returning at hour 13 and being released at hour 15 fails.
- The 14-hour release limit is a condition of the exception, distinct from the 14-hour driving window in 395.3(a)(2). Because (e)(1) exempts only from 395.8 and 395.11, the substantive driving limits of 395.3 (11-hour driving, 14-hour window, 60/70-hour) continue to apply to a short-haul driver. Meeting the 14-hour release test does not by itself satisfy 395.3, and vice versa.
- The exception does not apply to a driver-salesperson as to the return/release condition; that carve-out is explicit in (e)(1)(ii).

4. FULL QUALIFICATION CHECKLIST (all conditions must hold on the day claimed)
| # | Condition | Cite |
|---|-----------|------|
| 1 | Operates within 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location | 395.1(e)(1)(i) |
| 2 | Returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours (driver-salespersons excepted) | 395.1(e)(1)(ii) |
| 3 | Property-carrying: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty | 395.1(e)(1)(iii)(A) |
| 4 | Passenger-carrying: at least 8 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty | 395.1(e)(1)(iii)(B) |
| 5 | Carrier keeps accurate time records for 6 months: report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time, and prior-7-day totals per 395.8(j)(2) for new/intermittent drivers | 395.1(e)(1)(iv) |

Note on the property/passenger ambiguity: thresholds 1 and 2 are identical for property-carrying and passenger-carrying CDL drivers. The only difference is the off-duty block (10 vs. 8 consecutive hours). The answer to both asks therefore does not depend on resolving that ambiguity.

5. VARIANTS AND PITFALLS THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH THE ANSWER
(a) 395.1(e)(2) — property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL. Also a 150 air-mile radius, but there is NO 14-consecutive-hour release condition. Instead the driver must return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour and may not drive after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days, or after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7 consecutive days. Drivers using (e)(2) are expressly ineligible for (e)(1), (g) and (o). If the driver's vehicle does not require a CDL, ask 2 must be answered from (e)(2), not (e)(1).
(b) 395.1(p) — motion picture production site transportation: 100 air-mile radius. A different exception; not the short-haul RODS exception.
(c) SUPERSEDED FIGURES — 100 air miles / 12 hours. FMCSA's "Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service" still in circulation states the older rule: "Drive within a 100 air-mile radius ... Return to your work reporting location and are released within 12 consecutive hours." That reflects pre-2020 text. The 2020 hours-of-service final rule (effective September 29, 2020) expanded the short-haul exception, as FMCSA's own HOS rulemaking page states: "Expands the short-haul exception to 150 air-miles and allows a 14-hour work shift to take place as part of the exception." Any compliance document still using 100/12 for the CDL short-haul exception is out of date and will over-restrict drivers.
(d) The exception is day-by-day. If the driver exceeds the radius or the 14-hour release limit on a given day, the exception is lost for that day and a record of duty status must be completed for that day as soon as the exception no longer applies; the driver then falls back into the 395.8 RODS regime (current day plus the prior 7 days available for inspection).
(e) Because (e)(1) removes the 395.8 RODS obligation, a qualifying driver is not required to use an ELD (ELD use is tied to the duty to prepare RODS under 395.8(a)); the carrier's 6-month time records under (e)(1)(iv) take the place of the log. Those time records are mandatory, not optional, and are the enforcement artifact an inspector will request.

6. VERIFICATION STEPS FOR A COMPLIANCE REVIEWER
1. Confirm the driver holds a CDL-required CMV assignment; if not, switch the analysis to 395.1(e)(2).
2. Plot the 150-air-mile circle (172.6 statute miles) around the normal work reporting location and confirm no dispatch point, delivery point or planned diversion falls outside it.
3. Confirm dispatch and release both occur at that same location.
4. Pull the carrier time records and confirm report time and release time for each claimed day differ by 14 hours or less.
5. Confirm the 10-hour (property) or 8-hour (passenger) off-duty block separates consecutive duty days.
6. Confirm records are retained 6 months and include prior-7-day totals for newly hired or intermittent drivers.
7. Sample any day on which a limit was exceeded and confirm a RODS was created for that day.

SOURCES
- 49 CFR 395.1(e), eCFR current text (fetched 2026-11-16, sha256 1f7674313f0d).
- 49 CFR 395.1(e), GovInfo CFR-2024-title49-vol5 XML (sha256 a03f87b5824e) — identical wording.
- FMCSA, Hours of Service rulemaking page (sha256 ac634cac1266) — confirms 150 air-mile / 14-hour expansion.
- FMCSA Info Session slides, Apr 2024 (sha256 3637878be7ed) — restates 150 air miles / 14 consecutive hours and the consequence of exceeding either limit.
- FMCSA Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to HOS (sha256 90ea3715470c) — air-mile conversion factors; its 100-air-mile/12-hour passage is superseded and cited here only to flag the stale figure.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a/section-395.1 and 8 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2024-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2024-title49-vol5-sec395-1.xml. The first reads: "(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 5 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a/section-395.1 and 2 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2024-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2024-title49-vol5-sec395-1.xml. The first reads: "(A) After the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days;"

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT AND OCCUPANCY LIMITS (US, 14 CFR 61.113(i), as amended)

CURRENT LIMITS (in force on and after November 12, 2024)

1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 lb (maximum certificated takeoff weight, MTOW).
2. Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7 occupants (this is a limit on what the aircraft's design approval authorizes it to carry, not on how many people happen to be aboard).
3. Passengers on board: 6 passengers.

Basis: 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) as amended by Section 828 ("Expansion of BasicMed") of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Public Law 118-63; implemented by FAA Notice N 8000.386 (dated 11/14/24), which states the post-November 12, 2024 limits verbatim as: aircraft authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, MTOW no more than 12,500 pounds, and no more than six passengers on board. Confirmed by the FAA BasicMed page ("Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants; Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds ... Carries not more than six passengers") and by the FAA newsroom release "FAA Updates BasicMed Program" (Friday, November 15, 2024): "Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters."

SUPERSEDED LIMITS (November 12, 2024 and earlier — shown only to reconcile older citations)

| Limit | Pre-11/12/2024 | Current |
|---|---|---|
| Max certificated takeoff weight | 6,000 lb | 12,500 lb |
| Occupants aircraft may be authorized to carry | 6 | 7 |
| Passengers on board | 5 | 6 |

Older FAA material (AC 68-1A, the July/August 2017 FAA Safety Briefing "BasicMed Issue," and older FAQ answers such as the PA-32/Cherokee Six discussion) still carries the 6,000 lb / 6 occupant / 5 passenger figures. Those are correct only for flights conducted before November 12, 2024. Anyone reading a 6,000 lb or "five passengers" figure in current guidance should treat it as superseded.

OCCUPANTS vs. PASSENGERS — THE OFF-BY-ONE

- "Occupants" is a certification/authorization term: the total number of persons the aircraft's design approval permits it to carry, including required flightcrew. It is a property of the aircraft, not of the flight.
- "Passengers" is an operating term: persons carried aboard who are not required flightcrew. The pilot acting as PIC under BasicMed is not a passenger.
- Consequence: a 7-occupant airplane flown single-pilot may carry 6 passengers; the same airplane type certificated for two required pilot flightcrew members may be flown under BasicMed with 5 additional occupants on board (2 crew + 5 = 7 occupants, and 5 <= 6 passengers). The passenger cap binds independently: even in an aircraft authorized for 7 occupants, you may not board 7 passengers.

HOW "AUTHORIZED TO CARRY" IS DETERMINED

- Type-certificated aircraft: the aircraft's design approval — type certificate (TC), supplemental type certificate (STC), or amended TC (ATC) — establishes both the occupant authorization and the maximum certificated takeoff weight. Check the TCDS and any installed STCs; do not count seats. An aircraft certificated for more than 7 occupants does not qualify merely because only 7 seats are installed; it must be altered under a new design approval (STC/ATC) that restricts it to 7 or fewer.
- Experimental aircraft: not type certificated; 14 CFR 91.319(j) independently prohibits operating an experimental aircraft under BasicMed with more than the applicable occupant limit, and the operating limitation is set by the aircraft's own operating limitations.
- Helicopters: the 12,500 lb increase expressly excludes transport category helicopters.

SCOPE AND CAVEATS

- These are ceilings on what BasicMed allows, not a determination that a specific flight is legal. The pilot's own certificate and ratings, the aircraft's airworthiness and operating limitations, and any stricter limit in the aircraft's paperwork all continue to apply; the BasicMed figure is the outer bound.
- BasicMed does not apply to operations requiring a medical certificate (e.g., Part 121/135 operations, or any operation for compensation or hire).
- The three limits above are aircraft/occupancy limits only. The companion operating limits in 61.113(i)(2), unchanged by the 2024 expansion, are: at or below 18,000 ft MSL; within the United States (or another country in which BasicMed is authorized); indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots; and not for compensation or hire. The limits apply to the entire flight, from takeoff to touchdown — a BasicMed pilot cannot act as PIC for any portion of a flight that exceeds them, even if another pilot on board holds a medical certificate.
- Currency note: the values above are those in force as of this writing, following the November 12, 2024 effective date. If an answer is needed as of a specific past date, use the superseded column for dates before November 12, 2024.

ONE-LINE ANSWER

Under BasicMed a pilot may fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 12,500 lb or less (excluding transport category helicopters), authorized to carry no more than 7 occupants, carrying no more than 6 passengers.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 7 on faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/notice/n_8000.386.pdf and 6 on faasafety.gov/files/notices/2020/sep/ac_68-1a_basic_med.pdf. The first reads: "• The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants,"

question: M3
answer:
Federal FMCSA determination for a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle (for example, a motorcoach), under the standard rule set in 49 CFR 395.5, with no adverse-driving, short-haul, or other exception applied.

Scope: This is the federal interstate hours-of-service answer for a passenger-carrying CMV subject to Part 395. It is not a state intrastate determination; states may impose stricter rules. It addresses the three requested limits only. The separate 60/70-hour limits in 395.5(b) remain independently applicable and can prohibit driving earlier.

1. Maximum driving: 10 hours.
49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) prohibits a carrier from permitting or requiring, and prohibits a driver from driving, a passenger-carrying CMV more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty. This is a maximum of 10 hours of driving in the work period that begins after the 8-hour reset; it is not 10 hours per calendar day.

2. Off-duty reset: 8 consecutive hours off duty.
49 CFR 395.5(a) requires 8 consecutive hours off duty before the 10-hour driving period and before the 15-hour on-duty period. The baseline is one consecutive 8-hour off-duty period. For a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth, 49 CFR 395.1(g)(3) permits accumulation of the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty through two sleeper-berth periods meeting that provision. Time counts as off duty only if the driver is relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the vehicle, its accessories, passengers, baggage, and freight; otherwise it may be on-duty not driving.

3. On-duty cutoff: 15 hours on duty.
49 CFR 395.5(a)(2) prohibits driving for any period after the driver has been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty. Off-duty time is not included in the 15-hour on-duty period. Thus the driver may not drive after accumulating 15 on-duty hours, even if the 10-hour driving cap has not yet been reached.

How the limits interlock: The driver must stop driving at whichever comes first: 10 hours of driving or 15 hours on duty after the 8-hour reset. Separately, 395.5(b) prohibits driving after 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week, or after 70 hours on duty in 8 consecutive days if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week. Those weekly limits can stop driving before the daily 10/15 limits are reached.

Caveats that do not change the baseline values: The adverse-driving-conditions provision can extend the 10-hour driving limit and the 15-hour on-duty limit by up to 2 hours. The 150 air-mile/14-hour short-haul provision in 395.1(e) is a record-of-duty-status exemption, not a change to the 395.5 limits. The 30-minute break is a property-carrier requirement, not a passenger-carrier requirement under 395.5. Property-carrier values (11-hour driving, 10-hour off-duty reset, 14-hour window) do not apply to passenger-carrying CMV drivers.

Sources: 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1), (a)(2), and (b); FMCSA Summary of Hours of Service Regulations; FMCSA Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers.

question: M5
answer:
# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less

**Operator:** US on-demand charter operator certificated under 14 CFR Part 135
**Governing provision:** 14 CFR § 135.273, *Duty period limitations and rest time requirements* (paragraphs (a), (b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(3), (b)(10), (b)(11), (b)(14))

---

## 1. Short answer

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum rest after a scheduled duty period of **14 hours or less** | **9 consecutive hours** (scheduled) | § 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2 | Amount to which that rest may be **reduced** | **8 consecutive hours**, conditioned on a subsequent rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours** that is scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** | § 135.273(b)(3) |

Both are floors. The certificate holder may always schedule more; it may never schedule less than 8, and it may never schedule 8 unless the 10-hour compensatory rest condition is met and documented in the schedule.

---

## 2. Regulatory text relied on

**§ 135.273(a) — definitions**

- **Duty period** — "the period of elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder. The time is calculated using either Coordinated Universal Time or local time to reflect the total elapsed time."
- **Flight attendant** — "an individual, other than a flight crewmember, who is assigned by the certificate holder, in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications **or in addition to that minimum complement**, to duty in an aircraft during flight time and whose duties include but are not necessarily limited to cabin-safety-related responsibilities."
- **Rest period** — "the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise."

**§ 135.273(b)(1)** — "Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours."

**§ 135.273(b)(2)** — "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section **must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours**. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

**§ 135.273(b)(3)** — "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section **may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours**; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

**§ 135.273(b)(10)** — "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section."

**§ 135.273(b)(11)** — "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period."

**§ 135.273(b)(14)** — a flight attendant is not considered scheduled in excess of duty period limitations if the assigned flights are scheduled and normally terminate within the limitations but, due to circumstances beyond the control of the certificate holder (e.g., adverse weather), are not at the time of departure expected to reach destination within the scheduled time.

---

## 3. The requirement in full — conditions table

| Element | Requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | A **scheduled** duty period of 14 hours or less | (b)(1), (b)(2) |
| Base rest | **≥ 9 consecutive hours**, scheduled | (b)(2) |
| Placement of base rest | Between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | (b)(2) |
| Reduction floor | **8 consecutive hours** — no lower under any circumstance in paragraph (b) | (b)(3) |
| Condition of reduction | A subsequent rest period of **≥ 10 consecutive hours** | (b)(3) |
| Timing of the compensatory rest | Must be **scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** (measured from the START of the reduced rest, not its end) | (b)(3) |
| Placement of the compensatory rest | Between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | (b)(3) |
| Scheduling obligation | The rest must be *scheduled* — a compliant rest period that arises only by accident of actual flight time does not satisfy the rule | (b)(2), (b)(3) |
| No-assignment bar | No duty period may be assigned unless the minimum rest has actually been received | (b)(10) |
| No-duty bar | No duty of any kind may be assigned during a required rest period | (b)(11) |

### 3.1 What "rest" means for compliance

"Rest period" is defined as "the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise." Applied to this operator, the following do **not** count toward the 9 (or 8) hours and, if assigned, break the consecutive clock:

- deadhead or positioning travel under company direction;
- ground transportation the company requires or provides as an assigned duty;
- training, checking, or administrative tasks;
- reserve/standby status, on-call availability, or any requirement to remain reachable and respond;
- required check-in calls or app acknowledgements that constitute responsibility for duty;
- any flying, including flying for another certificate holder if that is a duty of this certificate holder.

Rest is measured in **consecutive clock hours**. It cannot be assembled from interrupted blocks.

### 3.2 What does *not* apply here — common mis-citations

- **§ 135.265 (9/10/11 hours keyed to scheduled flight time) is the flight-crewmember scheduled-operations rule.** It is not the flight-attendant rule and is not the default answer here. See § 4 for the § 135.273(c) election that could import it.
- **§ 135.273(b)(7)/(b)(8) (12 consecutive hours, reducible to 10) apply only to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 but not more than 16 hours** under (b)(4)–(b)(6). They are outside the premise of this question (14 hours or less).
- **§ 135.273(b)(9)** — the bar on scheduling more than 14 hours of duty "during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest period" — is expressly limited to an election to reduce rest to 10 hours under (b)(8). **It does not attach to the (b)(3) reduction to 8 hours.** Do not apply it to the 9→8 case.

---

## 4. Alternative compliance path the operator may have elected — § 135.273(c)

§ 135.273(c) permits a certificate holder, notwithstanding paragraph (b), to apply the **flight crewmember** flight time, duty and rest requirements of Part 135 subpart F to flight attendants for all its operations, provided it establishes written procedures that (i) apply to all flight attendants used in the operation and (ii) include the flight crewmember requirements contained in subpart F as appropriate to the operation, except that on-board rest facilities are not required.

If this operator has made that election in its manual, the answer changes from "9 hours, reducible to 8" to the flight crewmember rest table — **9, 10, or 11 consecutive hours keyed to scheduled flight time (less than 8 / 8 but less than 9 / 9 or more hours), reducible to 8, 8, or 9 hours respectively with a compensating rest period that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commencement of the reduced rest period.** Because this is an on-demand (unscheduled) operator, the applicable flight crewmember section would ordinarily be § 135.267 rather than § 135.265; the exact numeric table must be read from the section that actually governs the operation.

**Action:** confirm from the operator's approved manual/operations specifications whether the § 135.273(c) election has been made. **If it has not (the default assumption here), the answer is 9 hours, reducible to 8.** If it has, the flight crewmember table governs and the flight-attendant 9/8 rule does not.

---

## 5. Applicability check — does § 135.273 apply to this operator's cabin personnel?

- A flight attendant is **required** only when the aircraft has a passenger seating configuration of more than 19 (§ 135.107). Most Part 135 on-demand charter fleets do not trigger this.
- However, § 135.273 applies to any individual who meets the (a) definition, **including personnel assigned in addition to the minimum crew complement whose duties include cabin-safety-related responsibilities**. The FAA's June 10, 2014 memorandum, *Applicability of part 135 flight, duty, and rest rules to flight attendants assigned in addition to the minimally-required crew complement* (AFS-240 / AGC-220), holds expressly that "if an operator voluntarily assigns individuals to a crew on a part 135 operation and assigns cabin-safety-related responsibilities to those individuals during flight time, then those individuals are 'flight attendants' for purposes of § 135.273," and that § 135.273 "do[es] not distinguish between different types of flight attendants."

**Action:** inventory every cabin crewmember and confirm, per person, whether they are (i) required by the operations specifications minimum crew complement or (ii) assigned in addition to it with cabin-safety duties. Any person in either category is covered by § 135.273 and must be scheduled to the 9-hour / 8-hour rule.

---

## 6. Scheduling procedure (how a scheduler applies this)

**Step 1 — Determine the scheduled duty period.** Duty period runs from report time to release time as *scheduled*, per the § 135.273(a) definition, computed in UTC or local time consistently.

**Step 2 — Branch.**

- Scheduled duty ≤ 14.0 h → paragraph (b)(2)/(b)(3) applies. Go to Step 3.
- Scheduled duty > 14.0 h → **stop**; this question does not cover it. Paragraphs (b)(4)–(b)(9) apply (additional flight attendant requirements, 12-hour rest, reduction to 10 with the (b)(9) 14-hour restriction). Route to the duty-period-extension checklist.

**Step 3 — Default schedule.** Schedule **≥ 9 consecutive hours** of rest between release from the duty period and report for the next duty period. Record the rest block in the scheduling system with explicit start and end times.

**Step 4 — If a reduction is operationally needed, apply all four conditions, or do not reduce:**

1. Rest block ≥ **8** consecutive hours (never fewer);
2. A subsequent rest block of ≥ **10** consecutive hours is scheduled and recorded;
3. That subsequent rest block **begins no later than 24 hours after the START of the reduced rest block**;
4. Both blocks sit between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

**Step 5 — Arithmetic gate for Step 4.** Because the 10-hour rest must *begin* within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest, and the reduced rest consumes 8 of those hours, **the duty period that follows the reduced rest may not exceed 16 hours measured from the end of the reduced rest to the start of the compensatory rest** — and in any event may not exceed 14 hours under (b)(1). In practice: `8 + (following duty period) ≤ 24`, and the following duty period is separately capped at 14. A 14-hour following duty period yields 22 hours and is compliant.

**Step 6 — Verify no duty is assigned inside either rest block** ((b)(11)): no deadhead, no training, no calls, no standby.

**Step 7 — Verify the crew member actually received the minimum before the next assignment** ((b)(10)). If actual rest fell short of the scheduled block for any reason (delay, company contact, interrupted hotel), the next assignment may not be made until the minimum is actually received.

---

## 7. Worked example

**Compliant, reduced to 8 hours.**

- Duty period 1 (scheduled): 06:00–20:00 = 14.0 h. Compliant under (b)(1).
- Reduced rest: **20:00 Day 1 → 04:00 Day 2 = 8 consecutive hours.** Permitted under (b)(3) only with the conditions below.
- Duty period 2: 04:00–18:00 Day 2 = 14.0 h. Compliant under (b)(1).
- Compensatory rest: **18:00 Day 2 → 04:00 Day 3 = 10 consecutive hours.** It begins at 18:00 Day 2, which is **22 hours after the 20:00 Day 1 start** of the reduced rest — within the 24-hour limit. ✓
- No duty assigned in either rest block. ✓

**Compliant, no reduction.** Same duty period 1; rest 20:00 Day 1 → 05:00 Day 2 = 9 consecutive hours. No compensatory rest required (though the next rest period must itself meet (b)(2)).

**Non-compliant examples.**

- Rest 20:00 → 03:00 (7 hours). Violates the (b)(3) floor of 8. No authority to go below 8 for a ≤14-hour duty period.
- Rest 20:00 → 04:00 (8 hours) with the next rest only 8 hours long, or beginning at 21:00 Day 2 (25 hours after the reduced rest began). Violates the (b)(3) condition; the reduction was therefore never authorized.
- Rest 20:00 → 04:00 (8 hours) with the flight attendant required to complete a 30-minute company online training module at 22:00. Breaks the consecutive rest block and violates (b)(11).
- Scheduling a 9-hour rest but calling the flight attendant in at hour 7 for a flight. Violates (b)(10) and (b)(11) regardless of what the schedule said.

---

## 8. Documentation and audit posture

For each flight-attendant duty period, retain:

1. Scheduled report and release times, and the resulting scheduled duty period length (with the UTC/local basis used);
2. Scheduled rest block start and end times, and total consecutive hours;
3. Whether the rest was the (b)(2) base rest or a (b)(3) reduction;
4. For every reduction: the compensatory rest block, its start and end, and the computed interval between the **start** of the reduced rest and the **start** of the compensatory rest (must be ≤ 24:00);
5. Actual rest received, with any interruption or company contact annotated and the corrective action taken before the next assignment;
6. Any duty period that exceeded 14 hours in actuality but was scheduled within limits, with the circumstances-beyond-the-control basis documented under (b)(14).

Store these in the crew scheduling/tracking system under the operator's Part 135 recordkeeping program so the 9/8 rule can be demonstrated on demand during an inspection.

---

## 9. One-line answer for the ops manual

> A flight attendant assigned to a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less must receive a scheduled rest period of at least **9 consecutive hours** between the completion of that duty period and the start of the next. That rest may be reduced to no less than **8 consecutive hours** only if the flight attendant is also given a subsequent rest period of at least **10 consecutive hours** that is scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period**. (§ 135.273(b)(2), (b)(3))

question: M7
answer:
ANSWER

1) Current specification of HTTP/2: RFC 9113, "HTTP/2", June 2022, M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla) and C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.), IETF Stream, Standards Track, status Proposed Standard, ISSN 2070-1721. It was produced by the HTTPBIS working group as draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.

2) RFCs it obsoletes: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740 — exactly two, and no others.

EVIDENCE (RFC 9113 front matter, verbatim)

  Stream:      Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)
  RFC:         9113
  Obsoletes:   7540, 8740
  Category:    Standards Track
  Published:   June 2022
  ISSN:        2070-1721
  Authors:     M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla); C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.)

Abstract sentence, verbatim: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
Section 1, verbatim: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740.  Appendix B lists notable changes."
Appendix B, verbatim: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes."

Corroboration from the other side of the relationship — the rfc-editor.org info page for RFC 7540 carries the banner, verbatim: "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113.  This RFC was updated, see RFC 8740." The IETF Datatracker document page for RFC 9113 states, verbatim: "Obsoletes RFC 8740, RFC 7540" and "Was draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis (httpbis WG)".

WHAT EACH OBSOLESCENCE MEANS

- RFC 7540 (May 2015, Belshe/Peon/Thomson, "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)") was the original HTTP/2 specification. RFC 9113 replaces it in full: it is a revision (http2bis), not an addendum. Substantive changes listed in Appendix B include deprecation of the RFC 7540 priority scheme (the PRIORITY frame format and HEADERS priority fields are retained but their semantics now live only in RFC 7540, with [HTTP-PRIORITY] recommended instead), deprecation and removal of the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism from the document, and editorial realignment with the revised core HTTP semantics documents (concepts such as the 421 status code and connection coalescing moved into the core HTTP documents).
- RFC 8740 ("Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2") was an update to RFC 7540 that defined how TLS 1.3 is used with HTTP/2. RFC 9113 folds that content into the base specification, so RFC 8740 is obsoleted rather than left standing.

SCOPE DISCIPLINE (what is NOT in the answer)

- Obsoletes is not Updates. RFC 9113's header carries no Updates field, so there is nothing to add on that axis; the answer is the two-number Obsoletes list and nothing more. Note the asymmetry: RFC 7540 was updated by RFC 8740, but that is a statement about RFC 7540's history, not about RFC 9113's obsoletion list.
- RFC 9113 does not obsolete RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching), or RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1). Those are companion documents in the same 2022 HTTP revision set; RFC 9113 depends on and references them (the "[HTTP]" reference in Appendix B is to RFC 9110). HTTP/2 is an optimized expression of HTTP semantics defined elsewhere, so "HTTP/2 depends on RFC 9110" must not be written as "RFC 9113 obsoletes RFC 9110."
- RFC 9113 is itself current and not obsolete: it is not listed as obsoleted by any published RFC as of the lookup date below, and the RFC Editor index still serves it as the live HTTP/2 specification.

REPRODUCTION PROCEDURE (how to re-verify, and how to detect if this answer goes stale)

1. Fetch the authoritative front matter: curl -s https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.txt | sed -n '1,20p' and read the header block for the lines 'RFC:', 'Obsoletes:', 'Updates:', 'Category:', 'Published:'. The canonical source is the document's own header, not a search-result snippet.
2. Confirm currency, not just existence: curl -s https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ and check that no banner of the form "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC NNNN" appears. Apply the same check to rfc7540 and rfc8740 to confirm they still display the "now obsolete, see RFC 9113" banner.
3. Check the RFC Editor index for any later HTTP/2 document: search rfc-editor.org for title containing "hypertext transfer protocol" sorted by number descending, and look for any RFC numbered above 9113 that claims to specify or obsolete HTTP/2. As of the lookup date none exists.
4. Staleness rule: this answer is valid for the RFC Series state on the lookup date below. If a future RFC obsoletes RFC 9113, step 2's banner check on rfc9113 will start returning a successor number and this answer must be reissued with that number and its own Obsoletes list.

RECORDED CONTEXT

Lookup date: 2026-11-16 (UTC), per the fetch timestamps of the source pages. Sources consulted: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html, https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113, https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/. Status caveat worth carrying forward: RFC 9113 is a Proposed Standard, not an Internet Standard; the 2022 HTTP set did not advance HTTP/2 to Internet Standard status, so "current specification" here means "the RFC in force," not "the highest maturity level." Readers should also check the errata page at https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 for verified errata before treating any specific protocol detail as final; errata do not change the obsolescence relationships stated above.

question: M9
