# UK statutory minimum wage rates effective 1 April 2026

## Direct answers

| Ask | Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 March 2026) | Cash increase | % increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over | **£12.71 per hour** | £12.21 | +£0.50 | 4.1% |
| 2 | National Minimum Wage — workers aged 18 to 20 | **£10.85 per hour** | £10.00 | +£0.85 | 8.5% |

Both are in pounds sterling per hour, stated to the exact penny as fixed by the amending regulations. No rounding choice is required: the figures are set as exact amounts in the statutory instrument.

## Legal status of these figures

The rates are not a forecast. They have been through the full annual cycle:

1. **Recommendation** — Low Pay Commission recommendations made in October 2025, published as LPC advice to Government on 26 November 2025.
2. **Government acceptance** — GOV.UK states the Government "accepted in full the recommendations of the independent Low Pay Commission (LPC)" and that the increases "will be effective from April 2026".
3. **Legislation** — the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, laid before Parliament as a draft affirmative instrument under s.51(5) of the National Minimum Wage Act 1998, coming into force **1 April 2026**, extending to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

### Operative provisions of the draft SI (National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026)

- **Regulation 2(2):** in regulation 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (the national living wage), for "£12.21" substitute **"£12.71"**. → answers ask 1.
- **Regulation 2(3)(a):** in regulation 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21), for "£10.00" substitute **"£10.85"**. → answers ask 2.
- **Regulation 2(3)(b):** in regulation 4A(1)(c) (workers under 18), for "£7.55" substitute "£8.00".
- **Regulation 2(3)(c):** in regulation 4A(1)(d) (apprentice rate), for "£7.55" substitute "£8.00".
- **Regulation 2(4):** in regulation 16(1) (accommodation offset), for "£10.66" substitute "£11.10".

The Explanatory Note confirms in terms: "Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour" and "Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour".

Note on the age band: the 18–20 band is **not** restructured for April 2026 — reg 4A(1)(b) is amended in amount, not repealed or re-aged, so the existing "18 or over but not yet 21" band is the correct band for ask 2. (The LPC's 2026 uprating report records that "Government policy is to remove the 18-20 Year Old Rate", but that is a forward-looking policy intention and does not alter the rate applicable from 1 April 2026.)

## Full April 2026 rate table (for context and to prevent misattribution)

| Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Increase (£) | Increase (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £0.50 | 4.1 |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £0.85 | 8.5 |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 |
| Accommodation offset (per day) | £11.10 | £0.44 | 4.1 |

(GOV.UK also lists the already-announced April 2027 rates — 21+ £13.21, 18–20 £11.27, under-18 £8.31, apprentice £8.31 — which must not be used for an April 2026 question.)

## Arithmetic verification

- Ask 1: £12.21 + £0.50 = **£12.71**; 0.50 ÷ 12.21 = 4.095% → published as 4.1%. Consistent.
- Ask 2: £10.00 + £0.85 = **£10.85**; 0.85 ÷ 10.00 = 8.500% → published as 8.5%. Consistent.
- Both figures are internally consistent with the SI's substituted amounts, the LPC 2026 uprating report table, the GOV.UK rates page's "April 2026" row, and the ONS 2026 low/high pay bulletin.

## Source provenance (all fetched 2026-11-16)

1. **The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026** (draft SI) — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2026/9780348279030 — primary legislation source; gives £12.71 and £10.85 as the substituted amounts, in force 1 April 2026.
2. **GOV.UK, "Minimum wage rates for 2026"** (LPC advice to Government, published 26 November 2025) — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026 — Government announcement; NLW (21 and over) £12.71, 18–20 Year Old Rate £10.85.
3. **GOV.UK, "National Minimum Wage rates"** — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates — "April 2026: 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; Under 18 £8; Apprentice £8".
4. **Low Pay Commission, "The National Minimum Wage in 2026"** (published 1 April 2026) — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026 and PDF at https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/69cbe06e024cdf09254f3f92/2026_Uprating_report_v2.pdf — table "NMW Rate from April 2026": NLW (21 and over) £12.71, 18-20 Year Old Rate £10.85.
5. **ONS, "Low and high pay in the UK: 2026"** — https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/bulletins/lowandhighpayuk/2026 — independent confirmation: "£12.71 for employees aged 21 years and over; £10.85 for employees aged 18 to 20 years".

All five agree on both figures; there is no conflicting official figure.

## Points of caution for anyone using these numbers

- **Statutory vs voluntary.** These are the *statutory* National Living Wage / National Minimum Wage. They are not the voluntary "Real Living Wage" set by the Living Wage Foundation, which the ONS reports at £13.45 (outside London) and £14.80 (London) as at April 2026. The two are commonly confused; the Real Living Wage is not a legal minimum.
- **Effective date.** The rates apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after **1 April 2026**. Rates for the period 1 April 2025 – 31 March 2026 remain £12.21 (21+) and £10.00 (18–20).
- **Age determination.** Entitlement follows the worker's age; a worker aged 21 or over on the relevant date gets the NLW rate, and a worker aged 18, 19 or 20 gets the 18–20 rate. Apprentices under 19, or 19+ in the first year of their apprenticeship, are on the apprentice rate (£8.00) instead — an apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year is entitled to £12.71.
- **Accommodation offset.** £11.10 per day from 1 April 2026, a separate figure that reduces the cash minimum wage payable where living accommodation is provided; it is not an alternative hourly rate.
- **Currency/scope.** GBP, UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) — the SI extends to all four nations; there is no devolved variation in the statutory rate.

question: M11
answer:
# FMCSA Short-Haul Exception (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — Radius and Release Thresholds

## Answer

| Criterion | Value | Regulatory language |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum operating radius from the normal work reporting location | **150 air miles** (172.6 statute miles) | "The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location" — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i) |
| Maximum consecutive hours before the driver must be released from work | **14 consecutive hours** | "The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours" — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii) |

Both values come from the current eCFR text of 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) ("150 air-mile radius driver"), which exempts a qualifying driver from the record-of-duty-status requirement in § 395.8 and the supporting-documents requirement in § 395.11.

## Full text of the operative provision

> **(e) Short-haul operations —**
> **(1) 150 air-mile radius driver.** A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
> (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
> (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
> (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
> (iii)(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
> (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) the time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) the total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) the time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) the total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.

## How to apply the two thresholds

1. **Radius (150 air miles / 172.6 statute miles).** The circle is centered on the driver's *normal work reporting location* — the location where the driver reports to and is released from work. The driver must remain inside that radius for the entire duty tour. Per FMCSA's published short-haul guidance, as long as the driver starts and ends each shift at the same location, that location may differ from shift to shift; the radius is measured from the location used for that shift. "Air miles" are straight-line (great-circle) miles, not highway miles; the regulation equates 150 air miles to 172.6 statute miles.
2. **Release time (14 consecutive hours).** The 14-hour clock starts when the driver comes on duty. Within those 14 consecutive hours the driver must (a) return to the work reporting location and (b) be released from work there. It is a release deadline, not merely a driving limit — the driver must be off duty, at the reporting location, by hour 14. The exception at § 395.1(e)(1) is not available to a driver-salesperson.

## Points that do **not** change either answer

- **Property-carrying vs. passenger-carrying.** Both classes use the same 150 air-mile radius and the same 14-consecutive-hour release. The distinction appears only in the separating off-duty period: 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying, 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying (§ 395.1(e)(1)(iii)).
- **Adverse driving conditions.** The up-to-2-hour adverse-driving extension does not stretch the short-haul 14-hour release deadline. FMCSA's short-haul FAQ states that a short-haul driver who cannot return to the reporting location within 14 hours because of adverse conditions must record duty status for that day (paper log or ELD). Do not apply the 2-hour extension to this 14.
- **Exemption from the 30-minute break.** Drivers operating under § 395.1(e)(1) are also not required to take the 30-minute break after 8 cumulative hours of driving.

## Adjacent provisions — do not confuse them with the answer above

- **§ 395.1(e)(2) — property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL.** Also a 150 air-mile radius, measured from the location where the driver reports to and is released from work, and the driver must return to that location at the end of each duty tour. But the release structure differs: the driver may not drive after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days, and after the 16th hour on 2 days of any period of 7 consecutive days. A driver using (e)(2) is ineligible for (e)(1), (g), and (o). Where a single release figure is requested, 14 consecutive hours (the (e)(1) rule) is the governing answer.
- **§ 395.1(o) — split sleeper berth / 16-hour exception.** Allows release within 16 hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty, but only after returning to the normal work reporting location for the previous five duty tours, and not more than once in any 6 consecutive days (absent a 34-hour restart). This is a separate exception, not the short-haul exception.
- **§ 395.1(p) — motion picture production sites.** 100 air-mile radius. Unrelated to short-haul.

## Superseded history (for version control only — not the operative rule)

The 2020 hours-of-service final rule (FMCSA, effective September 29, 2020) amended the short-haul exception by extending the maximum radius from **100 air miles to 150 air miles** and the maximum duty period from **12 hours to 14 hours**. Any document still stating 100 air miles / 12 hours reflects the pre-2020 text and is out of date. Cite the current eCFR text of 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) for the 150 / 14 figures.

## Compliance obligations that survive the RODS exemption

The driver is excused from § 395.8 (RODS) and § 395.11 (supporting documents) — meaning no graph-grid log and no ELD — but the motor carrier must still maintain and retain for **6 months** accurate and true time records showing the driver's report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time, and (for drivers used for the first time or intermittently) the total time for the preceding 7 days. If the driver exceeds the 150 air-mile radius or is not released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception is lost for that day and the driver must complete a record of duty status (paper log or ELD) for that day.

## Basis and scope

- **Authority:** 49 CFR Part 395, Subpart A, § 395.1(e)(1), as published in the current eCFR (Title 49, Subtitle B, Chapter III, Subchapter B).
- **Corroborating FMCSA publications:** "Summary of Hours of Service Regulations" (FMCSA, last updated March 28, 2022) and the FMCSA/CSA HOS Visor Card, both of which restate the short-haul criteria as 150 air miles and a 14-hour maximum duty period.
- **Scope:** Federal interstate motor carrier operations subject to FMCSA jurisdiction. Intrastate operations may follow a state's own adoption of Part 395 (many states incorporate the federal 150/14 thresholds, but a specific state's intrastate variation is outside this answer).

The first reads: "(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 5 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a/section-395.1 and 2 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.1. The first reads: "(A) After the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days;"

question: M1
answer:
# BasicMed aircraft limits — current US rule

## 1. Direct answer

| Limit | Current value (ops on/after 12 Nov 2024) | Prior value (2017 – 11 Nov 2024) |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) | **12,500 lb** | 6,000 lb |
| Occupants the aircraft may be **authorized to carry** (design approval) | **7** | 6 |
| Passengers on board (operational limit) | **6** | 5 |

All three are conditions of 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1), as amended to implement § 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Pub. L. 118-63). The 12,500 lb figure **excludes transport category helicopters** (see § 5 below).

Source for the current values, quoted verbatim from FAA Notice N 8000.386 (11/14/24), ¶ 5a(2): *"Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: • The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, • The aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and • The aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board."* Corroborated by the FAA newsroom release of 15 Nov 2024 ("Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.") and by AOPA's July 2025 summary ("cannot have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of more than 12,500 pounds ... cannot be certified to carry more than seven occupants ... no more than six passengers on board").

## 2. Authority chain (so each number is traceable)

- Statute: 49 U.S.C. § 44836 (BasicMed), as amended by Pub. L. 118-63, § 828 ("Expansion of BasicMed").
- Rule: 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) — the three aircraft conditions; § 61.113(i)(2) — the flight (operating) conditions.
- Experimental aircraft: 14 CFR § 91.319(j) — parallel occupant cap for experimental airworthiness certificates.
- Guidance: AC 68-1A (BasicMed) and FAA Notice N 8000.386 (14 Nov 2024) for the post-expansion figures.

## 3. What each number means and how to verify it for a specific aircraft

**MTOW (12,500 lb).** This is the *maximum certificated* takeoff weight — the weight in the aircraft's design approval (type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended TC), not the weight you happen to operate at and not a derated/performance-limited figure. Check the TCDS or the STC/ATC. An aircraft whose design approval permits more than 12,500 lb is not a covered aircraft unless the design approval has been amended (e.g., by STC) to restrict it to 12,500 lb or less. N 8000.386 and AC 68-1A both make the point that the design approval governs; AC 68-1A ¶ 5.1.2: *"the aircraft's design approval would authorize the number of occupants the aircraft may carry and would contain the maximum certificated takeoff weight ... may be a type certificate (TC), a supplemental type certificate (STC), or an amended TC (ATC)."*

**Occupants authorized (7).** Also a design-approval attribute, and it **includes required flightcrew**. AC 68-1A ¶ 5.2.1: *"A covered aircraft may be authorized to carry up to six occupants (including any required flightcrew members) and may be operated with up to five passengers on board"* — read those numbers as 7 and 6 respectively for current operations. The AC's own worked logic still applies: a type certificated for one pilot can be flown with six additional occupants; a type certificated for two required pilots can be flown with five additional occupants. It is the *certificated* capacity that counts, not the number of seats currently installed — AC 68-1A and the BasicMed FAQ (Q33) make clear that an aircraft certificated for more occupants is ineligible even if seats are removed, unless the removal/alteration is reflected in a design approval (STC/ATC) or the configuration is one the TC expressly permits (e.g., the PA-32-260/300 six-seat configuration, or removal of the 7th-seat STC).

**Passengers on board (6).** This is an operational limit on the flight, separate from the certificated capacity. Passengers = occupants minus the pilot(s) actually required and aboard. One pilot aboard ⇒ up to 6 passengers. Two required flightcrew aboard ⇒ up to 5 passengers (7 occupants total either way). Non-required crew or extra pilots occupying seats are occupants and count against both caps; a second pilot who is not a required flightcrew member does not buy you a seventh passenger.

## 4. Worked checks

| Aircraft situation | Occupants authorized | Max passengers | Covered? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single-pilot type, 7 seats, MTOW 10,000 lb | 7 | 6 | Yes |
| Single-pilot type, 7 seats, MTOW 12,500 lb exactly | 7 | 6 | Yes (limit is "no more than") |
| Two-required-pilot type, 7 seats, MTOW 12,500 lb | 7 | 5 | Yes |
| Type certificated for 8 occupants, 7 seats installed | 8 | n/a | No — unless STC/ATC restricts design approval to 7 |
| MTOW 12,501 lb, 7 seats | 7 | n/a | No — unless STC/ATC restricts MTOW to ≤12,500 lb |
| Any transport category helicopter | — | — | See § 5 |

## 5. Caveat that changes the headline number: transport category helicopters

The 12,500 lb increase expressly excludes transport category helicopters. Operationally this means a pilot exercising BasicMed privileges in a transport category helicopter should plan against the pre-expansion **6,000 lb** MTOW limit; the occupant/passenger expansion is stated separately and is not subject to that carve-out. I flag this as an inference from the structure of the statutory carve-out as reported by the FAA release — confirm against the current text of § 61.113(i)(1) before relying on it for a specific helicopter, since the secondary sources I have do not restate the helicopter figure.

## 6. Version-control warning (the most common error on this question)

AC 68-1A as published 5/3/17 still reads, at ¶ 3.2: *"Fly with no more than five passengers ... maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than 6,000 lbs ... authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants."* Those are the **superseded** numbers. If you are reading a 2017-vintage AC, FAQ, or safety-briefing article, you are reading the pre-12 November 2024 rule. Use N 8000.386 / the amended § 61.113(i)(1) for anything dated on or after 12 Nov 2024. The same caution applies to AC 68-1A's quotation of § 91.319(j) ("more than six occupants" for experimental aircraft) — that text predates the expansion, so verify the current § 91.319(j) before applying an occupant count to an experimental aircraft rather than assuming it moved to seven.

## 7. The rest of the envelope (not asked, but these three numbers are not the whole limit set)

Per § 61.113(i)(2) and N 8000.386 ¶ 5b, the flight must be conducted:
- at or below **18,000 ft MSL**;
- at an indicated airspeed **not exceeding 250 knots**;
- **within the United States**, or within another country in which BasicMed is authorized (the FAA BasicMed FAQ Q23 states plainly: "No. You cannot fly outside the United States when operating under BasicMed." — treat the foreign-operation allowance as requiring affirmative authorization by the other state, and do not assume it);
- **not for compensation or hire**.

Also unchanged and worth stating because it is frequently confused with the aircraft limits: the limitations apply to the **entire flight** from takeoff to touchdown — a BasicMed pilot cannot act as PIC for any portion of a flight that exceeds them, even if another pilot with a medical certificate is PIC for the portion that does (FAA Safety Briefing, Jul/Aug 2017). BasicMed relief is limited to acting as PIC; a safety pilot who is not PIC needs a medical certificate.

## 8. Bottom line

A BasicMed pilot in the US today may fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of **12,500 lb or less** (transport category helicopters excepted), that is **authorized to carry no more than 7 occupants** including required flightcrew, carrying **no more than 6 passengers** on board — within the US, at or below 18,000 ft MSL and 250 KIAS, and not for compensation or hire.

question: M3
answer:
US FEDERAL HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS FOR A PASSENGER-CARRYING CMV DRIVER (MOTORCOACH)

Controlling authority: 49 CFR 395.5, 'Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles' (70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005; text unchanged in the 2025 CFR print and current on eCFR). Corroborated by FMCSA, 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers.' Scope: 49 CFR 390.3(a) applies Subchapter B to CMVs transporting property or passengers in interstate commerce.

1. ANSWERS

| Ask | Question | Answer | Unit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may they drive? | 10 | hours | 395.5(a)(1) |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | 8 | consecutive hours off duty | 395.5(a) |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | 15 | hours on duty | 395.5(a)(2) |

All three are read out of a single sentence structure, so they are only meaningful together: a driver may drive up to 10 hours, and may not drive at all after the 15th hour on duty, in each case measured from the end of a period of 8 consecutive hours off duty.

2. THE REGULATION, VERBATIM (49 CFR 395.5)

'Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 395.1:
(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—
(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or
(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.'

3. HOW THE THREE LIMITS OPERATE

- 10 hours (driving limit). This is a cap on driving time, not on total time worked, and it is measured from the end of the 8-consecutive-hour off-duty period — not '10 hours in a 24-hour day.' Driving in excess of 10 hours within the window is prohibited.
- 8 consecutive hours off duty (the reset). The period must be consecutive; it restarts both the 10-hour driving clock and the 15-hour on-duty clock. Time not consecutive (or interrupted by any on-duty work) does not start a new window.
- 15 hours (driving window / on-duty limit). Once the driver has been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, driving is prohibited for any period thereafter. Note the precise effect: the rule bars driving after hour 15, not all work — on-duty-not-driving work may continue, but it continues to consume the weekly 60/70-hour allowance and cannot be followed by driving.
- Outer weekly limits (395.5(b)) independently bar driving: 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week, or 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days if it does. There is no restart provision in 395.5; the 34-hour restart at 395.3(c) is property-carrier-only and must not be applied here. The 7- or 8-day period is the carrier-designated 24-hour period sequence for the driver's home terminal (395.8).

Sanity check on the numbers as stated: 10 driving hours is available inside the 15-hour on-duty window (10 <= 15); the daily figures (10, 15) and the weekly figures (60/7, 70/8) are quoted exactly as in the regulation and are not derived from one another, so no stated value violates a threshold stated elsewhere in this answer.

4. DEFINITIONS THAT DRIVE THE COUNT (49 CFR 395.2)

- On-duty time: all time from the time the driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work until relieved from work and all responsibility for performing work. Performing other compensated work for a person who is not a motor carrier is also on-duty time.
- Off-duty time: time the driver is relieved from work and all responsibility for performing work (the basis of the 8-consecutive-hour reset).
- Adverse driving conditions: snow, sleet, fog, other adverse weather, or unusual road or traffic conditions that the driver did not know and could not reasonably discover before beginning the run.

5. EXCEPTIONS UNDER 395.1 THAT CAN CHANGE THESE NUMBERS (do not assume them absent the facts)

- Adverse driving conditions (395.1(b)(1)): a driver who encounters adverse driving conditions may drive the period of time needed to complete the run, and afterwards must be off duty for at least 8 consecutive hours before driving again. This is a completion-of-run allowance keyed to the defined conditions; it is not a standing extension of the 10-hour cap.
- Sleeper-berth split (395.1(g)(3)): a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth may accumulate the equivalent of the 8 consecutive hours off duty using two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the conditions of 395.1(g)(3)(i)-(iv) are satisfied (including the paired-period driving-time and 15-hour constraints). Confirm the paragraph text before relying on it for a specific schedule.
- Travel / 'cushioning' time (395.1(j)): travel at the carrier's direction but not driving or otherwise working counts as on-duty unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival, in which case the entire period may be treated as off duty. Relevant to relief-driver movements.
- Alaska (395.1(b)): separate limits apply to drivers operating in Alaska; the passenger-carrying variant uses a 15-hour driving allowance following 8 consecutive hours off duty and a 20-hour on-duty outer limit (with 70/7 and 80/8 weekly caps). Do not apply these outside Alaska.
- Short-haul relief in 395.1(e) is written for property-carrying operations; do not assume it covers a motorcoach run without checking the paragraph.

6. SCOPE, JURISDICTION, AND COMMON MISAPPLICATIONS

- Interstate operations: the federal limits above govern. Intrastate-only motorcoach operation is not governed by 395.5 as a matter of federal law; the state's intrastate HOS rules apply and may differ or be stricter. Confirm the operation's interstate/intrastate status before quoting these numbers as compliance obligations.
- Stricter requirements are permitted: 390.3(d) allows an employer to impose more stringent safety requirements, and state law may be stricter; the federal figures are a floor, not a ceiling on carrier policy.
- Recordkeeping vs. HOS: a nonbusiness private motor carrier of passengers is exempt from the record-of-duty-status requirement (395.8(a)(1)), but the 395.5 driving limits still apply. A logging exemption is not an hours exemption.
- Property-carrier rules do not apply: the 11-hour driving limit, 14-hour window, 30-minute break, and 34-hour restart in 395.3 are for property-carrying CMVs. A motorcoach driver is measured by 10 / 15 / 8 and 60-7 / 70-8 only.
- Multiple-employer drivers: 395.5(b) applies 'regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services,' and 395.8(j) requires a signed statement of the prior 7 days' on-duty time when a driver is used intermittently. Part-time or multi-carrier motorcoach drivers do not get a fresh 60/70 clock per carrier.

7. WORKED EXAMPLE (arithmetic check)

Driver goes off duty at 22:00 and returns to duty at 06:00 — 8 consecutive hours off duty, so a new window opens at 06:00. That driver may drive no more than 10 hours (i.e., until 10 hours of driving is accumulated, at the earliest 16:00 if driving continuously), and may not drive at any time after 21:00 (15 hours on duty following the 06:00 start), even if only 9 driving hours have been used. Both limits bind independently; the earlier-applying one governs. The weekly 60/70-hour cap applies on top of both.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a/section-395.5 and 15 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395. The first reads: "(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty;"

question: M5
answer:
# Flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less — 14 CFR Part 135

## 1. Answer

| Item | Value | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Required rest after a scheduled duty period of **14 hours or less** | **At least 9 consecutive hours** (scheduled) | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| May be reduced to | **8 consecutive hours**, but only with a compensating subsequent rest | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |
| Condition on the reduction | Subsequent rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours**, scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period**, and occurring between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

So: **9 consecutive hours, reducible to 8 consecutive hours only when followed by at least 10 consecutive hours of rest that begins within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest.**

## 2. Why 135.273 applies (applicability, not assumption)

- 14 CFR 135.273(e) (subpart F introductory text): "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants **in all operations conducted under this part**." There is no on-demand/scheduled carve-out for the flight attendant rule; the scheduled-vs-on-demand split in 135.263(b)–(c) governs the *flight crewmember* rules (135.265/135.267/135.269), not 135.273.
- Part 135 does not *require* a flight attendant below a 20-seat passenger configuration (135.107), but that does not exempt one who is carried. FAA memorandum, June 10, 2014 (AFS-240 / AGC-200, "Applicability of part 135 flight, duty, and rest rules to flight attendants assigned in addition to the minimally-required crew complement") holds that an individual assigned to a Part 135 flight with cabin-safety-related responsibilities during flight time is a "flight attendant" under 135.273(a) **even if not required**, and that 135.273(b) and (c) "do not distinguish between different types of flight attendants." Voluntarily added cabin crew on a 19-seat-or-less charter aircraft are therefore covered.
- Definitional anchors in 135.273(a):
  - *Duty period* — elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder.
  - *Rest period* — "the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise."
  - *Flight attendant* — a non-flight-crewmember assigned by the certificate holder, per the ops-spec minimum complement or in addition to it, to duty in an aircraft during flight time, with cabin-safety responsibilities among the duties.

**Practical consequence:** the 9/8 rule is the default for this operator's cabin crew unless the operator has taken the 135.273(c) election described in §6 below.

## 3. The operative rule text (135.273(b)(1)–(3))

- **(b)(1)** No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a **scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours** (except under (b)(4)–(6), which allow longer duty only with extra flight attendants aboard — see §5).
- **(b)(2)** A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of **14 hours or less** under (b)(1) "must be given a scheduled rest period of **at least 9 consecutive hours**. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."
- **(b)(3)** That rest "may be scheduled or reduced to **8 consecutive hours** if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours**; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."
- **(b)(10)** No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under the section.
- **(b)(11)** No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during any required rest period.

Note the trigger is the **scheduled** duty period (14 h or less), and the rest is a **scheduled** rest period measured in consecutive hours free of all responsibility for work or duty.

## 4. Boundaries and common misapplications

1. **8 hours is a floor, not a target.** There is no provision reducing flight attendant rest below 8 consecutive hours for a 14-hour-or-less duty period. A 7-hour rest is a violation regardless of any follow-on rest.
2. **The 10-hour follow-on rest is mandatory, not optional.** Reduce to 8 without scheduling the ≥10-hour subsequent rest and the assignment is unlawful under (b)(3) and (b)(10).
3. **The 24-hour clock runs from the start of the reduced rest, not from release or report.** Reduced rest beginning 21:00 means the subsequent ≥10-hour rest must *begin* no later than 21:00 the next day.
4. **The 10-hour follow-on rest sits between two duty periods.** It must occur after completion of the scheduled duty period and before commencement of the subsequent duty period; it cannot be banked, deferred, or counted as the next pairing's ordinary rest.
5. **No duty during required rest (b)(11).** Post-flight paperwork, calls, simulator, training, positioning as duty, or reserve availability that constitutes a responsibility for work will erode the consecutive rest block and can void compliance. If the crew member is on a rest period, the certificate holder must leave them free of all responsibility for work or duty.
6. **There is no paragraph (b)(9)-style 14-hour cap attached to the 8-hour reduction.** The (b)(9) restriction (no duty period over 14 hours in the 24 hours after the reduced rest begins) is written expressly for the 10-hour reduction under (b)(8) that applies to duty periods over 14 hours. Do not import it into (b)(3) — but do not rely on its absence either: (b)(1) independently caps the following scheduled duty period at 14 hours, which is what keeps the 24-hour follow-on deadline achievable in practice.
7. **No weekly cumulative rest minimum for flight attendants in 135.273(b).** The 24-consecutive-hours-in-7-days relief in 135.265(d) is a flight crewmember requirement. Do not assume it binds cabin crew unless the operator has made the (c) election.
8. **This is not the Part 121 regime.** Part 121 cabin-crew rest (including its 24-hour/7-day and reduced-rest structures) does not apply to a Part 135 certificate holder; only 135.273 does.

## 5. Do not confuse with the over-14-hour tiers

For completeness (the question is limited to 14 hours or less, so these do **not** govern the answer):

| Scheduled duty period | Required rest | Reducible to | Follow-on rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| **14 h or less** | **9 consecutive hours** — 135.273(b)(2) | **8 consecutive hours** — (b)(3) | **≥10 consecutive hours, beginning ≤24 h after start of reduced rest** |
| More than 14 h up to 16 h (with at least one additional flight attendant) — (b)(4) | 12 consecutive hours — (b)(7) | 10 consecutive hours — (b)(8) | ≥14 consecutive hours, beginning ≤24 h after start of reduced rest; and no duty period over 14 h in the following 24 h — (b)(9) |
| More than 16 h up to 18 h (with at least two additional flight attendants) — (b)(5) | 12 consecutive hours | 10 consecutive hours | as above |
| More than 18 h up to 20 h (with at least three additional flight attendants, and a flight landing/taking off outside the 48 contiguous states and DC) — (b)(6) | 12 consecutive hours | 10 consecutive hours | as above |

If a duty period is extended past 14 hours, the rest requirement jumps to 12 hours and the reduction floor rises to 10 — the opposite direction from the 14-or-less case. Schedule to the 14-hour boundary deliberately.

## 6. The one election that would change the numbers — verify before relying

135.273(c) lets a certificate holder apply the **flight crewmember** flight time/duty/rest rules of Part 135 to its flight attendants instead, provided it establishes written procedures that (i) apply to all flight attendants in the operation, (ii) contain the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (except on-board rest facilities are not required), (iii) add one flight attendant per flight crewmember above the minimum in the type certificate data sheet, and (iv) **are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications**.

If, and only if, that election is in the ops specs, the governing numbers become the flight crewmember ones (e.g., 135.265(b): 9 consecutive hours for less than 8 h scheduled flight time, 10 for 8 to less than 9, 11 for 9 or more; reducible under 135.265(c) to 8, 8, and 9 respectively with follow-on rests of 10, 11, and 12 hours beginning within 24 hours). **Action for the operator: confirm no 135.273(c) election exists in the ops specs before scheduling to the 9/8 rule.** Absent that election, 9/8 is the rule.

## 7. Worked scheduling arithmetic

**Baseline (no reduction).** Scheduled duty 07:00–21:00 (14.0 h — inside the (b)(1) cap and inside (b)(2)'s "14 hours or less"). Release 21:00. Required rest 9 consecutive hours → 21:00 to 06:00. Earliest next report: **06:00**.

**With the 8-hour reduction.** Same pairing. Reduced rest 21:00 to 05:00 (8 h) → earliest next report **05:00**, permitted only if a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours is scheduled to begin no later than **21:00 the next day** (24 h after 21:00) and before the next duty period begins. Example: next duty 05:00–19:00 (14.0 h); rest from 19:00 → begins 19:00, which is earlier than the 21:00 deadline; 10 consecutive hours run 19:00–05:00. Compliant.

**Failure case to screen for.** Reduced rest starts 21:00; the following duty is delayed so it does not end until 21:30. The ≥10-hour subsequent rest cannot begin by 21:00 → the reduction was not available, and the pairing is non-compliant for both the reduction and the follow-on. Schedulers must treat the 24-hour deadline as a hard constraint on the *following* duty period's release time, not as a soft target.

**Second failure case.** Rest block 21:00–05:00 with a 04:30 company call or a 04:45 training module assigned inside it → rest is 7.5 hours and duty is assigned during required rest, violating (b)(3) and (b)(11).

## 8. Compliance procedure the operator should adopt

1. **Classify every cabin crew member as a "flight attendant" under 135.273(a)** in the ops manual, including crew carried in addition to (or without) a required complement who have cabin-safety duties during flight time. This closes the 2014 interpretation gap.
2. **Confirm the ops-spec status** of any 135.273(c) election. Record the determination (elected / not elected) in the manual so schedulers know whether 9/8 or the flight-crewmember table governs.
3. **Build the rest check into the pairing build, not the day of flight.** For each flight attendant pairing, compute: scheduled duty period length; if ≤14 h, enforce a 9-hour rest block; if reduced, flag the pairing and require entry of the planned ≥10-hour subsequent rest with its start time and verify start ≤ (reduced rest start + 24 h).
4. **Apply a company buffer** above the regulatory minimum (e.g., 10 hours standard, 9 hours as the internal floor) if the operation has any history of post-flight delays eroding actual rest; the regulation is a minimum, not a safe scheduling target.
5. **Keep duty/rest records** sufficient to demonstrate, for each flight attendant and each duty period, report time, release time, the rest block given, and (where reduced) the follow-on rest block and its start time. 135.273 itself prescribes no record form, but (b)(10)–(b)(11) are prohibitions the certificate holder must be able to disprove; maintain the records under the operator's 135.63 recordkeeping program and manual procedures, and make them retrievable for FAA inspection.
6. **Reconcile with the flight crew's own limits on the same pairing.** The pilots' 135.265/135.267 rest is computed separately and may be longer than the flight attendant's; the pairing must satisfy both, and the later constraint governs the report time.

## 9. Assumptions and caveats (state these to the requestor)

- The person is a "flight attendant" within 135.273(a) and the 2014 interpretation — i.e., assigned by the certificate holder with cabin-safety-related responsibilities during flight time. If the individual is carried purely as a passenger with no assigned duty, 135.273 does not reach them.
- The duty period is the **scheduled** duty period of 14 hours or less, with no unscheduled extension past 14 hours. If actual duty exceeds 14 hours, re-run against (b)(4)–(8) (12 hours, reducible to 10, with a 14-hour follow-on).
- The operator has **not** made a 135.273(c) election, and neither its ops specs, manual, nor any collective bargaining agreement or customer contract imposes a longer rest. Any such source overrides this answer upward.
- "Rest" means a period free of all responsibility for work or duty, per 135.273(a).
- Rule text as currently published in 14 CFR part 135 (eCFR / 2026 edition of CFR title 14 vol. 3), including the flight attendant duty/rest provisions of 135.273(b).
- Nothing here addresses flight time limits for the flight attendants themselves; 135.273(b) limits duty periods and rest, not flight hours. If the (c) election is in place, flight time limits apply too.

The first reads: "(1) A rest required under paragraph (b)(1) of this section may be scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 8 hours if the flight crewmember is given a rest period of at least 10 hours that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commenc"

ANSWER

1) Current specification of HTTP/2: **RFC 9113**, "HTTP/2", Standards Track, June 2022 (ISSN 2070-1721). Editor: Cory Benfield (Apple Inc.). It is the document the RFC Editor currently marks as the active HTTP/2 specification.

2) RFCs it obsoletes: **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** — exactly two.
   - RFC 7540, "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)", Belshe/Peon/Thomson, May 2015 (the original HTTP/2 specification).
   - RFC 8740, "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2", Benjamin, February 2020.

PRIMARY EVIDENCE (verbatim from the fetched records)

- RFC 9113 header block: "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740" — https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html (fetched 2026-11-16T01:24:18Z, sha256 82697578db79). The same "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740" line is carried on the RFC Editor info page and the Datatracker record.
- RFC 9113 Abstract: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." — https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ (sha256 fa8ab6496754) and https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ (sha256 ad12a3569026).
- RFC 9113 Appendix B (Changes from RFC 7540), first bullet: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes." — confirms RFC 8740 is folded in, not merely updated.
- RFC 9113 §11 (IANA Considerations): "This revision of HTTP/2 marks the HTTP2-Settings header field and the h2c upgrade token, both defined in [RFC7540], as obsolete." — consistent with 7540 being superseded.
- Corroboration that RFC 7540 is the superseded original: RFC 7540's own text describes it as an alternative to, but not an obsoleter of, HTTP/1.1 message syntax (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/, sha256 488ead20743d), i.e. it is the base document that RFC 9113 replaces.

HOW TO RE-VERIFY (procedure, ~2 minutes)

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/.
2. In the document header metadata, confirm the line reads exactly `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`. The count must be 2; if any additional number appears, the answer to ask 2 changes accordingly.
3. Confirm there is **no** `Obsoleted by:` line and no `Updated by:` line that would displace RFC 9113 as the current base specification. As of the fetch date 2026-11-16T01:24:18Z, none appeared in the retrieved record.
4. Cross-check the same fields on https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ ("Obsoletes" / "Obsoleted by" / "Updates" boxes). Datatracker and rfc-editor.org are generated from the same RFC metadata and must agree.
5. Do not accept secondary sources (vendor docs, Wikipedia, MDN) as authoritative for the obsoletes relationship; use them only as sanity checks.

SCOPE NOTES AND DISAMBIGUATION (what is deliberately NOT in the answer)

- "Obsoletes" vs "updates": the answer counts only the formal `Obsoletes:` relationship. RFC 9113's relationship to RFC 7540/8740 is obsolescence (full replacement), not an update. This is why the answer is a set of two, not a longer list.
- HPACK: RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2) is **not** obsoleted by RFC 9113 and is **not** part of the answer to ask 2. RFC 9113 continues to reference HPACK as a separate, still-current companion specification. Anyone reading "HTTP/2 specification" broadly should treat RFC 9113 (framing/connection/streams/TLS) + RFC 7541 (field compression) as the pair — but only RFC 9113 answers ask 1, and RFC 7541 is not in the ask-2 set.
- Extensions: documents such as RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2) and other HTTP/2 extensions were not obsoleted by RFC 9113 either; they remain in force on top of the base specification. They are excluded from ask 2. (Worth a glance at each one's own "Updates:" header if the reader needs the full dependency picture; that is outside the two asks.)
- HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) does not obsolete HTTP/2; it is a separate protocol. It is excluded.
- Date sensitivity: "current" is asserted as of the source fetch time, 2026-11-16T01:24:18Z. RFC statuses change only when a new RFC is published with an `Obsoletes:` line naming 9113; the step-3 check above is the guard. Errata against RFC 9113, if any are recorded, correct text but do not alter the obsoletes relationship and do not change either answer.
- RFC 7540's own `Obsoletes:` list (i.e. what the 2015 document itself superseded) is a separate historical question and is not part of either ask; the retrieved passages do not show that header, so nothing is asserted about it here.

ONE-LINE CITABLE FORM

RFC 9113 (June 2022) is the current HTTP/2 specification; per its own header and abstract it obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ ("Obsoletes: 7540, 8740").

(The last three rows are outside the two asks; they are included so the table is complete and so the age bands are unambiguous. Arithmetic check: 12.21 + 0.50 = 12.71; 10.00 + 0.85 = 10.85; 7.55 + 0.45 = 8.00; 10.66 + 0.44 = 11.10.)

Sources and currency

- Primary (law): The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357, made 19 March 2026, in force 1 April 2026 — legislation.gov.uk, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/made. Reg. 2(2) and reg. 2(3)(a); Explanatory Note.
- GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage rates' (the operational rates page): April 2026 row shows 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85 — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates.
- Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026', published 1 April 2026 — confirms £12.71 (21+) and £10.85 (18–20), and records that the increases follow LPC recommendations made in October 2025, accepted by the Government at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025.
- Low Pay Commission, 'Minimum wage rates for 2026', published 26 November 2025 — the Government accepted the LPC's recommendations in full.
- GOV.UK press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', published 1 April 2026.

Chain of authority: LPC recommended (27 October 2025) → Government accepted in full (announced 26 November 2025) → SI 2026/357 made (19 March 2026) → in force (1 April 2026). The figure to rely on is the one in the statutory instrument; the gov.uk pages agree with it.

Points of confusion to avoid

- Statutory National Living Wage vs the 'Real Living Wage'. £12.71 is the statutory NLW, enforced by HMRC and payable by all employers. The Real Living Wage is a separate voluntary benchmark set by the Living Wage Foundation on a different methodology and different annual timetable. It is not the answer to this question and the two must not be conflated in payroll or communications.
- 'National Living Wage' vs 'National Minimum Wage'. The NLW is simply the top band of the NMW, for workers aged 21 and over. The 18–20 rate is an NMW rate and is sometimes loosely called 'the minimum wage for young workers' — it is £10.85, not £12.71, and not the apprentice rate.
- Age threshold history: the NLW age threshold was 25 before April 2021, 23 from April 2021, and 21 from April 2024. It is 21 for the April 2026 rates.
- Apprentices aged 21+ in the first year of their apprenticeship, or aged under 19, are on the apprentice rate (£8.00), not the NLW; apprentices aged 19+ who have completed the first year move to the rate for their age (£12.71 if 21+).
- Accommodation offset: £11.10 per day is the maximum an employer may deduct (or count) for providing living accommodation; it is a daily figure, not hourly.

Forward look (outside the scope of this answer, given only to prevent mis-dating): the GOV.UK rates page also lists rates for April 2027 — 21 and over £13.21, 18 to 20 £11.27, under 18 £8.31, apprentice £8.31. Those are not the April 2026 rates and must not be used for the 2026–27 tax year.

Scope and caveats

- This covers the headline hourly rates only. It does not address apprentice/under-18 entitlements in detail, salary sacrifice and deductions, uniform and tool allowances, time-recording and 'time work' rules, or employer eligibility — all of which can change what must actually be paid.
- Rates are set annually with effect from 1 April. Anyone relying on these figures for a pay run after 31 March 2027 should re-check the then-current statutory instrument.

question: M11
answer:
# FMCSA Short-Haul Exception (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — Operational Limits

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Radius within which the driver must operate, measured from the normal work reporting location | **150 air miles** (the regulation's own equivalent: 172.6 statute miles / 277.8 km) |
| 2 | Consecutive hours within which the driver must return and be released from work | **14 consecutive hours** |

Both figures are from the exception that relieves the driver of the record-of-duty-status requirement, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), as currently in force.

## 2. Controlling regulatory text

> **§ 395.1(e) Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver.** A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
> (i) The driver operates within a **150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles)** of the normal work reporting location;
> (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, **returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours**;
> (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
> (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
> (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) the time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) the total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) the time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) the total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.

Corroborated by FMCSA's Summary of Hours of Service Regulations and the FMCSA HOS Visor Card: "A driver is exempt from the requirements of §395.8 and §395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours... must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours."

## 3. How each figure is measured

**Radius (150 air miles).**
- The unit is **air miles**, not road/statute miles: 1 air mile = 6,076 ft vs 5,280 ft for a statute mile (factor 1.15076). 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles = 277.8 km. This is the regulation's own conversion and must be used verbatim; do not substitute a road-mile or drive-distance ring.
- The center point is the **normal work reporting location** — the location where the driver reports to and is released from work — not the carrier's terminal generically and not the driver's home.
- The constraint applies to the **whole operation for the day**, not merely to driving: the vehicle and driver must remain inside the 150 air-mile ring at all times during the duty tour (the text is "the driver operates within," not "the driver drives within").
- Air miles are straight-line (great-circle) distance; a routing/geofence implementation should compute geodesic distance from the geocoded reporting location and compare against 150 air miles, not against accumulated odometer miles.

**Release limit (14 consecutive hours).**
- The clock is **consecutive hours**, running from the moment the driver comes on duty. It is the same 14-hour construct as the 395.3(a)(2) driving window: off-duty time taken inside the tour does **not** pause or extend it.
- Two events must both occur inside the 14 hours: the driver must **return to the work reporting location** and be **released from work** there. A driver who returns at hour 13 but is not released until hour 15 fails the condition; so does a driver released at hour 13 at a location other than the reporting location.
- The exception is a **RODS exception only** (it exempts from §§ 395.8 and 395.11). It does **not** exempt the driver from the underlying limits in § 395.3: the 11-hour driving limit, the 14-hour driving window, the 60/70-hour limit, and the 10-consecutive-hour off-duty requirement (property-carrying) all still apply, and the 10 hours off duty must separate each 14 hours on duty.
- Passenger-carrying drivers under (e)(1) need **8** consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty, not 10.
- A **driver-salesperson** is carved out of the (e)(1)(ii) release condition by the words "except a driver-salesperson" and is addressed by a separate provision in § 395.1. The 150 air-mile radius condition still reads on its face without that carve-out.
- Qualifying drivers under (e)(1) or (e)(2) are also not subject to the 30-minute break requirement of § 395.3(a)(3)(ii), per FMCSA guidance.

## 4. Distinguishing the neighboring provisions (do not cross-apply)

| Provision | Who / what | Radius | Time limit | Exempts from RODS? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **§ 395.1(e)(1)** — 150 air-mile radius driver | Any CDL or non-CDL driver of a property- or passenger-carrying CMV | **150 air miles** | **Released within 14 consecutive hours** | **Yes** (§§ 395.8, 395.11) |
| § 395.1(e)(2) — non-CDL property-carrying | Only property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL; driver must return to the reporting location at the end of each duty tour | 150 air miles | No driving after the **14th** hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days, and after the **16th** hour on 2 days of any 7 consecutive days | Yes (§§ 395.3(a)(2), 395.8, 395.11) |
| § 395.1(o) — 16-hour exception | Property-carrying; requires return to and release at the reporting location for the previous 5 duty tours, and no use in the previous 6 consecutive days | n/a | Released within **16** hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty | No — extends the window only |
| § 395.1(p) — motion picture production sites | Property or passenger transport to/from a theatrical or TV production site | **100 air miles** | Separate driving limits | No — exempts from § 395.3(a) only |

**Superseded values — flagged for anyone working from an older FMCSA PDF.** The 2015 and 2016 editions of FMCSA's *Interstate Truck Driver's Guide to Hours of Service* and FMCSA's New Entrant pages still print the pre-2020 figures for this exception: **100 air miles and 12 consecutive hours**. The 2020 hours-of-service final rule (published June 2020, effective September 29, 2020) amended § 395.1(e)(1) to 150 air miles and 14 hours. Any compliance document, geofence, or dispatch rule built on 100/12 is stale. The correct current pair is **150 / 14**; a mixed pair (150 with 12, or 100 with 14) matches no version of the rule and should be rejected on sight.

## 5. Correction to a common assumption

The short-haul exception at **(e)(1) has no day-count cap**. There is no rule limiting how many days in a rolling period a driver may use (e)(1), provided the 150 air-mile radius, the 14-consecutive-hour return-and-release, the applicable 10- or 8-hour off-duty separation, and the carrier's 6-month time records are all satisfied, and provided the driver still respects the 60/70-hour limit (with the 34-hour restart available under § 395.3(c)). The "5 days at 14 / 2 days at 16" day-count structure belongs to **(e)(2)**, and the "once every 7 consecutive days" structure belongs to **(o)**. Applying a day-count cap to (e)(1) would over-restrict lawful operations.

## 6. Conditions checklist for a carrier asserting (e)(1)

1. Driver operates entirely within 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location. [ ]
2. Driver returns to that location and is released from work there within 14 consecutive hours of coming on duty (driver-salespersons excepted). [ ]
3. Property-carrying: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty. Passenger-carrying: at least 8. [ ]
4. Carrier maintains and retains for 6 months accurate and true time records of: report-for-duty time each day, total hours on duty each day, release-from-duty time each day, and — for drivers used for the first time or intermittently — the total time for the preceding 7 days per § 395.8(j)(2). [ ]
5. Driver still complies with § 395.3 (11-hour driving, 14-hour window, 60/70-hour). [ ]

## 7. Failure handling

If on a given day the driver exceeds 150 air miles or is not returned and released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception simply does not apply for that day — the driver is not thereby in violation of the hours-of-service rules, but must complete a record of duty status for that day (FMCSA guidance, § 395.1(e) Q&A). The carrier should treat any excursion as a signal to switch that day to full RODS/ELD, not as an automatic violation.

## 8. Scope of this answer

This states the **federal interstate** rule in 49 CFR 395.1(e) as currently in force. It does not address state intrastate hours-of-service rules, which may set different radii or release periods, nor Canadian or Mexican rules. It also does not address the separate (e)(2), (o), or (p) provisions except to distinguish them above.

**Sources:** 49 CFR 395.1(e), eCFR (current) and govinfo CFR 2024/2025 editions; FMCSA *Summary of Hours of Service Regulations*; FMCSA HOS Visor Card (FMCSA-MCE-20-009); FMCSA *Interstate Truck Driver's Guide to Hours of Service* (2022 revision, and the superseded 2015/2016 editions cited only to identify the stale 100/12 figures).
cautions: The recompute vote reached no majority on ask 2; that part of the answer was not compared.

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.1 and 8 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2024-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2024-title49-vol5-sec395-1.xml. The first reads: "(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 5 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.1 and 2 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2024-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2024-title49-vol5-sec395-1.xml. The first reads: "(A) After the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 14 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.1 and 12 on ai.fmcsa.dot.gov/test/newentrant/mc/content.aspx?nav=logs. The first reads: "(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;"

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT AND OCCUPANT LIMITS (14 CFR 61.113(i), as amended)

Governing authority. BasicMed is the alternate qualification under 14 CFR 61.113(i), enacted by section 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (FESSA) and codified in the note to 49 U.S.C. 44703. Section 828(a)(4) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63) amended FESSA 2307(j) to enlarge the 'covered aircraft' envelope and amended 2307(a)(8)(A) to enlarge the passenger limit. Those statutory changes were self-implementing on 12 November 2024; the FAA conformed the regulation in the final rule published at 89 FR (doc. FAA-2024-26935, 18 November 2024) and issued Notice N 8000.386 dated 14 November 2024. All three answers below reflect the post-12-November-2024 rule, which is the rule in force.

THE THREE ANSWERS

1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 lb (maximum takeoff weight; for a type-certificated aircraft, the maximum certificated takeoff weight shown on the type certificate data sheet / design approval). Preamble: 'a covered aircraft ... has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds'; FAA BasicMed page, Aircraft Requirements: 'Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds.' Note the regulation itself omits the word 'certificated' (deliberately, so that experimental aircraft — which are not type certificated — can qualify); the metric is the aircraft's approved maximum takeoff weight, not the actual weight on a given flight. Up from 6,000 lb.

2. Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7. The test is the aircraft's authorized capacity under Federal law (its design approval — TC, STC, or ATC; for experimental aircraft, the operator's stated maximum per 14 CFR 91.319(j)), not the number of seats installed. Preamble: 'a covered aircraft may now be authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flight crewmembers)'; FAA BasicMed page: 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants.' Up from 6.

3. Passengers on board: 6. Preamble: 'and may be operating with up to 6 passengers on board'; FAA BasicMed page, Operating Requirements: 'Carries not more than six passengers.' Up from 5.

HOW THE THREE FIT TOGETHER
- The occupant figure (7) is a property of the aircraft; the passenger figure (6) is a limit on the flight. An aircraft authorized for 8 occupants does not become a covered aircraft merely because two seats are removed — the authorized count must be reduced by a new design approval (STC or amended TC). Conversely an aircraft authorized for 7 may fly with any mix of crew and passengers, but the non-crew count may not exceed 6.
- The passenger limit is derived by subtracting required flight crew from the occupant limit: 7 occupants − 1 required pilot = 6 passengers. In an aircraft type certificated for two flight crewmembers, the practical passenger maximum is 7 − 2 = 5.
- The weight and occupant tests are applied independently; both must be satisfied on the same aircraft.

EXCLUSION ADDED IN 2024. Transport category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under 14 CFR part 29 are excluded from the covered-aircraft definition regardless of weight or seat count (preamble: section 828(a)(4) 'added a third provision ... to exclude transport category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under part 29').

COMPANION OPERATING LIMITS (stated so the answer is not misleadingly partial; 14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)–(3))
- At or below 18,000 ft MSL.
- Indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots.
- Within the United States, or within another country in which BasicMed is authorized.
- Not for compensation or hire.
- VFR or IFR both permitted.
- The limits apply to the whole flight: a pilot operating under BasicMed may not act as PIC at any point in a flight that exceeds them, even if another pilot aboard holds a medical certificate and acts as PIC for part of it.

SUPERSEDED VALUES — DO NOT USE (shown only so stale sources are recognizable)
| Item | Pre-12-Nov-2024 | Current |
| Maximum takeoff weight | 6,000 lb | 12,500 lb |
| Occupants authorized | 6 | 7 |
| Passengers on board | 5 | 6 |
Sources still carrying the old numbers: AC 68-1A (3.2, 5.1.2, 5.2.1) and the July/August 2017 FAA Safety Briefing. Notice N 8000.386 states both sets explicitly, applying the new set 'on or after November 12, 2024'.

CITATIONS FOR VERIFICATION
- FAA, 'FAA Updates BasicMed Program' (15 Nov 2024): passenger limit 6 (from 5), occupants 7 (from 6), takeoff weight 12,500 lb (from 6,000 lb), excluding transport category helicopters.
- 89 FR, doc. 2024-26935 (18 Nov 2024), section B (Covered Aircraft Requirements) and section C (Passengers in Covered Aircraft).
- FAA BasicMed program page, 'Aircraft Requirements' and 'Operating Requirements'.
- FAA Notice N 8000.386 (14 Nov 2024), para. 5a (aircraft requirements, both before and on/after 12 Nov 2024) and 5b (flight requirements).

SCOPE NOTE (compliance). This is a restatement of the Federal aviation-medical operating limits; it is not a determination for a specific pilot, aircraft, or flight. State-law, insurer, employer, or club/rental restrictions can be more restrictive and are outside the scope of what was asked. Whether a particular aircraft meets the occupant test requires its type certificate data sheet or other design approval, which must be checked aircraft by aircraft.
