Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 6000 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/fr-2024-11-18/html/2024-26935.htm and 12500 on faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med. The first reads: "certificated takeoff weight of not more than 6,000 pounds."

question: M3
answer:
# Hours of service for a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach) — US federal rules

## Scope and authority

Governing rule: **49 CFR § 395.5, "Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles"** (Subpart A of Part 395, FMCSA), promulgated at 70 FR 50073 (Aug. 25, 2005) and unchanged in the current eCFR text. It applies "[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1."

Basis of scope: the request specifies a *passenger-carrying* commercial motor vehicle (motorcoach). Passenger-carrying and property-carrying CMVs are governed by different limits — § 395.5 (passenger) versus § 395.3 (property) — so the property-carrying figures (11-hour driving / 10-hour off-duty reset / 14-hour on-duty window) are **not** the answers here and should not be substituted. The figures below assume a driver subject to the standard rule set, with no § 395.1 exception invoked.

## The three answers

| # | Question | Answer | Regulatory text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** following 8 consecutive hours off duty | § 395.5(a)(1): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, "[m]ore than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty does the limit reset? | **8 consecutive hours off duty** | § 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2), both of which run "following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | **15 hours** on duty following 8 consecutive hours off duty | § 395.5(a)(2): no driving "[f]or any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |

Short form: **10 hours driving / 8 consecutive hours off duty to reset / 15 hours on duty.**

## How the three limits interact

- Driving time is a subset of on-duty time. The 10 driving hours must be consumed **within** the 15-hour on-duty window that opens after the 8 consecutive hours off duty. The 15-hour clock is elapsed on-duty time, not driving time, so non-driving on-duty work (loading, inspections, paperwork, waiting in readiness for work, compensated work for a non-motor carrier) burns the window without adding driving hours.
- The two prongs are independent stop conditions: driving must cease at whichever comes first — 10 hours of driving accumulated, or the 15th hour on duty.
- The 8-hour reset restarts both clocks together. There is no separate reset for the driving limit versus the on-duty limit.
- **Worked example.** Driver comes on duty at 06:00 after 8 consecutive hours off duty. The 15-hour window closes at 21:00; no driving is permitted at or after 21:00 regardless of how few driving hours were used. Within that window, driving may not exceed 10 hours. If the driver accumulates 10 driving hours at 19:00, driving stops at 19:00 even though 2 hours of the on-duty window remain. The driver may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty have been taken.
- **Additional cumulative gate (context, not the answer to ask 3).** § 395.5(b) separately bars driving after the driver has been on duty **60 hours in any 7 consecutive days** (carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week) or **70 hours in any 8 consecutive days** (carrier operates CMVs every day of the week), regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services. A compliant schedule must satisfy the 10-hour, 15-hour, and 60/70-hour limits simultaneously; the 15-hour answer above is the per-shift on-duty bar, and the 60/70-hour limits are a rolling multi-day bar that can stop driving earlier.

## Definitions that drive the calculation

- **On-duty time (§ 395.2)** — "all time from the time a driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work until the time the driver is relieved from work and all responsibilities for performing work." Compensated work for a person who is not a motor carrier also counts as on-duty time. A driver working more than one job of any kind must count that time as on-duty.
- **Off-duty time** — not separately defined in the regulations; in effect it is any time that is not on-duty time.
- **Travel time / "cushioning" (§ 395.1(j))** — travel at the carrier's direction while not driving and not assuming any other responsibility for the carrier counts as on-duty time **unless** the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival at destination, in which case the entire period may be treated as off duty. For relief drivers: if the driver is driven or uses public transportation to a layover point and then takes 8 consecutive hours off duty, the travel time may be recorded as off duty; if the driver drives him/herself in a non-CMV to the layover point, that time is on duty (not driving).

## Exceptions to check before relying on the base numbers

§ 395.5 is expressly "[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1." The base figures above are correct for the standard case; the following can change them or change how the reset is accumulated:

- **Sleeper berth (§ 395.1(g)(3))** — a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth as defined in § 393.76 may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the four requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met. This is a substitute method of accumulating the 8-hour reset, not a relaxation of the 10- or 15-hour limits.
- **Adverse driving conditions and other § 395.1 relief** — the FMCSA passenger-carrier guidance identifies further exceptions under § 395.1 (its passenger brochure references an exception at § 395.1(e)); any claimed exception should be verified against the current § 395.1 text and its conditions before it is relied on. None is assumed in the answers above.
- **Non-business private motor carriers of passengers** are not subject to the Part 395 recordkeeping requirements (logbook / ELD), though the driving limits themselves are stated without that carve-out.

## Records (adjacent obligation, not asked)

Drivers required to keep a record of duty status must do so, and most motor carriers of passengers and their drivers are subject to the ELD rule, including drivers domiciled in Canada or Mexico operating in the United States absent an exception. ELD exceptions include drivers required to prepare a record of duty status no more than 8 days in any 30-day period, driveaway-towaway operations where the vehicle is part of the shipment, and vehicles manufactured before model year 2000. Motor carriers of passengers must use only ELDs self-certified and registered on FMCSA's website.

## Answer as it would be stated to the driver

> You may drive **10 hours** after taking **8 consecutive hours off duty**. You may not drive **after you have been on duty 15 hours** following those 8 consecutive hours off duty. You also may not drive after **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days** (carrier not operating every day) or **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days** (carrier operating every day).

## Currency note

Text confirmed against the current eCFR § 395.5 and corroborated by the FMCSA "Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers" guidance and the FMCSA Motor Carrier Safety Planner § 6.4.3 as of 2026-11-16. The three figures have been stable since the 2005 rulemaking; verify against eCFR before relying on them for enforcement-sensitive work.

question: M5
answer:
# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135

## 1. Answer

| Ask | Requirement | Value | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum scheduled rest period owed to a flight attendant after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **9 consecutive hours** | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2 | That rest period may be scheduled or reduced to | **8 consecutive hours**, conditioned on a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

Applies to a Part 135 certificate holder that uses flight attendants, in on-demand (unscheduled) charter as well as scheduled operations — 135.273 is not limited to scheduled operations.

## 2. Controlling rule text (14 CFR 135.273)

> (b)(1) Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours.
>
> (b)(2) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
>
> (b)(3) The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
>
> (b)(10) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section.
>
> (b)(11) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period.

FAA public guidance states the same rule in plain language: "if you have a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, you must have at least nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest after your duty period before you have another duty period. However, under certain circumstances, our regulations allow a rest period of only eight consecutive hours. If your employer schedules you for an eight hour rest period, your next rest period must be at least 10 consecutive hours and must begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the eight hour rest period." (FAA, "What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?")

## 3. The 8-hour reduction is conditional — all four elements must hold

A reduced rest is lawful only if every one of the following is satisfied:

1. **Floor of 8, never lower.** The rest may be "scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours." Eight is the absolute floor for a duty period of 14 hours or less; 7 hours 59 minutes is not authorized by this section under any condition.
2. **A subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours** must actually be provided (not merely planned as a possibility).
3. **That subsequent rest must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.** The clock starts at the *beginning of the reduced rest*, not at the end of the duty period and not at the end of the reduced rest.
4. **The subsequent rest must fall between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period** — i.e., a genuine ground rest block, not time overlapping duty, deadhead, positioning, training, or administrative work.

Additional hard limits that travel with any reduced-rest schedule:

- **135.273(b)(10):** no duty period may be assigned at all unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section.
- **135.273(b)(11):** no duty of any kind — flight, deadhead, ground positioning, training, paperwork, phone contact that constitutes duty under the operator's manual — may be assigned during a required rest period. A "rest period" interrupted by duty is not rest.
- The rest must be **consecutive**; it cannot be assembled from fragments.

## 4. Worked example (shows the 24-hour trigger)

- **Base case:** Scheduled duty Day 1 ends 2100. Required rest = 9 consecutive hours, 2100 Day 1 → 0600 Day 2. Earliest subsequent duty start: 0600 Day 2.
- **Reduced case:** Scheduled duty Day 1 ends 2100. Operator schedules 8 consecutive hours of rest, 2100 Day 1 → 0500 Day 2. Duty Day 2 may begin 0500 Day 2.
  - The subsequent rest must **begin no later than 2100 Day 2** (24 hours after 2100 Day 1, the start of the reduced rest) and must be **at least 10 consecutive hours**.
  - Compliant construction: Duty Day 2 runs 0500–2030 Day 2; subsequent rest 2030 Day 2 → 0630 Day 3 (10 hours, begins 30 minutes inside the 24-hour limit).
  - Non-compliant construction: Duty Day 2 runs 0500–2300 Day 2; the subsequent rest cannot begin until 2300 Day 2, which is 26 hours after the reduced rest began — the reduction was therefore never available, and the original 9-hour rest was owed.

## 5. Applicability checks before relying on these figures

1. **Does the operation actually use flight attendants?** 135.273 governs certificate holders conducting Part 135 operations who utilize flight attendants. If a given aircraft/configuration does not require and does not carry a flight attendant, there is no flight attendant to rest and this section generates no rest obligation for that leg.
2. **Has the operator made a 135.273(c) election?** Section 135.273(c) permits a certificate holder, under written procedures approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in its operations specifications, to apply the Part 135 subpart F **flight crewmember** flight time, duty, and rest requirements to its flight attendants instead. If such an election is in effect, the 9/8 figures above do **not** govern; the applicable crew-member scheme (135.265 for scheduled operations, 135.267 for unscheduled operations) does. Confirm against the operator's ops specs and manual before applying this memo.
3. **Any exemption, deviation, or special authorization?** None is assumed here. An FAA-granted exemption or ops-spec authorization could alter the requirement and must be checked.
4. **"Scheduled" vs. actual.** Section 135.273(b)(2)-(3) constrain what the certificate holder may *schedule/assign*. If actual duty runs beyond the scheduled duty period and exceeds 14 hours, the analysis moves to 135.273(b)(4)-(7), which carry different rest figures and are outside the scope of this memo. The 9/8 answer is correct only for a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less.

## 6. Common errors this memo is written to prevent

- Treating 8 hours as freely available rest. It is available **only** with the paired 10-hour compensatory rest, correctly timed.
- Measuring the 24-hour window from the end of duty or the end of the reduced rest instead of from the **start** of the reduced rest.
- Scheduling the 10-hour compensatory rest to begin after the 24-hour deadline, which retroactively invalidates the 8-hour rest.
- Assigning any duty (deadhead, training, calls) inside a required rest period, contrary to 135.273(b)(11).
- Importing Part 121 flight attendant figures (121.467) or Part 135 flight crewmember figures (135.265/135.267) without confirming whether a 135.273(c) election is in force.

## 7. Self-verification of the stated values

- 9 consecutive hours is the base requirement for a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less — 135.273(b)(2). ✔
- 8 consecutive hours is the permitted reduction, and 8 < 9, so it is a genuine reduction and not a mislabeled base figure — 135.273(b)(3). ✔
- The compensatory rest is 10 consecutive hours, which is greater than the 9-hour base, consistent with the rule's structure. ✔
- The 24-hour trigger is stated as running from the beginning of the reduced rest period, matching the rule text, and the worked example places the subsequent rest inside that window. ✔
- No figure is stated for duty periods exceeding 14 hours, so no value in this memo conflicts with an unverified threshold. ✔

## 8. Bottom line for the operator

Schedule **at least 9 consecutive hours** of rest between the end of any scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less and the start of the next duty period. You may schedule or reduce that to **8 consecutive hours** only if you also give the flight attendant a subsequent rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours** that begins **no later than 24 hours after the start of the 8-hour rest** — and no duty of any kind may be assigned during either rest period.

question: M7
answer:
TECHNICAL NOTE — CURRENT HTTP/2 SPECIFICATION AND ITS OBSOLESCENCE SET

1. ANSWERS

Ask 1 — Current specification of HTTP/2: RFC 9113.
  Title:      Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)
  Editors:    M. Thomson (Ed.), Mozilla; C. Benfield (Ed.), Apple Inc.
  Date:       June 2022
  Category:   Standards Track (Proposed Standard; not yet an Internet Standard)
  Stream:     IETF
  ISSN:       2070-1721
  Canonical:  https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113
  Also at:    https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113 (HTML)
              https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html (HTTPWG copy)

Ask 2 — RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113: exactly two — RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.
  RFC 7540 — Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2), R. Peon and M. Belshe (Eds.), May 2015, Standards Track. This was the original HTTP/2 specification.
  RFC 8740 — Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2, D. Benjamin, February 2020, Standards Track. This was a narrow update to RFC 7540 adding TLS 1.3 guidance; its content is folded into RFC 9113 (Section 9.2), so the standalone document is retired.

Both facts come from a single authoritative field: the RFC 9113 header block, which reads "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740" and whose Abstract states "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." The same header block supplies the answer to Ask 1 (RFC 9113 is the document bearing that header). There is no inference step between the two answers.

2. OBSOLESCENCE CHAIN

  RFC 7540 (May 2015, HTTP/2)
      |  updated by (not obsoleted by)
  RFC 8740 (Feb 2020, TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2)
      |
      |  both obsoleted together by
      v
  RFC 9113 (Jun 2022, HTTP/2)   <-- current specification

Note the direction of the RFC 8740 relationship: RFC 8740 *updated* RFC 7540; it did not obsolete it. RFC 9113 then obsoletes both at once, because it merges the TLS 1.3 requirements into the main text and reissues the whole specification. Anyone who answers Ask 2 as "only RFC 7540" (the 'HTTP/2 predecessor' reading) is wrong against the header; anyone who answers "RFC 7540 and everything that referenced it" is also wrong, because obsolescence is not transitive through references.

3. WHAT RFC 9113 DOES *NOT* OBSOLETE (guard against over-broad answers)

  - RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2, May 2015): NOT obsoleted. RFC 9113 cites it normatively as [COMPRESSION]; HPACK remains the header-compression scheme for HTTP/2.
  - RFC 7301 (TLS ALPN): NOT obsoleted; still the negotiation mechanism HTTP/2 uses.
  - RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching), RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1): siblings published in the same June 2022 revision cycle, not obsoleted by 9113.
  - RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (requirement keywords): referenced, not obsoleted.
  - HTTP/1.1 message syntax: RFC 9113 explicitly states HTTP/2 is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, HTTP/1.1.

4. SUBSTANTIVE CHANGES THAT MOTIVATE THE OBSOLESCENCE (for reviewers who need the 'why')

  - TLS 1.3 support: defined per RFC 8740, which this document obsoletes (Appendix B).
  - Priority: the RFC 7540 priority scheme (PRIORITY frame, HEADERS priority fields) is deprecated. Frame formats and mandatory handling are retained for interoperability; the semantics remain described only in RFC 7540 Section 5.3. The successor scheme is RFC 9218 (Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP).
  - HTTP/1.1 Upgrade to h2c: removed from the specification; the h2c upgrade token and the HTTP2-Settings header field are registered as obsolete (Sections 3.1 and 11). Prior-knowledge h2c remains.
  - Experimental-use codepoint ranges for frame types and settings are opened to normal registration policy.

5. SCOPE, PROVENANCE AND CAVEATS

  - Definition of 'current' used here: the most recent Standards Track RFC specifying HTTP/2 as of the sources consulted (fetched 2026-11-16). This is not a project-pinned version; if a consumer pins an older revision, RFC 7540 remains the governing text for that pin.
  - 'Obsoletes' is read strictly as the explicit obsoletes-list in the RFC 9113 header, not as transitive obsolescence and not as 'documents superseded in practice'.
  - Errata: verified errata exist against HTTP/2 RFCs and should be consulted at https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata_search.php?rfc=9113 before treating the text as normative for implementation. Errata correct text; they do not change the RFC number or the obsoletes-list.
  - Drafts: draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis-* is the pre-publication draft of RFC 9113 (e.g., -02, June 2021, header "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740 (if approved)"). It is superseded by RFC 9113 and must not be cited as the current specification.
  - Successor check: no RFC obsoleting or replacing RFC 9113 appears in any consulted source; the HTTPWG copy at httpwg.org still serves RFC 9113 as the current HTTP/2 spec. A later revision would surface as a new 'Obsoletes: 9113' header — re-verify against https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 before relying on this answer far from the 2026-11-16 retrieval date.

6. ONE-LINE CITABLE FORM

  "HTTP/2 is specified by RFC 9113 (June 2022, Standards Track), which obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740."

# UK National Living Wage and National Minimum Wage — rates effective from April 2026

## Direct answers

| # | Question | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Annual increase |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | National Living Wage, workers aged 21 and over | **£12.71 per hour** | +£0.50 (+4.1%) |
| 2 | National Minimum Wage, 18–20 Year Old Rate | **£10.85 per hour** | +£0.85 (+8.5%) |

Both figures are **confirmed, announced rates** — not forecasts or projections. They take effect on **1 April 2026** and apply until 31 March 2027.

## Full April 2026 rate table (for context and to prevent band confusion)

| NMW rate | From 1 April 2026 | Increase (£) | Increase (%) | Previous (April 2025 – March 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £0.50 | 4.1 | £12.21 |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £0.85 | 8.5 | £10.00 |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 | £7.55 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 | £7.55 |
| Accommodation Offset (daily limit) | £11.10 | £0.44 | 4.1 | £10.66 |

**Out of scope — do not confuse:** the same GOV.UK rates page also lists indicative **April 2027** rates (21+ £13.21; 18–20 £11.27; under-18 £8.31; apprentice £8.31). Those are not the answer to this question and are shown here only so the two years are not mixed up.

## Status and provenance

- **Announced:** 26 November 2025 by the Government, accepting in full the Low Pay Commission's recommendations (LPC advice submitted October 2025).
- **In force:** from 1 April 2026; the LPC's impact report *The National Minimum Wage in 2026* was published 1 April 2026.
- **Authority:** GOV.UK / Low Pay Commission. The same two numbers (£12.71 and £10.85) appear identically in four separate GOV.UK locations, so there is no source conflict to reconcile:
  1. LPC press release, *LPC recommendations take the National Living Wage to £12.71*, 26 Nov 2025 — https://www.gov.uk/government/news/lpc-recommendations-take-the-national-living-wage-to-1271
  2. LPC, *Minimum wage rates for 2026* (advice to Government), 26 Nov 2025 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026
  3. LPC, *The National Minimum Wage in 2026*, 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026
  4. GOV.UK, *National Minimum Wage rates* (live rates table) — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates

## Applicability notes

- **Age band structure is unchanged for April 2026.** The NLW applies to workers aged **21 and over** (the threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and 23 to 21 in April 2024). Workers aged 20 and under remain on the age-related NMW rates. A separate 18–20 Year Old Rate therefore still exists for the whole of 2026/27.
- **Forward look (not part of the answer):** the LPC has set out a path to extend the NLW to 20-year-olds in **2027** and to 18- and 19-year-olds in **2028 or 2029**, subject to economic conditions and government policy. Anyone using these figures for multi-year planning should treat the 18–20 band as time-limited, but it is fully in force for April 2026.
- **Gap between the two rates:** £10.85 is **85.4%** of £12.71 — the gap narrowed from 81.9% in April 2025 (£10.00 / £12.21) but the rates are not aligned.
- **Regional scope:** these are UK-wide statutory rates; no regional or devolved variation applies.
- **Gross headline rates:** the figures are the statutory hourly minimums before tax, NI and pension deductions. The only permitted offset relevant here is the **accommodation offset** (£11.10 per day maximum for April 2026), which is a separate limit, not an adjustment to the hourly rates above.
- **Apprentice carve-out:** apprentices aged under 19, or aged 19+ in the first year of their apprenticeship, are entitled to the Apprentice Rate (£8.00), not the NLW/age rate — even if they are 21 or over. Once they are 19+ and have completed the first year, the full rate for their age applies.

## Verification procedure (how to re-confirm before relying on this)

1. Open https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates and locate the row labelled **April 2026** in the 'Current rates' table; read the '21 and over' and '18 to 20' columns. Expect **£12.71** and **£10.85**.
2. Cross-check against the statutory instrument commenced 1 April 2026 (the annual National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations for that uprating) if a legal citation is needed rather than a guidance citation.
3. Confirm the page has not been superseded: from 1 April 2027 the current-rates row rolls forward to April 2027 (£13.21 / £11.27), at which point the April 2026 figures move into the 'Previous rates' section — they remain correct for the 2026/27 year but would no longer be the live rate.
4. If any source disagrees with £12.71 / £10.85 for the 1 April 2026 uprating, treat GOV.UK and the LPC publications as authoritative over press summaries and re-check for a correction notice.

**Bottom line: £12.71/hour for workers aged 21 and over, and £10.85/hour for 18–20 year olds, both effective 1 April 2026.**

question: M11
answer:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION — THE TWO QUALIFYING THRESHOLDS
Governing provision: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), '150 air-mile radius driver' (current eCFR text, verified against the FMCSA Hours-of-Service summary page and FMCSA short-haul training materials).

ANSWERS
1. Radius: the driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation parenthetically equates this to 172.6 statute miles. This is an air-mile (great-circle) measure, not road miles; a route that stays under 172.6 statute miles of driving distance but exceeds 150 air miles point-to-point from the reporting location is outside the exception.
2. Release: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The clock runs from the time the driver comes on duty; the driver must both physically return to the reporting location and be released there inside that 14-hour window. There is no averaging across days and no extension of the 14-hour release requirement.

VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1))
'(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.'

SCOPE AND APPLICABILITY NOTES (needed to apply the two figures correctly)
- Carrier type: the 150 air-mile / 14-hour pair applies to both property-carrying and passenger-carrying CMV drivers. Carrier type changes only the required off-duty period separating duty periods — 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying, 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying — not the 150-mile radius or the 14-hour release window.
- Driver-salesperson: the release-within-14-hours condition in (e)(1)(ii) is expressly inapplicable to a driver-salesperson; the radius condition still governs.
- Effect of the exception: it exempts the driver from the record-of-duty-status requirement in 395.8 and the supporting-documents requirement in 395.11. It does not exempt the carrier from the 6-month time-record obligation in (e)(1)(iv), which must capture report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time, and (for new or intermittent drivers) the preceding 7 days' totals.
- Exceeding a threshold: if on a given day the driver goes outside the 150 air-mile radius or is not released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception is unavailable for that day and the driver must record duty status for that day (paper log or ELD). FMCSA guidance applies the ELD rule by frequency: 8 or fewer days in the last 30 may be logged on a paper graph grid; more than 8 days in the last 30 requires an ELD for that day.
- Adverse driving conditions do not enlarge the 14-hour release threshold. The adverse-driving-conditions provision extends the driving window and driving time by up to 2 hours, but FMCSA's published short-haul Q&A states that a short-haul driver who cannot return to the reporting location within 14 hours because of an adverse driving condition must record duty status for that day. The 14-hour figure above therefore stands as the operative release threshold.
- Measurement of the reporting location: the location must be the same at the start and end of the shift, but it need not be the same location from shift to shift (FMCSA short-haul Q&A). The radius is measured from that day's normal work reporting location.

PROVISIONS THAT ARE NOT THE ANSWER (flagged to prevent misapplication)
- 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2), property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL: also a 150 air-mile radius and a return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour, but it has no single 'released within X consecutive hours' figure; instead the driver may not drive after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days, or after the 16th hour on 2 of those days. The 14/16-hour driving cutoffs in that provision are not the release threshold asked about here.
- 49 CFR 395.1(o), the 16-hour window for certain property-carrying drivers: a separate exception with its own five-duty-tour precondition; its 16-hour figure is not the short-haul release threshold.
- 49 CFR 395.1(p), motion picture production sites: a 100 air-mile radius provision; not applicable to the short-haul exception.

BOTTOM LINE
A driver qualifies for the RODS-free short-haul exception only if the driver operates within 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location and returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours, while also meeting the applicable consecutive-off-duty requirement and the carrier's 6-month time-record obligation.

The first reads: "(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;"

The first reads: "(A) After the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days;"

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — 14 CFR 61.113(i) (current text, as amended November 2024)

1. ANSWERS

  Ask 1 — Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 pounds (maximum certificated takeoff weight, inclusive ceiling).
  Ask 2 — Occupents the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7 (inclusive ceiling).
  Ask 3 — Passengers on board: 6 (inclusive ceiling).

  Source text (14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), eCFR current / GPO CFR 2025 title 14 vol 2):
  'The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupents, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter.'

2. WHAT EACH NUMBER MEANS (the definitions matter for compliance)

  - Maximum takeoff weight = the aircraft's MAXIMUM CERTIFICATED TAKEOFF WEIGHT under its design approval (TC, STC, or ATC), NOT the actual weight of a given flight. The FAA's BasicMed page states it as 'maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds.' An aircraft whose certificated MTOW is 12,500 lb is inside the rule; 12,501 lb is outside it. A light aircraft flown heavy is a weight-and-balance problem, not a BasicMed eligibility problem.
  - Occupents authorizated = the number the aircraft's design approval permits it to carry, including required flightcrew. It is a property of the aircraft, not of the flight.
  - Passengers on board = the actual count on a given flight, excluding the PIC (and excluding other required flightcrew, who are occupents but not passengers).
  - Arithmetic check: 6 passengers + 1 PIC = 7 occupents — exactly at the ceiling, permitted. The two limits are deliberately set so that a 7-seat aircraft flown by a single PIC can be filled with 6 passengers.
  - Additional, separate disqualifier: a transport-category rotorcraft certificated under part 29 is prohibited regardless of its weight or seat count. This is an independent condition, not a numeric threshold.

3. FULL AIRCRAFT/OPERATING CONDITION SET (§ 61.113(i)(1)–(3)) — for context, the three asked items are items 1–3

  1. Aircraft authorized to carry not more than 7 occupents.
  2. Maximum certificated takeoff weight not more than 12,500 lb.
  3. No more than 6 passengers on board.
  4. Not a transport-category rotorcraft certificated under part 29.
  5. Flight, including each portion, not above 18,000 ft MSL.
  6. Not outside the United States unless authorized by the country concerned.
  7. Not above 250 knots indicated airspeed.
  8. No compensation or hire.
  9. Pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license, meets § 61.23(c)(3), and carries in the logbook the completed § 68.7 CMEC and the § 61.23(c)(3) course-completion certificate.

  Experimental aircraft: § 91.319(j) separately caps BasicMed operation of experimental aircraft at the same occupent ceiling; it should be read consistently with the amended § 61.113(i)(1) figure of 7.

4. VERSION CONTROL — DO NOT APPLY THE OLD NUMBERS

  The FAA's Advisory Circular AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17), quoted in the research fetches, still carries the pre-amendment limits: 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight, 6 occupents, 5 passengers. Those figures were superseded by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 and the FAA's 15 November 2024 update (FAA newsroom, 'FAA Updates BasicMed Program'), which state: passengers increased to six from five, occupents to seven from six, and maximum takeoff weight to 12,500 lb from 6,000 lb, excluding transport-category helicopters. Any checklest, kneeboard card, or self-assessment built on AC 68-1A is out of date and must be corrected to 12,500 lb / 7 occupents / 6 passengers.

5. RESULTING COMPLIANCE STATEMENT

  A flight is within BasicMed aircraft limits if and only if: certificated MTOW ≤ 12,500 lb; design approval authorizes ≤ 7 occupents; actual passengers on board ≤ 6; and the aircraft is not a part 29 transport-category rotorcraft. The three requested values are therefore 12,500 lb, 7 occupents, and 6 passengers, current as of the November 2024 amendment.

question: M3
answer:
# Hours of Service — Driver of a Passenger-Carrying CMV (e.g., Motorcoach), Interstate, US

**Governing rule:** 49 CFR § 395.5, *Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles* (49 CFR Part 395, Subpart A), subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1. Current as published on eCFR and identical in the 2019 printed CFR edition and on FMCSA's own passenger-carrier guidance, so the numbers are stable across editions.

---

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer | Regulatory basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** | § 395.5(a)(1) — no driving "more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty may they drive again? | **8 consecutive hours off duty** | § 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) — both limits are measured from "8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours on duty** | § 395.5(a)(2) — no driving "for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |

### The rule in one sentence
After **8 consecutive hours off duty**, the driver may drive up to **10 hours**, and may not drive at all once **15 hours on duty** have elapsed — whichever comes first ends driving for that shift.

---

## 2. Verbatim regulatory text (§ 395.5)

> **§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.**
> Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:
>
> (a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
>
> (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
>
> (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
>
> (b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—
>
> (1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or
>
> (2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.
>
> [70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005]

---

## 3. How the three limits interlock

The 8-hour off-duty period is a single reset that starts two independent clocks:

- **Driving clock:** 10 hours of driving accumulated after the reset.
- **On-duty clock (the "window"):** 15 consecutive hours measured from coming on duty after the reset.

Both clocks run from the same 8-consecutive-hour off-duty reset. Driving stops at whichever is reached first:

- Driver drives 6 hours, then sits on duty (loading, paperwork, waiting) for 9 hours → **15-hour window expires; no further driving**, even though only 6 of the 10 driving hours were used.
- Driver drives 10 hours within the first 12 hours of the shift → **10-hour driving limit reached; no further driving**, even though 3 hours of the 15-hour window remain.

Neither limit may be exceeded by borrowing from the other. On-duty time that is not driving still consumes the 15-hour window. The regulation does not prescribe a minimum off-duty break *within* the shift for passenger carriers (unlike the 30-minute break in the property-carrying rule at § 395.3(a)(3)(ii)); the only mandatory rest is the 8 consecutive hours between shifts.

---

## 4. Weekly (cumulative) limits — context, not the answer to ask 3

§ 395.5(b) adds a separate cumulative ceiling. These are **not** the 15-hour daily window and should not be conflated with ask 3:

| Carrier operates CMVs… | On-duty ceiling | Rolling period |
|---|---|---|
| Not every day of the week | **60 hours** | any 7 consecutive days |
| Every day of the week | **70 hours** | any 8 consecutive days |

Driving is prohibited after the ceiling is reached, regardless of how much daily driving time remains. The 60/70-hour limits are on-duty hours, not driving hours, and include on-duty-not-driving time.

---

## 5. Common errors this answer is written to prevent

1. **Property-carrying rules substituted for passenger rules.** The property rule, § 395.3, is **11 hours driving / 10 consecutive hours off duty / 14-hour window**, plus a 30-minute break after 8 hours and a 34-hour restart. **None of those apply here.** For passenger-carrying CMVs the figures are **10 / 8 / 15**. The 2019 govinfo PDF snippet in the source set that shows "10 consecutive hours off duty" and "14 consecutive hours" is § 395.3, the *property* rule, and must not be used.
2. **The 34-hour restart.** The 34-hour restart provision in § 395.3(c) belongs to the property-carrying rule; the passenger rule at § 395.5 contains no restart provision. A passenger carrier driver recovers weekly capacity only by the passage of the 7- or 8-day window, not by a 34-hour reset.
3. **The 14 in the short-haul exception.** § 395.1(e) exempts drivers operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released within **14** consecutive hours from the record-of-duty-status requirement. That 14 is a recordkeeping threshold, **not** a driving window. The 15-hour driving prohibition still applies.
4. **Confusing "8 hours off" with "8 hours sleeper berth."** § 395.1(g)(3) permits a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth to accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty using two rest periods meeting § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv). This is a way to *satisfy* the 8-hour reset, not a reduction of it.
5. **Treating off-duty as any non-driving time.** Off-duty time requires the driver to be relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the vehicle, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage, and freight. A driver who remains responsible for the coach or passengers during a meal stop is not off duty.

---

## 6. Exceptions that can move the numbers (§ 395.1)

The base answers above are the general limits. The following are the only common variations; each is stated with its effect on the 10 / 8 / 15 figures:

| Provision | Effect on the three figures |
|---|---|
| § 395.1(b)(1) — adverse driving conditions | The **10-hour driving** and **15-hour on-duty** limits may each be extended by up to **2 hours** (to 12 and 17) when the driver encounters unusually adverse conditions that could not reasonably have been known. It does **not** extend the 60/70-hour limits, and the 8-hour off-duty reset is unchanged. |
| § 395.1(e) — short-haul / 150 air-mile | Recordkeeping exemption only. **10 / 8 / 15 unchanged.** |
| § 395.1(g)(3) — sleeper berth (passenger) | Two rest periods may accumulate the equivalent of the **8 consecutive hours off duty**. The 8-hour figure itself is unchanged. |
| § 395.1(k) — State of Alaska | Allows alternate 20-hour driving/off-duty cycles under specified conditions. Not applicable outside Alaska. |
| § 395.1(h) — State of Hawaii | Special rules; not applicable outside Hawaii. |
| § 395.1(d) — oilfield / § 395.1(m) — construction | Property-oriented special provisions; not applicable to passenger carriers in the ordinary case. |

**Scope caveat.** These are the **federal interstate** limits. A driver operating **intrastate only** is governed by the state's own rules (many states adopt the federal passenger limits by reference, but some do not), and non-business private motor carriers of passengers are exempt from the record-of-duty-status requirement (though not from the driving limits). If the operation is intrastate, the state authority must be checked before relying on 10 / 8 / 15.

---

## 7. One-line compliance check a carrier or dispatcher can apply

For each driver, each shift:

1. Confirm **≥ 8 consecutive hours off duty** immediately before the shift. If not, no driving.
2. Track driving hours; at **10.0 hours of driving**, stop driving.
3. Track elapsed time since coming on duty; at **15.0 hours on duty**, stop driving regardless of driving hours remaining.
4. Track the cumulative on-duty total; at **60 hours in 7 days** (carrier not operating every day) or **70 hours in 8 days** (carrier operating every day), stop driving regardless of 1–3.

Whichever of steps 2, 3, or 4 triggers first ends driving until the applicable reset is satisfied.

question: M5
answer:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — 14 CFR Part 135 flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less

1. SHORT ANSWER

| Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Rest owed after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | At least 9 consecutive hours | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| To what that rest may be reduced | To 8 consecutive hours, but only with a compensatory subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours that begins no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

Both figures are regulatory minimums for a required flight attendant. The 8-hour figure is a hard floor; there is no provision allowing less.

2. WHY THIS RULE GOVERNS

14 CFR 135.261(e) (the applicability section of Part 135 Subpart F) states: "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part." Section 135.273 is therefore not limited to scheduled passenger operations, nor to the 135.265/135.267/135.269 flight-crewmember framework. An on-demand (unscheduled) Part 135 charter operator is squarely within it. The flight-crewmember rest rules in 135.263-135.271 do not supply the answer for cabin crew; 135.273 does.

The rule applies to a "flight attendant," defined in 135.273(a) as an individual, other than a flight crewmember, assigned by the certificate holder in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under its operations specifications, or in addition to that minimum, to duty in an aircraft during flight time, whose duties include cabin-safety responsibilities. If the person is carried but is neither part of the required complement nor assigned cabin-safety duties, 135.273 does not apply — but in that case there is no regulatory rest minimum at all, only company policy.

Part 121 flight attendant rest rules (121.467) do not apply to a Part 135 certificate holder and were not used here.

3. THE TWO PARAGRAPHS, VERBATIM

135.273(b)(1): "Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours."

135.273(b)(2): "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

135.273(b)(3): "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

4. CONDITIONS ATTACHING TO THE 8-HOUR REDUCTION — ALL FOUR MUST BE MET

A reduction from 9 to 8 hours is lawful only if every element below is satisfied. Miss any one and the rest owed is 9 hours.

(a) Floor: the reduced rest is at least 8 consecutive hours. Eight is the minimum; 7 hours 59 minutes is non-compliant.
(b) Compensatory rest: the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours.
(c) Timing: that subsequent rest period is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the BEGINNING (not the end) of the reduced rest period.
(d) Placement: the subsequent rest period occurs between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period — i.e., it is a real, scheduled, logged rest period in the sequence, not a notional credit.

Additional operative constraints in the same section:
- 135.273(b)(10): no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section.
- 135.273(b)(11): no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during any required rest period.
- 135.273(a): "Rest period means the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise." Deadhead travel, positioning, training, phone availability, or any assigned task inside the rest window destroys the rest period.
- Duty period means the elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder.

5. WHAT THE REDUCTION IS NOT (common scheduling errors)

- 135.273(b)(9) does NOT attach to the (b)(3) reduction. Paragraph (b)(9)'s bar on scheduling a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of a reduced rest period is expressly limited to an election to reduce rest to 10 hours "as authorized by paragraph (b)(8)." No equivalent next-day 14-hour cap is imposed by (b)(3). Do not import it into the 8-hour case, and do not drop it from the (b)(8) case.
- The 9-hour and 8-hour figures are for scheduled duty periods of 14 hours or less only. For scheduled duty periods exceeding 14 hours, 135.273(b)(4) through (b)(9) contain a separate regime. Those paragraphs are outside the scope of this question and their figures must not be conflated with 9/8; a scheduler must branch on the duty-period length before applying a rest value.
- "Scheduled" is the trigger. Under 135.273(b)(14), a flight attendant is not considered scheduled for duty in excess of the limitations if the flights were scheduled and normally would terminate within the limitations but, due to circumstances beyond the certificate holder's control (e.g., adverse weather), were not at departure expected to reach destination within the scheduled time. That relieves the duty-period-limit exposure; it does not relieve the rest obligation. The 9-hour (or properly reduced 8-hour) rest is still owed before the next assignment.
- 135.273(c) alternative: a certificate holder may elect, by written procedures applying to all its flight attendants, to apply the Part 135 flight-crewmember flight time and duty/rest requirements to flight attendants (rest facilities on board not required). If such an election is in place, the rest values change to the flight-crewmember scheme (135.265: rest tied to scheduled flight time, reducible under 135.265(c) with compensatory rest). This memo assumes no such election, no OpsSpec deviation, no exemption, and no collective bargaining agreement more restrictive than the regulation. Any of those would have to be checked against the specific certificate.

6. WORKED EXAMPLE

Scheduled duty period ends 2100 local on Day 1.

- Baseline (no reduction): 9 consecutive hours → next duty period may not commence before 0600 Day 2.
- Reduced: rest 2100 Day 1 to 0500 Day 2 (8 consecutive hours). Next duty period 0500-1500 Day 2. The compensatory subsequent rest must be at least 10 consecutive hours and must BEGIN no later than 2100 Day 2 (24 hours after 2100 Day 1, the start of the reduced rest). A rest from 1500 to 0100 Day 3 satisfies both tests: it begins 6 hours inside the deadline and runs exactly 10 consecutive hours.
- Non-compliant variant: next duty 0500-1700 Day 2, rest 1700 Day 2 to 0300 Day 3. The rest is 10 hours but begins at 1700, which is still within the 24-hour window (2100 Day 2 deadline), so this one is actually compliant on timing — the failure mode to watch is a rest that begins after 2100 Day 2, or one that runs only 9 hours.

7. SCHEDULING AND RECORDS PROCEDURE

1) Identify each person as a 135.273 flight attendant (OpsSpecs complement or assigned cabin-safety duties) before applying any rest value.
2) Compute the scheduled duty period (report to release) and branch: 14 hours or less → apply 9 hours; more than 14 hours → apply the separate (b)(4)-(b)(9) regime, not this memo.
3) Default to 9 consecutive hours. Use 8 only as an affirmative, documented election with the 10-hour compensatory rest already placed on the schedule inside the 24-hour window measured from the start of the reduced rest.
4) Verify the rest window contains no duty, no deadhead, no training, no on-call availability, and no required contact — rest means free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.
5) Record, per pairing: scheduled duty start/end, rest start/end, whether reduced, the compensatory rest start/end and the elapsed time from reduced-rest start to compensatory-rest start (must be 24 hours or less). Retain with the crew schedule and duty logs.
6) Re-check after any irregular operation: a delay that pushes the actual duty period past 14 hours does not retroactively authorize the 8-hour rest, and a delay that eats into a scheduled rest requires recomputing from the actual rest obtained.

8. SCOPE AND CAVEATS

This answer assumes the current published text of 14 CFR Part 135 as reflected in the eCFR and the 2025 govinfo compilation, a required flight attendant, no 135.273(c) election, no applicable exemption or OpsSpec relief, and no more-restrictive CBA. Confirm the currency of the regulation and check the specific certificate's operations specifications and any exemptions before relying on it operationally. State, local, or foreign jurisdiction rest requirements are not addressed.

question: M7
answer:
# HTTP/2: current specification and what it obsoletes

## Answer

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, M. Thomson, Ed. and C. Benfield, Ed., Proposed Standard |
| RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113 | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** (exactly two) |

**As of:** the source pages below were retrieved 2026-11-16 (UTC). RFC status can change; re-check the RFC Editor info page for RFC 9113 before relying on this in a dated document.

## 1. The current specification: RFC 9113

Evidence (primary, RFC Editor):

- `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/` — header block reads: "RFC 9113: HTTP/2 … June 2022. M. Thomson, Ed., C. Benfield, Ed. Proposed Standard".
- `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/` — banner: "This RFC is now obsoleted, see RFC 9113."
- The RFC Editor's HTTP/2 subject page (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/`) lists 9113 as the HTTP/2 core document, with 7540 shown only in its historical role.

So the replacement chain for the core document is **RFC 7540 (May 2015) → RFC 9113 (June 2022)**, and 9113 is the current one. Note the maturity level: 9113 is a **Proposed Standard**, not a full Internet Standard — do not describe it as "the HTTP/2 standard (STD)" in downstream text.

Also worth recording: 9113 is a *revision* of 7540, not a from-scratch design; it keeps the frame layout and HPACK (RFC 7541) and changes TSL 1.3 handling, deprocates the priority scheme, deprocates the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade / h2c path, and tightens field validation (Appendix B of RFC 9113).

## 2. What RFC 9113 obsoletes: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740

Direct quote, appearing verbatim in both the info page and the XML source (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.xml`):

> "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

Expanded:

| Obsoleted RFC | Title | Publication | Why it is in the Obsoletes list |
|---|---|---|---|
| RFC 7540 | *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)* | May 2015, Belshe, Peon, Thomson (Ed.) | The original HTTP/2 core specification, wholly repleaced by 9113. |
| RFC 8740 | *Using TSL 1.3 with HTTP/2* | February 2020, D. Benjamin | It was a patch on 7540 (forbidding TSL 1.3 post-handshake auth); its content is folded into 9113. Confirmed by RFC 9113 Appendix B: "Use of TSL 1.3 was defined based on [RFC 8740], which this document obsoletes." |

That is the complete list. The Obsoletes header names exactly those two documents; no others.

## 3. Relations that are frequently conflated — keep them apart

- **Obsoleted vs. updated.** RFC 7540 was *updated* by RFC 8740 **and** *obsoleted* by RFC 9113. The errata listing for 7540 shows both lines side by side: "Obsoleted by: RFC9113 / Updated by: RFC8740". These are distinct relations; 8740 never obsoleted 7540.
- **Obsoletes vs. updated-by, for 9113 itself.** In the pages retrieved, RFC 9113 carries **no** "Updated by" and **no** "Obsoleted by" notice. Report it as current *as of the retrieval date*, not as current forever.
- **Transitive obsoletion is not in scope** (and would add nothing here anyway): 9113's Obsoletes list is read literally, as the two documents named above. Nothing named in that list itself obsoleted a further RFC that would need to be carried forward.
- **Companion documents are not obsoleted.** RFC 7541 (HPACK) is still the current header-compression spec and is cited normatively by 9113; RFC 8441 (WebSockets over HTTP/2), RFC 8336 (the ORIGIN frame) and RFC 8164 (Opportunistic Security for HTTP/2, Historic) are separate documents in the HTTP/2 subject area and are **not** in 9113's Obsoletes header. Do not list them as obsoleted. (Their own Updates/Updated-by relations are a different question and are not asserted here.)

## 4. How to re-verify in under a minute

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/`. Check two things: (a) no "Obsoleted by" banner at the top (if one appears, the answer to ask 1 has changed — follow it); (b) the sentence "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." in the abstract.
2. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/` and confirm the banner "This RFC is now obsoleted, see RFC 9113."
3. For the authoritative header rather than the HTML rendering, use the XML (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.xml`) and read `<obsoletes>` in the front matter; it should contain exactly two entries, 7540 and 8740.
4. If citing in a document that must be stable, write the as-of date next to the claim.

## 5. Citation-ready form

> RFC 9113, *HTTP/2*, M. Thomson, Ed., C. Benfield, Ed., June 2022, Proosed Standard. Obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740. (Verified against the RFC Editor, 2026-11-16.)

Out of scope by the stated assumptions, and therefore not answered here: which RFCs *update* HTTP/2 without obsoleting it, and any transitive-obsoletion chain.

UK NATIONAL MINIMUM WAGE / NATIONAL LIVING WAGE — RATES EFFECTIVE 1 APRIL 2026

1. HEADLINE ANSWERS

1.1 National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over): £12.71 per hour.
    Previous rate (1 April 2025 – 31 March 2026): £12.21. Increase: 50p, 4.1%.

1.2 National Minimum Wage, 18–20 Year Old Rate (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21): £10.85 per hour.
    Previous rate: £10.00. Increase: 85p, 8.5%.

Both rates take effect on 1 April 2026 and apply throughout England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland (SI 2026/357, reg. 1(3)).

2. LEGAL BASIS

The rates are set by the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357, made 19 March 2026 and coming into force 1 April 2026. The instrument amends the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/621):

  - reg. 2(2): in regulation 4 (the national living wage), for '£12.21' substitute '£12.71'.
  - reg. 2(3)(a): in regulation 4A(1)(b) (18 or over but not yet 21), for '£10.00' substitute '£10.85'.
  - reg. 2(3)(b): in regulation 4A(1)(c) (under 18), for '£7.55' substitute '£8.00'.
  - reg. 2(3)(c): in regulation 4A(1)(d) (apprentice rate), for '£7.55' substitute '£8.00'.

The figures implement in full the Low Pay Commission's recommendations submitted to Government on 27 October 2025 and accepted at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025. These are final, in-force statutory rates — not projections or draft recommendations.

3. FULL TABLE FOR CONTEXT (all effective 1 April 2026)

  Band                              | Rate    | Cash increase | % increase
  ----------------------------------|---------|---------------|-----------
  National Living Wage (21 and over)| £12.71  | £0.50         | 4.1
  18–20 Year Old Rate               | £10.85  | £0.85         | 8.5
  16–17 Year Old Rate               | £8.00   | £0.45         | 6.0
  Apprentice Rate                   | £8.00   | £0.45         | 6.0
  Accommodation Offset             | £11.10 | £0.44         | 4.1

(Only the first two rows are responsive to the request; the remainder are supplied so the two headline figures are not misapplied in payroll or contract drafting.)

4. WHO EACH RATE APPLIES TO

4.1 NLW at £12.71: workers aged 21 and over. The NLW age threshold has been 21 since April 2024 (it was 25 before April 2021 and 23 from April 2021 to March 2024). 'National Living Wage' in this answer means the statutory NLW only.

4.2 18–20 Year Old Rate at £10.85: workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21. Age is determined by the worker's age on the relevant pay reference period, not by length of service.

4.3 Apprentice interaction (frequent compliance error): an apprentice is entitled to the £8.00 apprentice rate only if aged under 19, or aged 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year of their apprenticeship is entitled to the full £12.71 NLW. An apprentice aged 21 in the first year of their apprenticeship is entitled to £8.00.

5. CAVEATS AND COMMON CONFUSIONS

5.1 The statutory National Living Wage is not the 'Real Living Wage' published by the Living Wage Foundation (a voluntary rate, separately calculated and higher). Any figure attributed to the Living Wage Foundation should not be used for HMRC national minimum wage compliance.

5.2 Rates are statutory hourly minimums. They are not annual salaries; any annualised figure (e.g. 'worth £X a year') depends on assumed hours and should not be presented as a statutory amount.

5.3 The rates apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026. Workers whose pay reference period straddles 1 April are dealt with under the usual pay reference period rules in the 2015 Regulations; the April 2026 rate applies from the first pay reference period beginning on or after that date.

5.4 For forward planning only: the same GOV.UK rates page lists indicative April 2027 figures of £13.21 (21 and over), £11.27 (18–20), £8.31 (under 18), £8.31 (apprentice). These are not the answer to this request and are subject to the 2027 uprating cycle.

6. SOURCES

  - The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357 — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/made
  - Low Pay Commission / GOV.UK, 'Minimum wage rates for 2026' — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026
  - GOV.UK press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/news/national-living-wage-increases-to-1271-per-hour
  - Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026', 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026
  - GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage rates' — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates

question: M11
answer:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — THE TWO REQUESTED CONDITIONS

CURRENT, IN-FORCE ANSWER (applicable to duty tours on or after September 29, 2020; verified against 49 CFR 395.1 as published in the 2024 edition of the CFR and on eCFR 'current'):

1. RADIUS — 150 air miles. The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. (150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles, the conversion FMCSA states parenthetically in the rule itself.)

2. RELEASE TIME — 14 consecutive hours. The driver (other than a driver-salesperson) must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

CONTROLLING TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), quoted):

"(e) Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
 (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
 (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
 (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
 (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
 (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

§ 395.8 is the records-of-duty-status (RODS) requirement and § 395.11 is the supporting-documents requirement; the exemption from those two sections is what the question describes as 'frees a driver from keeping records of duty status.'

WHY THESE AND NOT OTHER FIGURES — THREE CONFLATIONS TO AVOID

(a) Superseded pre-2020 figures. Before the June 1, 2020 final rule (compliance date September 29, 2020), § 395.1(e)(1) read 100 air miles and 12 consecutive hours. FMCSA's own summary of that rule states it 'extends the maximum duty period allowed under the short-haul exception from 12 hours to 14 hours' and 'extends the maximum radius of the short-haul exception from 100 to 150 air-miles.' Older guidance still in circulation (e.g., the 2015 Driver's Guide to HOS, which lists '100 air-mile radius driver ... report and return to work reporting location within 12 consecutive hours' at § 395.1(e)(1)) is out of date on both numbers. For current operations the answers are 150 and 14. If a specific historical duty tour is being adjudicated, the date of the tour controls: tours before September 29, 2020 → 100 air miles / 12 hours; tours on or after → 150 air miles / 14 hours.

(b) The non-CDL variant, § 395.1(e)(2). Operators of property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL under Part 383 also get a 150 air-mile radius, but the time condition is written differently: the driver must return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour and must not drive after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days, nor after the 16th hour on 2 days of any period of 7 consecutive days. The 16-hour figure there is a two-days-per-week outer driving limit, not a general release time, and it does not convert the short-haul release condition into 16 hours. The 14-hour release answer above is from (e)(1).

(c) Other 100 air-mile provisions. § 395.1(o) (16-hour driving window, five duty tours, once per 7 consecutive days) and § 395.1(p) (motion picture production sites) each use a 100 air-mile radius for different relief and are not the general short-haul RODS exception. State, port, and drayage rules may impose different limits and do not alter the federal figures.

ADDITIONAL CONDITIONS THAT QUALIFY THE TWO NUMBERS (stated so the two figures are not read as the whole exception)

Meeting 150 air miles and 14 hours is necessary but not sufficient. A driver also needs: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty (property-carrying) or at least 8 consecutive hours (passenger-carrying); and the motor carrier must maintain and retain for 6 months accurate and true time records of report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time, and — for drivers used for the first time or intermittently — total time for the preceding 7 days per § 395.8(j)(2). The return-and-release condition does not apply to a driver-salesperson. Note also that § 395.1(e)(1) contains no 8-consecutive-days-in-30-days usage cap; that kind of frequency limit belongs to other exceptions, not this one.

PRACTICAL MEASUREMENT NOTES

Radius is measured in air miles, not road miles: 6,076 feet per air mile versus 5,280 feet per statute mile. FMCSA states 100 air miles = 115.08 statute miles and 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles (277.8 km). The radius is measured from the normal work reporting location, and the 14-hour clock runs from coming on duty, with the driver both returning to that location and being released from work by hour 14.

The first reads: "(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;"

The first reads: "(A) After the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days;"
