answer:
# BasicMed (United States) — aircraft limits

**Scope of this note:** the three aircraft-related eligibility limits in the FAA BasicMed rule, as currently in force. Other BasicMed operating limits are included only as context. This is a statement of the regulatory limits, not a determination that any particular pilot or aircraft qualifies.

---

## 1. Bottom line (current, effective 12 November 2024)

| # | Limit | Current value | Governing text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maximum **certificated takeoff weight** of the aircraft | **12,500 lb** (not more than) | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as expanded by PL 118-63 §828 |
| 2 | **Occupants** the aircraft may be **authorized to carry** | **7** (not more than) | same |
| 3 | **Passengers on board** during the flight | **6** (not more than) | same |

All three are upper bounds stated as "not more than"; an aircraft certificated at exactly 12,500 lb, or at exactly 7 occupants, is within the rule. There is no lower bound in the rule other than what the aircraft's own airworthiness documents permit.

---

## 2. Authority and why these are the current numbers

**Statute.** BasicMed was created by §2307 of the 21st Century Cures Act (PL 114-255) and implemented by the FAA at 14 CFR 61.113(i), 61.23(c)(3), 14 CFR part 68, and 14 CFR 91.319(j).

**Expansion.** §828 ("Expansion of BasicMed") of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63) raised all three aircraft limits, effective 12 November 2024. The FAA's implementing notice, **Notice N 8000.386 (dated 11/14/24)**, sets out both sets of numbers and states verbatim:

> "(2) Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024:
> • The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants,
> • The aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and
> • The aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board."

**Agency confirmation.** FAA newsroom release, Friday 15 November 2024, *FAA Updates BasicMed Program*:

> "Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters."

**Current FAA BasicMed page** (licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med), under "Aircraft Requirements" and "Operating Requirements":

> "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants; Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds ... Carries not more than six passengers."

Three independent FAA sources — one dated after the effective date and one current web page — agree on 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers. That is the answer.

---

## 3. Superseded figures — DO NOT USE

For the period 1 May 2017 through 11 November 2024 the limits were:

| Limit | Old value | New value |
|---|---|---|
| MTOW | 6,000 lb | 12,500 lb |
| Occupants | 6 | 7 |
| Passengers | 5 | 6 |

These old numbers are **still printed** in FAA documents that have not been revised:

- **AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17)** — §3.2 ("no more than five passengers", "6,000 lbs", "no more than 6 occupants"), §5.1.2, §5.2.1 ("up to six occupants ... up to five passengers on board").
- **FAA Safety Briefing, July/August 2017, "The BasicMed Issue"** — "6,000 pounds or less ... not more than six occupants ... Max Passengers (five)".
- **AOPA, July 2021** — "six-place airplane, and five passengers ... 6,000 pounds".

Anyone citing AC 68-1A or the 2017 briefing as the current limit will get the pre-2024 numbers. If your compliance documentation, SOP, or training material cites the AC, it needs a revision note.

---

## 4. How each limit is measured

**Limit 1 — "maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds."**
It is the *certificated* MTOW in the aircraft's design approval (type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended TC), or the equivalent figure in the operating limitations for a non-type-certificated aircraft. It is **not** the actual weight at brake release. A 12,500 lb airplane that happens to be light is fine; a 12,500 lb airplane that is overloaded is an airworthiness violation under part 91, not a BasicMed violation. 12,500 lb is also the traditional "small aircraft / large aircraft" dividing line in 14 CFR 1.1, so the expansion now admits essentially the whole small-airplane fleet (e.g., a Cessna 208 Caravan at ~8,000 lb MTOW, most turboprop singles and light twins).

**Limit 2 — "authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants."**
The count that matters is the **occupant capacity in the design approval**, not the number of seats actually installed. AC 68-1A §5.1.2 makes the principle explicit (quoting the pre-2024 version): "the aircraft's design approval would authorize the number of occupants the aircraft may carry." The 2017 briefing gives the classic trap: "Certain aircraft, such as variants of the Piper PA-32 and PA-34 ... do not qualify under BasicMed because they are certificated to carry more than six occupants, even if they only have six seats installed." Under the current rule those same aircraft are measured against 7 — a PA-32-300 certificated for 7 occupants (1 pilot + 6) now qualifies.

**Occupants vs. passengers — the distinction the rule turns on.**
"Occupants" includes the pilot flying under BasicMed and any other required flight crew. "Passengers" excludes required flight crew. The two limits are separate and both must be satisfied:

| Aircraft certificated for | Required flight crew | Max passengers permitted by limit 3 | Permitted by limit 2? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 occupants | 1 pilot | 6 | Yes — 7 − 1 = 6 |
| 7 occupants | 2 pilots | 5 | Yes — 7 − 2 = 5 |
| 7 occupants | 1 pilot | 7 | **No** — exceeds limit 3 |
| 8 occupants | 1 pilot | 6 | **No** — exceeds limit 2 |

So a 7-occupant, single-required-pilot aircraft is the case that uses both limits to their full extent; any aircraft requiring two pilots can carry at most 5 passengers even though 6 are allowed by limit 3.

**Aircraft altered to fit.** An aircraft certificated above the limits can be brought inside them by a new design approval (STC or amended TC). AC 68-1A §5.1.2 states the principle — "if an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of more than 6,000 pounds is altered to have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of less than 6,000 pounds, then that aircraft would likewise meet the requirements" — and the same logic now applies with 12,500 lb and 7 occupants substituted. The alteration must be reflected in the design approval; a logbook entry or a removed seat row is not enough.

**Experimental / non-type-certificated aircraft.** Occupancy is governed by 14 CFR 91.319(j) rather than §61.113(i)(1); AC 68-1A §5.1.3 states that §91.319(j) "prohibits a person from operating an experimental aircraft under BasicMed carrying more than six occupants." **Verify before relying on this one:** the 2024 expansion raised the §61.113(i)(1) figure to 7, and the FAA BasicMed web page now states the 7-occupant limit generically ("any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants"), but I did not have the amended §91.319(j) text in front of me. Confirm the current eCFR text of §91.319(j) before operating an experimental aircraft with 7 occupants under BasicMed.

---

## 5. Exclusions and traps

1. **Transport category helicopters.** The FAA newsroom release states the MTOW increase to 12,500 lb is "excluding transport category helicopters." For those, the 6,000 lb limit continues to apply. Do not apply 12,500 lb to a transport category rotorcraft.
2. **The limit applies to the whole flight.** Per the 2017 FAA Safety Briefing, Congress made the limitations apply to the entire flight: "Even if the pilot you are flying with holds a valid medical certificate and has the ability to operate beyond the constraints of BasicMed, you cannot act as PIC at any time during that flight if those limitations are exceeded." You cannot split a flight to get around the weight/occupant/passenger caps.
3. **State law does not change these numbers.** These are federal aircraft-eligibility limits; no state varies the 12,500 lb / 7 / 6 figures. States differ only on recognition of BasicMed for state-law purposes, which is outside this question.
4. **BasicMed vs. a medical certificate.** These limits are conditions of the BasicMed privilege. A pilot operating on a valid FAA medical certificate is not bound by them.

---

## 6. Related BasicMed operating limits (context only — not the ask)

From §61.113(i)(2) and the FAA BasicMed page, a flight under BasicMed must be conducted:

- at or below **18,000 ft MSL**;
- at an indicated airspeed **not exceeding 250 knots**;
- **within the United States**, or within another country in which BasicMed is authorized;
- **not for compensation or hire** (flight instruction is permitted and the CFI may be compensated for the instruction);
- day or night, VFR or IFR;
- not during a medical deficiency (14 CFR 61.53).

---

## 7. Pre-flight verification checklist for a specific aircraft

1. Pull the aircraft's **TCDS or other design approval (TC/STC/ATC)** from the FAA website — not the POH, not the seat count.
2. Read the **maximum certificated takeoff weight**; it must be ≤ **12,500 lb** (≤ 6,000 lb if a transport category helicopter).
3. Read the **occupant capacity** in the design approval; it must be ≤ **7**.
4. Count **required flight crew** for the planned operation; planned passengers must be ≤ **6** and ≤ (7 − required crew).
5. Confirm the flight will stay within 18,000 ft MSL, 250 KIAS, US airspace, and no compensation or hire.
6. For an experimental aircraft, check the current text of 14 CFR 91.319(j) (see §4 above).

---

## 8. Sources

- FAA, *BasicMed* — https://www.faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med ("not more than 7 occupants"; "not more than 12,500 pounds"; "not more than six passengers").
- FAA Newsroom, *FAA Updates BasicMed Program*, 15 Nov 2024 — https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/faa-updates-basicmed-program.
- FAA Notice **N 8000.386**, 11/14/24 — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Notice/N_8000.386.pdf (the two-tier table and the 12 Nov 2024 effective date).
- FAA **AC 68-1A**, 5/3/17 — https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_68-1A.pdf (**superseded figures**; still useful for the definitions in §5.1.2, §5.1.3, §5.2.1).
- FAA Safety Briefing, July/August 2017, *The BasicMed Issue* — https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med/JulAug2017.pdf (**superseded figures**; useful for the whole-flight rule and the "certificated for more occupants than seats installed" trap).
- 14 CFR 61.113(i), 61.23(c)(3), part 68, 91.319(j); PL 114-255 §2307; PL 118-63 §828.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 6 on faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/advisory_circular/ac_68-1a.pdf and 7 on faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/notice/n_8000.386.pdf. The first reads: "Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants."

# Hours of service — driver of a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach), US interstate operation

**Authority: 49 CFR § 395.5(a)** (Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles), issued under 49 CFR Part 395, Subpart A. Text as currently published on eCFR (fetched 2026-11-16) and repeated verbatim on FMCSA's 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' page.

## Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Basis (49 CFR § 395.5(a)) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** | (a)(1): no driver shall drive 'more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty' |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty may they drive? | **8 consecutive hours off duty** | (a)(1) and (a)(2): both limits are measured 'following 8 consecutive hours off duty' |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours** | (a)(2): no driving 'for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty' |

Plain-language statement for the driver: *You get 10 hours of driving inside a 15-hour on-duty window, and both clocks restart only when you take 8 consecutive hours off duty.*

## How the three numbers fit together (and the traps to avoid)

1. **Two clocks, one reset.** The 10-hour driving limit and the 15-hour on-duty limit both run from the end of the same 8-consecutive-hour off-duty period. Eight hours off duty is the only thing that restarts both.
2. **The 15-hour clock is a window, not a driving allowance.** It counts *all* on-duty time — pre-trip inspection, fueling, loading bags, waiting at terminals, paperwork, yard moves — not just wheels-turning time. A driver who drives only 6 hours but is on duty 15 hours and 1 minute may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty.
3. **'On duty' includes other employment.** § 395.5(b) applies 'regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services,' and FMCSA's passenger page states: 'All compensated work for a motor carrier or a non-motor carrier is on-duty time.' A second job counts.
4. **Do not use the property-carrying numbers.** Property-carrying CMVs run 11 driving / 10 off duty / 14 on-duty window under § 395.3. The passenger numbers are 10 / 8 / 15. The regulation itself draws this line in § 395.1 (short-haul time records): '(A) A property-carrying … driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; (B) A passenger-carrying … driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty.' Mixing the two sets is the single most common error on this question.
5. **The 10 is a maximum, not a target.** 10 driving hours and 15 on-duty hours are independent ceilings; whichever is reached first stops the driver. Because 10 < 15, a driver who drives the full 10 hours will typically still have window time left, but may not exceed 10 driving.

## Additional ceilings that also stop the driver (not asked, but binding)

Under **§ 395.5(b)**, no passenger-carrying CMV driver may drive after:
- **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days**, if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days**, if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.

These are cumulative on-duty totals across all carriers, and they override the daily numbers: a driver with window and driving time remaining is still barred once the 60/70-hour total is reached.

## Scope conditions and caveats (compliance notes)

- **Assumed in scope:** US interstate (or otherwise federally regulated) for-hire or private motor carrier of passengers; no emergency declaration, waiver or exception in effect; current rule as published, not a historical or pending version.
- **Sleeper berth — affects the '8 hours' answer in form, not in substance.** Per § 395.1(g)(3), a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty using two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the four conditions of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)-(iv) are met. The requirement remains '8 hours of off-duty-equivalent rest'; only the way it is accumulated changes. If the carrier uses split sleeper-berth rest, the compliance analysis must test the four conditions, not just add the two periods.
- **Short-haul / 150 air-mile provision — does not change 10/8/15.** § 395.1(e) exempts qualifying drivers (within 150 air miles of the normal work-reporting location, released within 14 consecutive hours) from the *record-of-duty-status/logbook* requirement. It is an paperwork relief, not a relief from the driving, off-duty or on-duty limits. The 14-hour figure in that provision is a condition of eligibility for the exemption — it is **not** the on-duty driving cutoff, which remains 15.
- **Adverse driving conditions — flagged, not quantified.** § 395.5 is expressly '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1', and § 395.1(b) contains an adverse-driving-conditions exception. The text of § 395.1(b) was not among the passages retrieved for this answer, so no numeric extension is stated here; a carrier relying on that exception must read § 395.1(b) in the current eCFR before doing so. The 10/8/15 figures above are the base rule.
- **Alaska is a separate regime.** The 15-hours-following-8-off-duty / 20-hours-on-duty figures that appear in § 395.1 are the **Alaska** passenger-carrying rules, not the general rule. They do not apply to operations in the 48 contiguous states or DC.
- **State variations and cross-border operations.** This answer states the federal rule only. Canada (Sleeper berth / daily limits under the provincial and federal HOS regimes) and Mexico have different limits; a driver crossing a border is subject to the more restrictive applicable regime in practice. State-level intrastate passenger rules can also differ.
- **Record-keeping is a separate obligation.** A driver subject to Part 395 must keep a record of duty status (ELD for most carriers of passengers); non-business private motor carriers of passengers are relieved of the logbook/RDS requirement but **not** of the driving limits. Exceeding 10/8/15 is a violation whether or not a log is required.

## Worked illustration (for training or audit use)

Driver reports for duty 06:00, takes 8 hours off duty from 22:00 to 06:00 the previous night (restart satisfied). Drives 06:30-10:30 (4.0 h driving). On duty at terminal 10:30-13:00. Drives 13:00-19:00 (6.0 h driving; cumulative 10.0 h — **driving cap reached at 19:00**). On-duty clock at 19:00 stands at 13.0 h, so window time remains, but the driver may not drive further. Had the driver instead taken a 3-hour break at midday, the on-duty clock would still have hit 15 hours at 21:00, ending driving at that point even with driving hours unused. Either ceiling — 10 driving or 15 on duty — ends the shift; 8 consecutive hours off duty restarts both.

## Source record

- 49 CFR § 395.5 (eCFR, current) — subsections (a)(1), (a)(2), (b)(1), (b)(2).
- 49 CFR § 395.1 — sleeper-berth equivalence (g)(3); short-haul (e); Alaskа and adverse-conditions provisions distinguished.
- FMCSA, 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' (carrier-safety guidance restating § 395.5 and the on-duty-includes-all-compensated-work point).
- FMCSA Safety Planner § 6.4.3 'Passenger-Carrying Operations (395.5)' (same three limits, plus the multiple-employer on-duty note).

The first reads: "(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/part-395 and 8 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a/section-395.1. The first reads: "(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;"

# Flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less — 14 CFR Part 135

## Answers

| # | Ask | Answer | Authority |
|---|-----|--------|-----------|
| 1 | Rest required after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **At least 9 consecutive hours** of scheduled rest | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2 | Floor to which that rest may be reduced | **8 consecutive hours**, conditioned on a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(3) |

Both figures are *consecutive* hours of rest, and the rest must fall between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.

## Governing text

§ 135.273(b)(2):

> "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

§ 135.273(b)(3):

> "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

## Conditions attached to the reduction to 8 hours — all four must hold

1. **The reduced rest is still consecutive.** Eight consecutive hours; not eight hours split, not eight hours minus a phone call or a deadhead report.
2. **A subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours is provided.** This is compensatory rest, given after the duty period that follows the reduced rest.
3. **That subsequent rest is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the *beginning* of the reduced rest period.** The clock runs from the start of the reduced rest, not from its end and not from the end of the following duty.
4. **Both rest periods occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period** — i.e., they sit in the rest windows, not inside duty.

The reduction is a *scheduling election*. The regulation says the 9-hour period "may be scheduled or reduced to 8" — the operator may build an 8-hour rest into the pairing from the outset, or may reduce it in actuality. It is not conditioned on a delay, a mechanical, weather, or any other operational event.

## Worked timeline (verification of the 24-hour trigger)

- Day 1, 07:00 — report; scheduled duty period 14 hours; release 21:00.
- Baseline (no reduction): 9 consecutive hours of rest 21:00 D1 → 06:00 D2. Earliest next report 06:00 D2.
- Reduced: 8 consecutive hours of rest 21:00 D1 → 05:00 D2. Earliest next report 05:00 D2, **provided**:
  - the compensatory rest of ≥10 consecutive hours begins no later than **21:00 D2** (24 hours after 21:00 D1, the beginning of the reduced rest), and
  - that compensatory rest occurs after completion of the D2 duty period and before the next duty period.
- Practical consequence: the D2 duty period must be complete and the flight attendant released into the 10-hour rest by 21:00 D2. Any scheduling that pushes the second release past 21:00 D2 breaks the (b)(3) condition and the 8-hour rest becomes non-compliant retroactively.

## Related prohibitions the operator must also satisfy

- **§ 135.273(b)(10):** no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under the section.
- **§ 135.273(b)(11):** no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during any required rest period — this forecloses using the flight attendant for positioning, training, phone contact, or administrative tasks inside the 9- or 8-hour window.
- **§ 135.273(b)(1):** no assignment to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours, except as permitted by (b)(4)–(b)(6) (additional flight attendants) — the 9/8 rest figures above are the ones keyed to the ≤14-hour case.

## What does NOT govern this answer — common traps

1. **Flight crewmember rest rules.** § 135.267 (unscheduled one- and two-pilot crews) requires, in substance, 10 consecutive hours of rest and permits reduction to a floor of 8 or 9 hours depending on scheduled flight time. Those numbers are for *flight crewmembers*, not flight attendants. Using § 135.267(c) here would wrongly produce "10 hours, reducible to 8." The correct flight-attendant baseline is 9, not 10.
2. **The over-14-hour flight attendant pair.** § 135.273(b)(7)/(b)(8) sets an 11-hour rest reducible to 10 consecutive hours for flight attendants assigned to duty periods exceeding 14 hours (up to 16 with an additional flight attendant). That pair is inapplicable to the ≤14-hour case asked about; do not answer 11/10.
3. **"Delays beyond the control of the certificate holder."** § 135.273(b)(14) provides that a flight attendant is not considered scheduled in excess of the duty period limitations where flights were scheduled and normally would terminate within the limits but, due to circumstances beyond the certificate holder's control (e.g., adverse weather), were not expected at departure to reach destination within the scheduled time. That provision relieves a *duty-period-limitation* exceedance; it is not the trigger for reducing rest. The reduction authority in (b)(3) is conditioned on compensatory rest, not on delay. An operator that reduces to 8 hours on the theory that a delay justifies it, without scheduling the 10-hour compensatory rest within 24 hours, is out of compliance.
4. **The election to use flight crewmember rules.** § 135.273(c) permits a certificate holder to apply the flight crewmember flight time/duty/rest requirements of Part 135 to flight attendants for all operations, but only if it establishes written procedures applying to all flight attendants used in the operation and includes the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (rest facilities on board not required), with the corresponding operations specification. If the operator has made that election, the numbers in this memo are displaced by the flight crewmember scheme. Confirm the election status before applying 9/8.
5. **Contractual overlays.** A collective bargaining agreement or company manual may impose more rest than the regulation; the regulatory figure is a floor. This answer states the regulatory minimum only.

## Applicability confirmation

§ 135.273 governs duty period limitations and rest for flight attendants of certificate holders operating under Part 135. "Flight attendant" is defined in § 135.273(a) as an individual, other than a flight crewmember, assigned by the certificate holder in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications or otherwise required by the regulations. The question presupposes a flight attendant is assigned to the crew, so the section applies to that individual. The scheduled-vs-unscheduled distinction that matters elsewhere in subpart F (§ 135.261 allocating §§ 135.265/135.267/135.269) does not change the flight attendant rest figures — § 135.273 applies to flight attendants independent of that allocation, subject only to the § 135.273(c) election described above.

## Compliance evidence the operator should retain

- Pairing/duty sheets showing scheduled duty period length and scheduled rest, by flight attendant and date.
- Actual release and report times (the (b)(3) conditions are measured against actual times: beginning of the reduced rest, beginning of the subsequent rest).
- Where 8-hour rest is used: a record pairing each reduced rest with the specific ≥10-hour compensatory rest and demonstrating that the compensatory rest began within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest.
- Evidence that no duty was assigned during required rest ((b)(11)) — no training, positioning, or administrative assignments logged inside the rest window.
- The written procedures and operations specification amendment, if the § 135.273(c) election is in effect.
- Records retention consistent with Part 135 recordkeeping requirements (verify the current text of § 135.63 for the applicable duty/rest record provisions and retention period before finalizing the record schedule).

## Bottom line

Nine consecutive hours, reducible to eight consecutive hours only if the flight attendant is given a subsequent rest of at least ten consecutive hours that begins no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest. Eight is the floor; nothing in § 135.273 authorizes less for a duty period of 14 hours or less.

The first reads: "(1) A rest required under paragraph (b)(1) of this section may be scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 8 hours if the flight crewmember is given a rest period of at least 10 hours that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commenc"

# HTTP/2: current specification and its obsoleted RFCs

## Answers

1. **The current specification of HTTP/2 is RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, Standards Track, edited by M. Thomson (Mozilla) and C. Benfield (Apple Inc.).
2. **RFC 9113 obsoletes two RFCs: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.**

## Evidence (primary sources)

### RFC 9113 header block

Quoted from the RFC Editor's info page and the IETF Datatracker's HTML rendering of RFC 9113:

```
Stream:  Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)
RFC:     9113
Obsoletes:  7540, 8740
Category:  Standards Track
Published:  June 2022
ISSN:     2070-1721
Authors:   M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla)
           C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.)
```

The abstract states it explicitly: *"This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."*

Appendix B (*Changes from RFC 7540*) repeats the relationship for the TLS 1.3 content: *"Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes."*

### Independent corroboration from the other direction

The RFC Editor errata search for RFC 7540 displays, on every errata record:

```
⚠ This RFC has been obsoleted!
Obsoleted by: RFC9113
Updated by:   RFC8740
```

This confirms both directions of the graph: 7540 → obsoleted by 9113, and 8740 → had *updated* 7540 (a different relation, see below).

## Documentation notes and edge cases

- **Obsoletes ≠ updates.** RFC 8740 (*Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2*) *updated* RFC 7540; RFC 9113 then *obsoleted* both 7540 and 8740, folding the TLS 1.3 rules into the base specification. So 8740 belongs in the obsoletes list even though its own relationship to 7540 was an update. Do not conflate the two header fields.
- **Obsoletes ≠ obsoleted by.** RFC 9113 obsoletes 7540 and 8740. RFC 9113 is not itself obsoleted by anything in the groundling; it is the leaf of the chain 7540 → 9113.
- **Not in scope: HTTP semantics RFCs.** RFC 9113 does **not** obselete RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching), or RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1). The same caution appears in RFC 7540's own abstract: *"This specification is an alternative to, but does not obselete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax."* HTTP/2 is an alternative expression of HTTP semantics, not a replacement for the semantics documents.
- **Not in scope: extensions.** RFC 7541 (HTTP/2 *Negotiation* / Upgrade Token) is a distinct document and is not named in RFC 9113's Obsoletes header. Only the two RFCs in the header count.
- **Errata do not change the obsoletes relationship.** The errata records for RFC 7540 (e.g. Errata-ID 5031 Verified, 4535 Held for Document Update, 4645/5249 Rejected) are editorial/technical corrigenda to the obsoleted text; none alters which RFC is current, and RFC 9113 carries its own errata process via its info page.
- **Meaning of "current".** "Current" here is asserted as of the source-fetch date (2026-11-16) using the RFC Editor and IETF Datatracker as the authoritative index. No successor RFC to 9113 appears in the groundling. If a later revision is published, it would appear as an `Obsoletes: 9113` entry in that new RFC's header; the answer should then be re-derived by the same procedure below, not patched by hand.
- **Status nuance.** The RFC Editor info page lists RFC 9113 as **Proposed Standard**; the document's own Status of This Memo calls it an *Internet Standards Track document*. Both are consistent — Standards Track is the stream, Proosed Standard the current maturity level. Neither affects the obsoletes answer.

## Reproducible verification procedure

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113` (or `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113`).
2. Read the header block. Confirm `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`.
3. Confirm the abstract sentence *"This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."*
4. Cross-check by opening the errata search for RFC 7540 (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata_search.php?rfc=7540`) and confirming the banner `Obsoleted by: RFC9113`.
5. Optional negative check: confirm RFC 9113's header does **not** list 9110/9111/9112 or 7541, which would indicate scope creep beyond the two obsoleted RFCs reported here.

## One-line answer

> RFC **9113** is the current specification of HTTP/2; it obsoletes RFC **7540** (the original HTTP/2 specification, May 2015) and RFC **8740** (Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2).

question: M9
answer:
UK statutory minimum wage rates in force from 1 April 2026

HEADLINE ANSWER

| Age band | Statutory rate name | Hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 March 2026) | Cash increase | % increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21 and over | National Living Wage (NLW) | £12.71 | £12.21 | £0.50 | 4.1% |
| 18 to 20 | National Minimum Wage (18–20 Year Old Rate) | £10.85 | £10.00 | £0.85 | 8.5% |

So: NLW for workers aged 21 and over = £12.71 per hour; NMW for 18–20 year olds = £10.85 per hour. Both effective 1 April 2026.

LEGAL BASIS

- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357. Made 19 March 2026; coming into force 1 April 2026; extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
- Regulation 2(2): in regulation 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (S.I. 2015/621) (the national living wage), for '£12.21' substitute '£12.71'.
- Regulation 2(3)(a): in regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations, for '£10.00' substitute '£10.85'. The Explanatory Note confirms regulation 4A(1)(b) is 'the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21)'.
- Because the instrument was made on 19 March 2026 and commenced on 1 April 2026, these are the rates actually in force from that date, not projections or recommendations awaiting implementation.

CORROBORATION (all four agree with the instrument)

1. Low Pay Commission advice to Government on 2026 minimum wage rates, published 26 November 2025: recommends NLW (21 and over) £12.71 and 18–20 Year Old Rate £10.85 from 1 April 2026. Government accepted the recommendations at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025.
2. Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026', published 1 April 2026: NLW (for those aged 21 and over) £12.71; 18–20 Year Old Rate £10.85; 16–17 Year Old Rate £8.00; Apprentice Rate £8.00; Accommodation Offset £11.10.
3. GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates': April 2026 row — 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; Under 18 £8; Apprentice £8.
4. GOV.UK press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', published 1 April 2026: same table of rates.

SCOPE AND APPLICATION NOTES (needed to apply the figures correctly)

- Geographic extent: UK-wide. The rates are set by UK secondary legislation and extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland; there is no separate national rate for Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.
- Effective date: the rates apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026. 'April 2026' in the question is read as rates in force from 1 April 2026, the standard annual uprating date.
- Age determination: the worker's age on the first day of the pay reference period determines the band. A worker aged 21 or over on that date is entitled to the NLW (£12.71); a worker aged 18, 19 or 20 is entitled to the 18–20 Year Old Rate (£10.85).
- Apprentice override: the apprentice rate (£8.00 from 1 April 2026) applies instead of the age-band rate where the worker is aged under 19, or is aged 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21 in the first year of their apprenticeship is therefore entitled to £8.00, not £12.71; an apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year is entitled to £12.71. The figures above assume a non-apprentice worker, as the question's age-band framing implies.
- Accommodation offset: where an employer provides living accommodation, the maximum daily offset from 1 April 2026 is £11.10 (up from £10.66), which reduces the amount of pay that counts towards the minimum wage but does not change the hourly rate itself.
- Statutory vs 'Real Living Wage': these are the statutory rates enforceable under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998. They are not the voluntary Real Living Wage promoted by the Living Wage Foundation, which is set independently, is higher, and is not a legal minimum. The two are commonly confused; the values above are the statutory ones.
- Completeness for the same date (not requested, supplied for context only): 16–17 Year Old Rate £8.00; Apprentice Rate £8.00; Accommodation Offset £11.10. Rates already announced for 1 April 2027 are NLW £13.21 and 18–20 rate £11.27 — these do not apply in the 2026/27 year.

CONFIDENCE

High. The values are taken from the operative statutory instrument and independently confirmed by the Low Pay Commission's recommendation, its post-implementation report, the GOV.UK rates page and a GOV.UK press release. Arithmetic cross-checks against the published cash and percentage increases are exact (12.21 + 0.50 = 12.71; 10.00 + 0.85 = 10.85). No ask is blocked.

question: M11
answer:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1))

1. THE TWO VALUES

Ask 1 — Radius: the driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The rule states the statute-mile equivalent in the same sentence: 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles. Air miles are straight-line (great-circle) distance, not highway/road miles; a route that is 180 road miles but 140 air miles from the reporting location is inside the radius.

Ask 2 — Release from work: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

2. CONTROLLING TEXT (quoted verbatim; eCFR current 49 CFR 395.1 and govinfo CFR-2025-title49-vol5 sec. 395-1 agree word for word)

"(e) Short-haul operations —
(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing:
(A) The time the driver reports for duty each day;
(B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day;
(C) The time the driver is released from duty each day;
(D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

Corroborating restatements in the record: FMCSA "Summary of Hours of Service Regulations" — "the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours... must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours." FMCSA HOS Final Rule page and "Get To Know The New Rule" — the exception was lengthened "from 12 to 14 hours" and "from 100 air miles to 150 air miles."

3. SCOPE OF THE RELIEF GRANTED

Satisfying (e)(1) exempts the driver from 49 CFR 395.8 (records of duty status) and 395.11 (supporting documents). It does NOT exempt the driver from the underlying hours-of-service limits in 395.3 (11-hour driving, 14-hour window, 60/70-hour), from 395.5 for passenger carriers where applicable, or from 395.13 (out-of-service). The exemption is from the paperwork, not from the driving limits.

4. CONDITIONS THAT MUST ALL HOLD — radius and release time alone do not create the exemption

(a) Radius: every point of operation on the tour within 150 air miles of the normal work reporting location. Ask 1.
(b) Return and release: returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours. Ask 2. Carve-out: a driver-salesperson is not required to meet the return/release condition in (e)(1)(ii), but must still meet the radius and the other conditions.
(c) Off-duty separation: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty for a property-carrying CMV driver; 8 consecutive hours for a passenger-carrying CMV driver.
(d) Records: the employing motor carrier maintains and retains for 6 months accurate and true time records of (i) time the driver reports for duty each day, (ii) total hours on duty each day, (iii) time released from duty each day, and (iv) total time for the preceding 7 days per 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.

If any day fails (a), (b) or (c), the driver must complete a RODS for that day (395.8) and is subject to the standard 395.3 limits, including the 30-minute break after 8 cumulative hours of driving without a 30-minute interruption.

5. HOW THE 14 CONSECUTIVE HOURS ARE COUNTED (the usual point of dispute)

Clock starts when the driver comes on duty / reports for duty at the normal work reporting location; clock stops when the carrier releases the driver from duty at that same location. It is a single continuous 14-hour span: off-duty time taken inside the span does not stop or extend the clock. Being released at hour 14:01 at the yard is a failure of the exception for that day, even if total driving was small. The measurement is from the start of the duty tour, not from the start of driving, and not from the end of the previous tour.

6. MEASUREMENT OF THE RADIUS / WHAT IS THE 'NORMAL WORK REPORTING LOCATION'

- The rule defines the point as 'the location where the driver reports to and is released from work, i.e., the normal work reporting location.' It is a fixed, carrier-designated location, not wherever the driver happens to start a given day.
- Measure straight-line air miles from that point to the furthest point actually reached during the tour (including the return leg). Do not measure by odometer.
- A driver with multiple terminals: each terminal can serve as a normal work reporting location only if the carrier designates it and the driver in fact reports to and is released from it; a driver who rotates reporting points must satisfy the 150-mile radius measured from the applicable designated location on each tour, and the carrier should document the designation. Shifting the designation day-to-day to capture a wider route is not a defense; the designation must reflect the driver's actual normal reporting point.

7. NEIGHBORING PROVISIONS THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH (e)(1)

- 395.1(e)(2) — property-carrying CMVs for which no CDL is required: also a 150 air-mile radius, but a different structure: return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour; no driving after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days and after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7; 6-month time records. A driver using (e)(2) is expressly ineligible to use (e)(1), (g) or (o).
- 395.1(o) — 16-hour exception: requires return to and release at the normal work reporting location for the previous five duty tours, release within 16 hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty, and no use of the exception in the previous 6 consecutive days (unless a new 7/8-day period began with 34+ consecutive hours off duty).
- 395.1(p) — motion picture production site transportation: 100 air-mile radius; a different, narrower provision.
- Superseded thresholds: 100 air miles and 12 hours are the pre-2020 short-haul values quoted in the older fact-sheet comparison table. They are not the current answer and should not be used in a compliance document.

8. SCOPE NOTE

This answer states the federal interstate rule (49 CFR Part 395). A state intrastate analog may set different radius or duty-period thresholds, and a driver operating intrastate under state rules should be checked against that state's adoption. The request asks for the federal short-haul thresholds, which are the values given above.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a/section-395.1 and 8 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2025-title49-vol5-sec395-1.xml. The first reads: "(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 5 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a/section-395.1 and 2 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2025-title49-vol5-sec395-1.xml. The first reads: "(A) After the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days;"

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — CURRENT FEDERAL RULE (effective 12 November 2024)

Governing authority: 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as amended to implement Section 828 ("Expansion of BasicMed") of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Public Law 118-63. The FAA's implementing guidance is Notice N 8000.386 (dated 11/14/24) and the BasicMed pages at faa.gov; AC 68-1A (5/3/17) remains the structural advisory circular but its numeric limits are superseded.

=== THE THREE LIMITS ===

1) MAXIMUM CERTIFICATED TAKEOFF WEIGHT: 12,500 pounds.
   The aircraft must have a maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) of not more than 12,500 lb. (Was 6,000 lb before 12 Nov 2024.)
   Caveat: the FAA's 15 Nov 2024 announcement states the increase to 12,500 lb applies "excluding transport category helicopters" — i.e., transport-category helicopters remain subject to the 6,000 lb ceiling. For every other aircraft category the figure is 12,500 lb.

2) OCCUPANTS THE AIRCRAFT MAY BE AUTHORIZED TO CARRY: 7 occupants.
   The aircraft must be "authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants." (Was 6 before 12 Nov 2024.)
   "Authorized to carry" is a design-approval quantity, not a seat count: it is set by the aircraft's type certificate (TC), supplemental type certificate (STC) or amended TC (ATC), as read from the Type Certificate Data Sheet. An aircraft certificated for more than 7 occupants does not qualify even if fewer seats are installed (the classic example being certain Piper PA-32/PA-34 variants under the old 6-occupant rule). Conversely, an aircraft altered by STC/ATC to a certificated capacity of 7 or fewer does qualify.

3) PASSENGERS ON BOARD: 6 passengers.
   The flight must be conducted carrying not more than 6 passengers. (Was 5 before 12 Nov 2024.)

=== WHY 7 OCCUPANTS AND 6 PASSENGERS ARE DIFFERENT NUMBERS ===
"Occupants" includes the pilot in command and any other required flightcrew member; "passengers" excludes them. The two limits therefore interact as follows (arithmetic checked against both limits):
 - Aircraft type certificated for one required pilot: 1 pilot + up to 6 passengers = 7 occupants. Both limits satisfied exactly.
 - Aircraft type certificated for two required flightcrew: 2 crew + up to 5 passengers = 7 occupants. Occupant limit satisfied exactly; passenger count (5) is within the 6 limit. Note that 2 crew + 6 passengers = 8 occupants would breach the 7-occupant limit, so 6 passengers is NOT available in a two-crew aircraft.
 - In every case the binding passenger figure is 6, and the aircraft's certificated occupant capacity is 7.

=== SCOPE / CHARACTER OF THE LIMITS ===
These are operational limits on the pilot exercising BasicMed privileges, not limits on the aircraft's own certification or airworthiness. The same aircraft flown by a pilot using an FAA medical certificate is not subject to them.

Experimental (amateur-built/experimental) aircraft: occupant carriage is separately addressed by 14 CFR 91.319(j), which cross-references the BasicMed occupant limit; read the current codified text of 91.319(j) rather than the 2017 AC, whose "six occupants" phrasing predates the 2024 amendment.

=== ADJACENT BASICMED OPERATING LIMITS (context, not part of the three answers) ===
Entire flight within the United States (or another country that authorizes BasicMed); at or below 18,000 ft MSL; indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots; not operated for compensation or hire. Limitations apply to the whole flight from takeoff to touchdown — a BasicMed pilot may not act as PIC for any portion of a flight that exceeds them, even if another pilot on board holds a medical certificate and acts as PIC for the rest of the flight.

=== EFFECTIVE-DATE WARNING (the usual source of error) ===
Any source dated before 12 November 2024 — including AC 68-1A, the FAA Safety Briefing July/August 2017 article, and older third-party summaries — will state 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers. Those figures are superseded. Use 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers for any flight conducted on or after 12 November 2024.

=== HOW TO VERIFY ===
Check the current text of 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) on eCFR (paragraph (i)(1) for the aircraft/occupancy limits, (i)(2) for the altitude/airspeed/geographic limits, (i)(3) for logbook carriage), cross-check the FAA BasicMed page (faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med, "Aircraft Requirements" and "Operating Requirements" bullets), and for a specific airframe read the occupant capacity and MTOW from its Type Certificate Data Sheet.

=== ONE-LINE ANSWER ===
Under BasicMed (on or after 12 November 2024) a pilot may fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 lb, authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, with not more than 6 passengers on board (transport category helicopters remain limited to 6,000 lb).
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 7 on faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/notice/n_8000.386.pdf and 6 on faasafety.gov/files/notices/2020/sep/ac_68-1a_basic_med.pdf. The first reads: "• The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants,"

question: M3
answer:
HOURS OF SERVICE — DRIVER OF A PASSENGER-CARRYING COMMERCIAL MOTOR VEHICLE (MOTORCOACH), UNITED STATES

GOVERNING AUTHORITY
49 CFR 395.5 (Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles), made subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 49 CFR 395.1. This is the passenger-carrying rule set; it is NOT the property-carrying rule set in 49 CFR 395.3 (which is 11 hours driving / 10 consecutive hours off duty / 14-hour window and must not be substituted). Assumes interstate operation, no waiver or exemption in force, and a driver required to keep a record of duty status.

THE THREE ANSWERS

1. Maximum driving time — 10 HOURS.
   Sec. 395.5(a)(1): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV "more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."
   The 10 hours is accumulated driving time within the duty period, not necessarily consecutive; it may be taken in one block or split into many blocks.

2. Consecutive hours off duty required before a new driving period — 8 CONSECUTIVE HOURS.
   Same provision. The 8 hours may be off-duty time, sleeper-berth time, or any combination of the two, but there must be no on-duty time and no driving time at any point inside those 8 hours. Only a full 8-consecutive-hour break restarts both the 10-hour driving clock and the 15-hour on-duty clock.

3. On-duty hours after which driving is no longer permitted — 15 HOURS ON DUTY.
   Sec. 395.5(a)(2): no driving "for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."
   This is a driving cutoff, not a work cutoff. After the 15th on-duty hour the driver may continue non-driving work, but may not drive again until another 8 consecutive hours off duty have been taken.

HOW THE 15-HOUR LIMIT IS MEASURED (passenger rule — differs from property rule)
The passenger rule is written as "having been on duty 15 hours," i.e. 15 accumulated hours of on-duty time (driving time plus on-duty-not-driving time) counted from the end of the last 8-consecutive-hour break. Off-duty time taken during the day (meal break, nap) does NOT count toward the 15 hours. FMCSA's own worked example in the Interstate Passenger-Carrying Driver's Guide: on duty at 06:00, work 7 hours, 1 hour off for lunch, work 8 more hours until 22:00 = 15 on-duty hours; the driver must not drive after 22:00 but may do other work. Do not describe this using the property-carrier 14-hour "elapsed window" semantics, where an off-duty break does not pause the clock — the passenger provision is drafted and administered as an on-duty accumulation.

ADDITIONAL CAPS THAT CAN BIND EARLIER (weekly limits — 49 CFR 395.5(b))
A driver may not drive after having been on duty:
  - 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days, if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
  - 70 hours in any 8 consecutive days, if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.
These are on-duty (not driving-only) totals and include work for any other motor carrier or non-motor-carrier employer. The 10-hour daily driving maximum is therefore an upper bound per duty period, not an entitlement on every duty day: the 60/70-hour cap can stop driving sooner. There is NO 34-hour restart in the passenger rule set — the 34-hour restart lives in 49 CFR 395.3(c), which applies to property-carrying CMVs. A passenger driver gets back under 60/70 by letting on-duty hours age out of the rolling 7- or 8-day window.

DEFINITIONS THAT DRIVE THE COUNT (49 CFR 395.2)
- Driving time: time spent at the controls of a CMV in operation.
- On-duty time: all time from coming on duty until going off duty, including driving, waiting to be dispatched, inspecting/ servicing the vehicle, loading/unloading, remaining in readiness to operate, and all compensated work for a motor carrier or non-motor-carrier employer.
- Off-duty time: not separately defined; in effect any time that is not driving time, on-duty time, or sleeper-berth time. FMCSA guidance: a meal or routine stop counts as off duty only if the driver is relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the bus, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage and freight being carried.

COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE (how to apply the three numbers to a duty day)
Step 1 — Start the clocks. At the end of 8 consecutive hours off duty (off duty, sleeper berth, or combination, with no work inside the 8), the driver comes on duty. Two clocks start: DRIVE (10 h) and ON-DUTY (15 h).
Step 2 — Add every on-duty minute (driving + on-duty not driving) to the ON-DUTY clock. Do not add off-duty breaks to it.
Step 3 — Add driving minutes only to the DRIVE clock.
Step 4 — Stop driving when EITHER clock is exhausted: DRIVE reaches 10:00, or ON-DUTY reaches 15:00. Whichever happens first controls.
Step 5 — Also track the rolling 60-in-7 or 70-in-8 on-duty total; stop driving when that total is reached even if both daily clocks have room.
Step 6 — Restart only with 8 consecutive hours off duty (or a qualifying equivalent under Step 7). Nothing else resets the clocks; a short break does not.

WORKED EXAMPLE
Off duty 22:00–06:00 (8 consecutive hours) -> clocks start 06:00.
06:00–11:00 drive (5:00 drive / 5:00 on duty)
11:00–11:30 on-duty not driving, pre-trip/inspection (5:00 / 5:30)
11:30–12:00 off duty, lunch (5:00 / 5:30 — off duty does not advance the 15-hour clock)
12:00–17:00 drive (10:00 / 10:30)
Result: DRIVE clock exhausted at 10:00 -> no further driving, even though only 10:30 of the 15 on-duty hours are used. The driver may perform non-driving work until the ON-DUTY clock reaches 15:00, and may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty.

EXCEPTIONS AND HOW THEY INTERACT (49 CFR 395.1) — none changes the three numbers unless it is actually invoked
- 150 air-mile short-haul (395.1(e)): a driver operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released from duty within 14 consecutive hours or less is exempt from the record-of-duty-status (logbook/ELD) requirement. This is a paperwork exemption only; it does not raise the 10-hour driving limit or the 15-hour on-duty cutoff. Do not treat it as a change to the three answers.
- Passenger sleeper berth (395.1(g)(3)): a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth may accumulate the equivalent of the 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two qualifying sleeper-berth periods. Where this is relied on, the split-rest conditions in 395.1(g)(3)(i)-(iv) must all be met and the current eCFR text should be read before use; absent a qualifying split, the plain 8-consecutive-hour rule applies.
- Adverse driving conditions: relief under 395.1(b) extends the time needed to complete the run; it does not enlarge the 10-hour driving maximum. After an adverse-conditions run, a passenger-carrying driver must be off duty at least 8 consecutive hours before driving again.
- Travel/cushioning time (395.1(j)) and relief drivers: travel to a layover counts as on-duty time unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival, in which case it may be recorded as off duty. Time driving oneself in a non-CMV to a layover is on duty, not driving.
- Multiple-employer drivers (395.8(j)): all compensated work for any employer is on-duty time; obtain the signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty before using the driver.

COMMON MISAPPLICATIONS TO AVOID
- Using 11 / 10 / 14 (property-carrying, 395.3) instead of 10 / 8 / 15 (passenger-carrying, 395.5). This is the single most likely error.
- Confusing the 8-consecutive-hour reset with the 34-hour restart. The 34-hour restart does not exist for passenger-carrying drivers; weekly limits are satisfied by hours aging out of the rolling window.
- Treating the 15-hour limit as a limit on all work. It is a limit on driving only; non-driving work may continue.
- Counting off-duty breaks toward the 15-hour on-duty total, or assuming a mid-day break extends the 15 hours (it does not — it simply is not counted as on-duty time).
- Assuming the 10 driving hours are available every day regardless of the 60/70-hour weekly total.

VERIFICATION SOURCES
49 CFR 395.5 (eCFR and Cornell LII text, both quoted identically above); 49 CFR 395.1 (exceptions, incl. (e), (g)(3), (j)); 49 CFR 395.2 (definitions); FMCSA brochure FMCSA-E-06-006, July 2022, "Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers"; FMCSA "Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service."

SCOPE LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
Applies to US interstate operations under FMCSA rules for passenger-carrying CMVs. Intrastate drivers may be subject to a state rule set that differs (some states adopt the federal passenger rules, some do not); a specific state's requirements are outside this answer. School bus, transit, and other statutory exemptions under 395.1 were not evaluated and could change the applicable limits if one applies.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.5 and 15 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395. The first reads: "(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty;"

question: M5
answer:
PART 135 FLIGHT ATTENDANT REST AFTER A SCHEDULED DUTY PERIOD OF 14 HOURS OR LESS

1. CONTROLLING RULE
§135.273 (Duty period limitations and rest requirements: flight attendants). Applicability is set by §135.261(e): 'Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part.' It therefore applies to an on-demand charter operator under §135.267 just as it applies to a §135.265 scheduled operator. The §135.265(b) rest table (9/10/11 consecutive hours keyed to scheduled FLIGHT TIME) is a flight CREWMEMBER table and does not govern a flight attendant unless the operator makes the §135.273(c) election described in item 6.

2. ASK 1 — REST AFTER A SCHEDULED DUTY PERIOD OF 14 HOURS OR LESS
Value: 9 consecutive hours, scheduled.
Basis: §135.273(b)(2) — 'a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'
The 14-hour figure is the band ceiling in §135.273(b)(1) ('no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours', except the extended-duty paragraphs (b)(4)-(b)(6)). A duty period of exactly 14 hours sits inside the band, so 9 hours is the base rest.

3. ASK 2 — TO WHAT IT MAY BE REDUCED
Value: 8 consecutive hours (the floor; no lower figure exists in the rule).
Conditions, all of which must hold (§135.273(b)(3)):
  (a) the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours;
  (b) that subsequent rest period is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the BEGINNING of the reduced rest period (the 24-hour clock runs from the start of the reduced rest, not its end);
  (c) that subsequent rest period occurs between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
Supporting prohibitions: §135.273(b)(10) — no duty period may be assigned unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section; §135.273(b)(11) — no duty may be assigned during any required rest period.

4. VALLEY TABLE (every figure cross-checked)
| Item | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Base scheduled rest, duty ≤14 h | 9 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(2) |
| Floor to which that rest may be reducible | 8 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Compensatory subsequent rest required if reducible to 8 | at least 10 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Deadline for compesatory rest to begin | no later than 24 h after beginning of reduced rest | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Base scheduled duty period ceiling | 14 h | §135.273(b)(1) |
Checks: 9 > 8 (a reduction, not an increase); 8 meets but does not breach the 8-hour floor; 10 meets but does not breach the 10-hour compesatory minimum; 24 h is a deadline measured from the beginning of the reduced rest.

5. COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE FOR THE OPERATOR
Step 1 — Determine the SCHEDULED duty period (the published/assigned schedule), not the actual duty period. The band and the rest trigger are keyed to the scheduled figure. If the scheduled duty period exceeds 14 h, paragraphs (b)(4)-(b)(6) and the 12-hour rest of (b)(7) apply instead, and this answer does not cover it.
Step 2 — If the scheduled duty period is 14 h or less, build the pairing with at least 9 consecutive hours of rest between completion of that duty period and commencement of the next one.
Step 3 — If 8 hours is used, the schedule must show, in the same pairing or the immediately adjacent one, a compesatory rest block of at least 10 consecutive hours that begins no later than 24 hours after the reduced rest began and falls between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.
Step 4 — Before publishing, chek that no duty is assinged during either rest period (§135.273(b)(10), (b)(11)).
Step 5 — Record the reduced rest and the compesatory rest in the crew scheduling system so the 24-hour deadline can be audited; the deadline is a hard scheduling constraint, not a crew-room discretion.

6. WORK ED EXAMPLE (arithmetic chek)
Scheduled duty period ends 21:00 Day 1. Reduced rest begins 22:00 Day 1 and runs 8 hours to 06:00 Day 2 (8 h = the floor, not fewer). The compesatory rest of at least 10 consecutive hours must be scheduled to begin no later than 22:00 Day 2 (22:00 Day 1 + 24 h = 22:00 Day 2) and must sit between the completion of the Day 1 duty period and the commencement of the next duty period. A 10-hour block beginning 22:00 Day 2 satisfies (a) 10 ≥ 10 and (b) start exactly at the 24-hour deadline, not past it. A 10-hour block beginning 23:00 Day 2 would breach the deadline even though it is long enough.

7. TRAPS / COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID
- Applying §135.265(b)'s 9/10/11-hour table (keyed to scheduled flight time) to a flight attendant. Wrong section; the flight attendant table is keyed to scheduled DUTY period.
- Reducing to 8 h without the at-least-10-hour compesatory rest, or without the 24-hour deadline. Both are conditions of the reduction, not suggestions.
- Measuring the 24 hours from the end of the reduced rest rather than its beginning. That overstates the available window by the length of the reduced rest.
- Treating 14 h as the actual duty period. The trigger is the scheduled duty period; a late-running flight that pushes actual duty past 14 h does not by itself move the crew into paragraph (b)(7), but it must be tracked against the schedule.
- Assuming any discretion below 8 h, or a 'ad hoc' reduction for unforeseen circumstances. The rule contains no such provision for flight attendants; 8 h is the absolute floor.
- Confusing §135.273(b)(9) (the 14-hour cap that follows a 10-hour reduction under (b)(8), which belongs to the over-14-hour band) with the 8-hour reduction in (b)(3). (b)(9) does not attach to a ≤14-hour duty period.

8. ELECTION CAVEAT (§135.273(c)) — VERIFY, DO NOT ASSUME
An operator may apply the flight crewmember flight time/duty/rest rules of Part 135 to its flight attendants if it establishes written procedures that apply to all its flight attendants, include the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (rest facilities on board not required), add one flight attendant per excess flight crewmember, and are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in its ops specs. If — and only if — this operator holds that election, the applicable rest becomes §135.265(b)'s table keyed to scheduled flight time (9 h for less than 8 h scheduled flight time; 10 h for 8 to less than 9 h; 11 h for 9 h or more), reducible under §135.265(c) to 8/8/9 h with compesatory rests of 10/11/12 h beginning no later than 24 h after the beginning of the reduced rest. Absent that election, the answer stated in items 2 and 3 governs. Chek the ops specs and the approved procedures before applying either table; do not blend them.

9. SCOPE NOTES
This is the regulatory minimum. A collective bargaining agreement or company policy may be more restrictive and would control as a matter of employment/contract, but it does not change the Part 135 floor. The answer covers a flight attendant serving as cabin crew only; a crewmember who also serves as a flight crewmember is governed by the flight crewmember rest rules for that function, and augmented-crew, deadhead transportation and rest-facility questions are outside this ask.
